fundamental.thesis: Asian Paints is a large decorative paints franchise with growing industrial and international businesses, but its market is under structural competitive pressure from Birla Opus. Revenue growth has accelerated from +2.8% in H1 FY26 to +17.5% in H1 FY27 (₹20,518 cr), and PAT rose 23.9% to ₹2,645 cr, but the quality of growth weakened in Q2: derived revenue was about ₹9,976 cr (+16.9%), PAT margin fell from 14.8% in Q1 to about 10.9%, and PBDIT margin fell 202 bps YoY to 15.6%, below the 18-20% full-year guided band; decorative growth was also price-led in H1 (volume +6.4% vs value +14.5%), and CFO/PAT dropped from 1.66x to 0.72x. On the sector card's consumer-franchise P/E yardstick, valuation is fair but at the top of the range, with trailing P/E of 58.9x against a 30-60x norm and forward P/E of 45.4x; the P100 peer rank is inflated by steel, metals and other cyclicals, and the price-based inputs and the 102% dividend yield and 17.85 debt/equity readings look unreliable, so they carry little weight. The biggest risk is that raw material inflation, the TiO2 anti-dumping duty and intense competition stop price increases from restoring margins while earnings estimates are already being cut (FY EPS -1.8% over 30 days).

Tata Steel is one of India's largest integrated steelmakers, with high-margin Indian operations and loss-prone European arms in the Netherlands (TSN) and the UK (TSUK). Q2FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹65,436 cr (+11.5% YoY) and PAT ₹3,700 cr (+16.3% YoY), a 5.7% PAT margin; revenue growth slowed from +14.3% in Q1 but stays well above FY26's +6.2%. EBITDA margin widened from 15.4% to 16.3% and consolidated EBITDA/tonne rose from ₹12,898 to ₹13,462, but India EBITDA/tonne fell from ₹19,162 to ₹17,790 and India EBITDA margin from 26.8% to 25.0%, which suggests domestic spreads are softening. PAT quality is uncertain because a ₹3,457 cr exceptional gain from the TMILL stake revaluation was booked in Q2, and it is unclear whether the ₹3,700 cr PAT includes it. On the sector card's yardstick for steel (EV/EBITDA), the trailing 10.4× is above the 5–8× mid-cycle range, but a forward P/E of 10.8× against a 23.5× trailing P/E and rising sell-side EPS estimates (+8.9% for next FY over 30 days) offset that, so the grade is fair. The headline peer discount (P13 on EV/EBITDA) is not used because the peer set includes paint companies, whose multiples do not apply to steel. The biggest risk is Europe: the auditor has issued a modified opinion on the consolidated results, citing TSN's going-concern uncertainty and an impairment risk it cannot quantify, with regulatory clarity not expected until about March 2027.

fundamental.thesis: Tech Mahindra is a tier-1 Indian IT services company with a large Communications vertical and a multi-year margin turnaround underway, aiming for a 15% EBIT margin in FY27. Q2FY27 revenue rose 15.6% YoY to ₹16,180 cr and PAT rose 33.9% to ₹1,610 cr. Growth picked up sharply from +4.2% in Q1FY27 and +8.3% in Q3FY26, but constant-currency growth was only +7.2%, so roughly half the headline jump comes from the weaker rupee. Margins are genuinely improving: PAT margin rose from 7.8% to 9.5% to 9.9% over three quarters, EBIT margin is 14.8% (up 260 bps YoY), new deal wins of $1,023M are up 25.4% YoY, and FCF of ₹2,874 cr is 2.16x PAT. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, as the IT sector card suggests. Trailing P/E is 27.8x, inside the 22–30x IT band and at P62 among peers. Forward P/E is 17.6x, right at the peer median (P50), and EV/EBITDA is 13.9x (P33). That makes it fair, not cheap. The main risk is that much of the growth and margin gain depends on the rupee and on cost cuts, while AI-driven price deflation in legacy work and weaker European auto clients cap underlying constant-currency growth.

Hindalco is India's integrated aluminium and copper major, and through its wholly owned subsidiary Novelis it is the world's largest flat-rolled aluminium producer, so its earnings move closely with global aluminium (LME) prices. Q2FY27 consolidated revenue hit a record ₹91,708 cr (+38.8% YoY) and PAT ₹7,533 cr (+58.9% YoY, 8.2% margin), with growth speeding up across like-for-like quarters from +13.9% in Q3FY26 to +32.0% in Q1FY27 to +38.8% now; upstream aluminium posted a record 52% EBITDA margin at USD 2,125/t, and non-LME-linked businesses also grew EBITDA 50% to ₹6,860 cr. Much of this is price-driven rather than volume-driven, and about 150 bps of the PAT growth came from a lower tax rate (25% vs 29%). Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for a commodity cyclical, the stock trades at 9.3x: that is above the 5–8x mid-cycle band in the sector card and is being earned on near-peak spreads, so I grade it fair rather than cheap, even though it sits at P7 versus peers and a forward P/E of 10.3x looks low. The low peer ranking is misleading because the peer median is inflated by paint and adhesive consumer franchises, and the stock is already at 85% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is a reversal in LME prices hitting a balance sheet that is becoming more stretched: net debt/EBITDA has risen to 1.80x from 1.23x, H1 capex was ₹20,719 cr (+83%), H1 free cash flow was negative ₹16,519 cr, and Novelis's Bay Minette plant has slipped to first coil in Q4FY27.

fundamental.thesis: Dr Reddy's is a large Indian generics maker with heavy US exposure, plus a fast-growing India branded business and emerging-market and biosimilar franchises. The latest quarter extracted from filings is Q1 FY27; Q2 FY27 results were filed on 23 Oct but not yet extracted, and the yfinance Q2 revenue of 4,150 cr is about half the normal run-rate, so it is treated as suspect. In Q1 FY27 revenue fell 5.6% YoY to 8,070 cr, down from +3.0% in FY26, and PAT fell 69% to 435 cr (5.4% margin, down from 12.8%), partly because of a 223 cr semaglutide inventory provision. Even after stripping that one-off, US revenue fell 35% while India formulations grew a healthy 17%, and cash conversion was very weak (CFO/PAT 0.23x, FCF of -22 cr). fundamental.thesis: IndusInd Bank is a mid-sized private lender, heavy on vehicle finance (28% of loans, 58% retail), that is still rebuilding after the FY26 accounting-discrepancy year in which full-year PAT fell 65% to ₹891 cr and ROA dropped to 0.17%. Per the H1FY27 filing, total income rose 26.8% YoY to ₹23,873 cr and PAT rose 36.4% to ₹2,279 cr, but this flatters the core business: the comparison base includes a Q2FY26 loss, Q1FY27 includes a one-off ₹868 cr IFR transfer, and operating profit actually fell 7.9% YoY to ₹10,323 cr. Loan growth has recovered from -8.5% (FY26) to +11% YoY, but NIM has slipped to 3.23% from 3.39–3.48%, credit cost is elevated at 1.4%, cost-to-income is high at 57.9%, and annualised Q2 ROE is only 7.4%. Using the bank yardstick (P/B with ROE, ignoring the distorted 80× trailing P/E), a P/B of 1.08× (P29 vs peers, 26% below the 1.5× median) fits sub-par returns of about 7% ROE, so the valuation is fair rather than cheap; the cheap case only holds if ROE recovers toward 12%+. The biggest risk is that the earnings recovery stalls as NIM compression and above-normal vehicle and microfinance credit costs hold ROA under 1%.

Eicher Motors owns Royal Enfield, which holds about 87% of India's mid-size (250-750cc) motorcycle segment, and has an equity stake in the VECV commercial-vehicle JV, which makes it a direct play on the premiumisation theme in the Auto sector card. Revenue growth in the latest reported quarter (Q1FY27) was +31.6% YoY to ₹6,632 cr, up from +14.8% in Q1FY26 (with +45.0% and +23.0% in Q2/Q3FY26), so growth is strong but lumpy; PAT grew more slowly, +21.4% to ₹1,463 cr, and PAT margin has drifted down from 23.9% to 22.0% over the window (the 31.0% EBITDA margin print looks definitionally inconsistent with the earlier 24-25% series, so I am not treating it as real expansion). On P/E, the yardstick the sector card names for OEMs, the stock trades at 37.9x trailing, above the card's 18-30x OEM range and about 40% above the peer median of 27.1x (P80). Forward P/E is 28.8x (P83), and EV/EBITDA of 33.7x and P/B of 8.3x are both the highest in the peer set (P100), so the verdict is expensive even after allowing a premium-mix quality premium. The biggest risk is that this rich multiple meets Q2FY27 results on 13 Nov (two days away; our data is one quarter stale): any further PAT-margin slippage from input costs or festive-season marketing spend could trigger a de-rating, since the stock already sits near 79% of its 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Life Insurance is India's second-largest private life insurer with a 10.9% individual WRP market share, distributing through a 59% bancassurance channel anchored by parent HDFC Bank across ULIPs (43% of mix), participating (27%), and a rapidly-growing protection segment. The sector card prescribes P/EV as the primary yardstick for life insurers, but the extracted embedded value figure (₹615 cr) is implausibly low against a ₹1.2L cr market cap and cannot be reliably used; on peer-relative forward P/E (46x, P50 in the Insurance – Life peer set), HDFCLIFE is fairly valued, though P/B of 6.85x against ROE of only 11.3% is stretched, and the stock's position at 11% of its 52-week range offers a modestly improved entry. The single biggest risk is the combination of rising expenses-of-management ratio (21.2% in FY26 to 22.2% in H1FY27) and declining VNB margin, which signals new business profitability erosion that may constrain embedded value compounding even as top-line premiums accelerate.

On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card uses for premium retailers, the stock trades at 55.3x, the most expensive in its peer group (P100) and 152% above the 21.9x median; trailing P/E of 85.4x is at P88, so valuation is expensive, though inside the card's 60-100x+ range for premium franchises and with forward P/E (55.8x) well below trailing. The biggest risk is that a high multiple meets weak profit growth: if Q2's gap between strong sales and flat profit continues alongside slower inventory turns (4.95x vs 6.11x), the stock is exposed to the 25-40% de-rating the card warns these names suffer on a single guidance reset.

fundamental.thesis: Shriram Finance is one of India's largest retail NBFCs, mainly lending against commercial vehicles, and it now has a 20% strategic shareholder in MUFG Bank, which put in ₹39,618 cr of fresh equity. In Q2 FY27 (H1 minus Q1 from the filings), revenue was about ₹13,774 cr, up 15.6% YoY, and PAT was ₹3,684 cr, up 59.1% YoY. Revenue growth has eased from +19.1% to about +16% while PAT margin widened from 19.0% to 26.7%, partly because the MUFG equity lowers borrowing needs, so the PAT jump overstates the gain in underlying loan economics (loan growth is ~15%). Valuation is graded on P/B plus ROE, the lender yardstick: P/B of 2.56x against ROE of 16.4% (diluted by the new capital) is fair rather than cheap, with P/B at P33 and trailing P/E of 16.8x at P44 among credit-services peers, and forward P/E of 12.9x plus +3.7% upward EPS revisions support the earnings path. The main watch-point is asset quality: gross NPA has crept up from 4.54% to 4.65% standalone and impairment charges rose 27.5% against roughly 15% loan growth, even though net NPA and provision coverage are improving.

fundamental.thesis: Avenue Supermarts (DMART) is India's dominant value-format grocery retailer (~500 stores, FY26) built on an everyday-low-price model with best-in-class inventory turnover (4.93× for H1FY27), giving it durable structural advantages in organised grocery. H1FY27 revenue grew +16.4% YoY to ₹38,439 cr (steady within a consistent +13–16% band over six periods), but PAT grew only +10.0% to ₹1,603 cr as PAT margin contracted to 4.17% from 4.4% — finance costs surged 84% to fund aggressive expansion, the Avenue E-commerce subsidiary dragged ₹166.62 cr in losses, and CFO/PAT collapsed from 0.96× (H1FY26) to 0.34× (H1FY27), signalling a meaningful deterioration in earnings quality. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary valuation yardstick (capital-intensive retail with PAT margins distorted by lease and e-commerce costs), DMART trades at 52.4× EV/EBITDA — P100 (most expensive) among 13 Consumer Discr. peers and +51% above the sector median — while trailing P/E of 89.1× is also P100 and +73% above sector median; sell-side EPS estimates have been revised down -3.1% over 90 days, a textbook pre-derating signal. The biggest risk is that the quick-commerce threat from Blinkit erodes SSSG momentum just as e-commerce losses widen and leverage builds, triggering the 25–40% multiple reset the sector card explicitly flags for any guidance disappointment at these premium valuations.

On the P/B-versus-ROE yardstick for lenders, the stock looks expensive at 4.62x book with ROE of 19-20%, which is at P89 of peers and 51.5% above the 3.0x median, although strong growth and low-priced state-owned peers such as PFC and RECLTD explain part of the premium; the 26.77x trailing P/E (P78) appears to use FY26 EPS, and is closer to 23x on my estimate of trailing-twelve-month PAT. fundamental.thesis: Siemens is one of India's leading electrical, automation and mobility equipment makers, with a net cash position of about ₹8,113 cr. That positions it squarely in the transmission, data-centre and rail capex cycle. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹5,734 cr, accelerating from +14.6% and +14.8% in the prior two periods, and new orders jumped 37.8% to ₹6,228 cr, with the order backlog up 12% to ₹47,034 cr (roughly 2x annualised revenue). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this order-book business, 52.8x is about 55% above the 34x peer median (around the 76th percentile), and trailing P/E of 76.5x sits at the top of even the 50–80x electricals band. With full-year EPS estimates cut 4.5% over 90 days, the stock looks expensive, and the biggest risk is that orders keep growing but margins don't, leaving the premium multiple to de-rate.

Dabur is a mid-sized Indian FMCG company selling Ayurvedic health, personal care and juice brands, with a fast-growing international arm. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 11.6% YoY to Rs 3,563 cr, and Q2 PAT works out to about Rs 505 cr (H1 Rs 1,096 cr less Q1 Rs 591 cr, a 14.2% margin), so top-line growth has picked up from +5.0% in FY26 to +7.3%, +10.6% and +11.6% over the last three quarters. However, domestic volume growth was only 5.5% against 10.7% value growth, so roughly half the growth is price and mix rather than more units sold, and PAT margin slipped from 15.7% in Q1 to about 14.2% in Q2 as input costs bit. On valuation, using P/E and EV/EBITDA as the card prescribes for FMCG, a trailing P/E of 39.4x sits at the bottom of the 40-60x sector band and in the cheapest quintile of peers (P20, about 10% below the 43.8x median), which makes it marginally cheap, but EV/EBITDA of 29.2x is only P40 (about 6% below the median), so the discount is modest, not deep, and the sector card warns that cheap FMCG often reflects a structural growth gap.

fundamental.thesis: Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

Using P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, the stock looks fair: trailing P/E of 24.7x sits inside the 22-30x IT band and exactly at the peer median (P50), EV/EBITDA of 14.7x is also at the median, and the forward P/E of 18.3x assumes earnings growth that recent revenue growth only partly supports; the stock sits at 30% of its 52-week range. The technical view is a hold, since the stock is stretched after a 33% one-month run with ADX near 49. In today's mean-reverting momentum regime, chasing that strength in a midcap is a poor entry. With no position and only about ₹18k of cash, we pass for now and would revisit near the 3,950 support (SMA20) once the Q2 figures confirm growth is re-accelerating.

fundamental.thesis: L&T Technology Services is a mid-cap engineering R&D services firm with 417 active clients, about 60% of revenue from North America and two-thirds on time-and-materials contracts, so it is directly exposed to the AI-driven pricing reset in IT services. The newest usable numbers are two quarters old: Q4FY26 revenue of Rs 2,858 cr grew +8.3% YoY with PAT of Rs 346 cr (12.1% margin), slower than full-year FY26 revenue growth of +14.0% (about Rs 10,996 cr; the table appears to report this in INR million, not crores). The Q1FY27 and H1FY27 figures, including the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-19, were not extracted, so the current trajectory cannot be confirmed. Supporting points are FY26 large-deal wins of USD 855 mn (+40%), CFO/PAT of 1.14x and ROE of about 20%. On valuation, a trailing P/E of 28.2x sits inside the 22-30x IT band but is a +14.5% premium to the peer median (P75), and EV/EBITDA of 18.3x is +24.9% above the peer median (P83), so we grade it expensive versus peers even with the price near its 52-week low (15% of range). The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps slowing toward the low single digits as AI deflates T&M engineering billing, which would not justify the premium multiple or the roughly 40% EPS growth implied by a forward P/E of 20x.

Glenmark is a mid-cap pharma company with three engines: India branded formulations, a growing US and Europe generics and specialty business (its Ryaltris nasal spray grew secondary sales +50% and is now sold in 55 markets), and a new oncology licensing push that includes the AbbVie deal ($700M upfront, $1,925M total value). The latest quarter cannot be read reliably: the extracted trend table mixes inconsistent scopes (FY26 revenue of ₹1,698 cr against Q4FY26 at ₹3,771 cr and Q3FY26 at ₹390 cr). The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been extracted yet. The only Q2FY27 figure is yfinance (revenue ₹1,306 cr, PAT ₹264 cr, down from ₹483 cr in Q1), which is sanity-check only and likely standalone, so no trustworthy YoY growth can be stated beyond a 'decelerating' revenue signal and weak India secondary sales growth of just 1.5% in Q4FY26. On valuation, using P/E with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the trailing P/E of 37.9x sits inside the 28–40x pharma band and near the peer median of 36.4x (P62). EV/EBITDA of 14.0x is cheap versus peers (P15, 35% below the median of 21.4x), and the forward P/E of 24.7x implies earnings growth, so the overall grade is fair, with the stock already at 83.5% of its 52-week range. The biggest risks are that the AbbVie upfront payment may be inflating trailing earnings as a one-off, and that sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 5.9% in 30 days while 10 of 12 analysts still rate it buy, a classic pre-derating pattern. Two snapshot figures look like data errors and were ignored: the 31% dividend yield and the 5.65 debt/equity ratio.

fundamental.thesis: Laurus Labs is a vertically integrated API and CDMO business with a dominant ARV generics franchise (41% of FY26 revenue) and a rapidly scaling CDMO segment (30%+ of FY26 revenue, targeting 50% by FY30) supported by 8,200 kl reactor capacity, 110 active CDMO pipeline projects, and zero critical audit findings across 132 inspections — a credible China+1 CDMO beneficiary. FY26 revenue grew +23% YoY to ₹6,813 cr with PAT up +148% YoY to ₹890 cr (PAT margin 13.1%); CDMO small-molecule delivered +38% growth and 9M CDMO grew +50%, though full-year revenue growth decelerated modestly from the +30% pace seen in 9MFY26 to +23% for the full year, while EBITDA margins expanded to 26.8% with very strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.82x FY26). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive CDMO/API model, the stock trades at 52.5x vs a sector median of 21.4x — a 145% premium — and ranks P100 (most expensive) across trailing P/E (96.6x), forward P/E (67.2x), P/B (19.8x), and EV/EBITDA in its 14-stock peer group, with the stock at 99.1% of its 52-week range: unambiguously expensive even granting a deserved CDMO re-rating premium. A ₹3,000 cr capex programme (nearly 3× the prior ₹1,000 cr guidance) must convert to contracted CDMO revenue without material slippage while the stock prices in near-flawless execution, with a pending US generics tariff review and inherent CDMO quarter-to-quarter lumpiness creating headline risk at this multiple.

fundamental.thesis: Mankind Pharma is a mainly India-focused branded drug maker, ranked #1 by prescriptions for nine straight years with a 15.2% share and limited direct exposure to US tariffs. Q2 FY27 is not reported separately in the data, but H1 less Q1 implies revenue of about Rs 4,337 cr (about +17% YoY) and PAT of about Rs 716 cr (about +38%), with quarterly revenue growth accelerating from +11.5% in Q3 FY26 to +11.8%, +12.9% and about +17%, and H1 PAT margin up 210 bps to 15.4%, backed by cash generation of 1.41x CFO/PAT. Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, the stock is expensive: the listed 50.5x P/E appears to use FY26 EPS and is about 43x on my trailing-12-month estimate, still above the 28-40x sector range, while EV/EBITDA of 28.0x is 31% above the peer median (P77); I ignored the implausible 8.0% dividend yield and used net debt of 1.1x EBITDA (FY26) rather than the 38.11 debt/equity flag, which looks like a percentage. The biggest risk is that this premium assumes the Q2 jump will last, yet the source of the step-up is not visible in this data, Consumer Healthcare grew only 2.6% in H1, and FY26 volume growth was just 2.3%.

fundamental.thesis: Fortis Healthcare runs a large hospital network of about 6,300 operational beds plus a diagnostics arm of about 400 labs, and it grows through occupancy, revenue per patient and adding beds. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 17.3% YoY to Rs 2,735 cr, with growth essentially flat over five periods (17.3% to 17.8%, with only a slight recent easing), helped by 72% hospital occupancy and about 7% growth in revenue per patient, but PAT fell 2.5% to Rs 320 cr and PAT margin dropped from 14.1% to 11.7%; lower exceptional gains (Rs 3 cr vs Rs 24 cr) explain only about 1 point of that drop, and even excluding them PAT grew only about 4% by my pre-tax-unadjusted estimate. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock is expensive at 35.6x vs a sector median of 23.3x (P81), and a trailing P/E of 69.3x vs a forward P/E of 40.9x implies about 69% EPS growth, although the mostly pharma peer set makes the comparison imperfect and the 34% consensus upside looks overstated because the 52-week position implies a price near Rs 957, or about 15% upside to the Rs 1,098 mean target. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps failing to reach profit while FY EPS estimates, already cut 5.8% over 90 days, fall further against a valuation that needs a sharp earnings rebound.

fundamental.thesis: Ajanta Pharma is a branded-generics maker focused on chronic therapies: about 66% of revenue comes from branded generics across India (30%), Asia (18%) and Africa (18%), and US generics add 29%. In India it ranks #1 in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 companies, growing about 1.27x the Indian pharma market (16.7% vs 13.2%). Growth is speeding up. Revenue growth rose from +14% (Q2FY26) to +20% (Q3FY26) and +25% (Q1FY27), and reached about +32.5% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr, implied from H1 ₹3,420 cr less Q1 ₹1,626 cr). Implied Q2 PAT of ₹388 cr is up about 49%, and PAT margin widened to about 21.6% from 19%, though cash conversion is only moderate (CFO/PAT 0.86x in H1). On the healthcare yardstick of trailing P/E plus peer rank, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28-40x sector band and at P46 vs peers, and forward P/E of 26.3x signals expected earnings growth. EV/EBITDA of 24.3x (P69) and P/B of 8.3x (P77) carry a premium that a 25% ROE broadly justifies. The biggest risk is the 29% US generics exposure: generics are tariff-exempt for now, but the pending US Commerce review of generics plus forex losses already hitting reported profit could stall the margin gains, and management has given no forward guidance.

MRF is India's largest tyre maker, with a net-cash balance sheet (about ₹1,850 cr net cash, AAA rating reaffirmed), and it sells to both the replacement market and car and bike makers. Sales are growing but profits are shrinking. Q2 FY27, derived as H1 minus Q1 from the filings, shows revenue of about ₹8,660 cr (+17.4% YoY vs about ₹7,378 cr) but PAT of about ₹387 cr (-26% YoY vs about ₹526 cr). The quarterly EBITDA margin slid from 17.8% in Q3 FY26 to 14.1% in Q1 FY27 and about 10.4% in Q2 FY27, as raw materials rose to 72.7% of revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses: at 11.1x EV/EBITDA and 22.5x trailing P/E, MRF is the cheapest of its auto-parts peers (P0, about 42% below the 19.1x median EV/EBITDA), but its P/E sits inside the 18–28x auto band, so I grade it fair. The discount is largely explained by falling earnings, with next-year EPS estimates cut 21.6% in 30 days. The biggest risk is further margin erosion from rubber and crude costs, together with a 32% jump in inventory and negative H1 free cash flow (₹-371 cr), which could mean demand softness or channel build-up.

drivers: H1FY27 results (filed 1d ago): profit fell 14.3% YoY to ₹882 Cr, and operating margin shrank 268 bps (14.92% to 12.24%), even though revenue grew 13.4%. Sales are rising but earning less per rupee.

Offsetting positives: net cash of ₹1,850 Cr, AAA rating reaffirmed by CARE, and demand described as strong in both domestic and export markets. These limit downside but don't fix the profit trend.

fundamental.thesis: Exide Industries is India's leading lead-acid battery maker, serving automotive OEMs, the replacement market, inverters/solar, industrial and export customers, and it is building lithium-ion cell capacity through its subsidiary EESL, whose 6 GWh gigafactory was commissioned in September 2026. Growth has sped up sharply: revenue went from +4.1% in FY26 to +9.4% in Q4 FY26, +17.7% in Q1 FY27 and +18.9% for H1 FY27 (Rs 10,331 cr), while H1 PAT rose 46.7% to Rs 794 cr. Working back from the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 FY27 revenue was about Rs 4,803 cr (about +20% YoY) and PAT about Rs 443 cr (about 9.2% margin, up from 6.3% in Q1), helped by a 270 bps EBITDA margin expansion in Q2 and auto OEM sales growing 25%+ for a fourth straight quarter. I grade valuation on EV/EBITDA, the auto sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive names: at 18.6x it is close to the auto-parts peer median of 19.1x (P40), so the stock is fair; the 40x trailing P/E sits at P80 among peers and above the 18-28x ancillary range, but the 23.9x forward P/E prices in the earnings growth, and the stock already trades at 80% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the Rs 5,352 cr put into the lithium-ion business, which is holding ROE down at 6.2% until that plant scales profitably, alongside high lead and sulphur input costs and a tough comparison against last year's post-GST demand surge.

fundamental.thesis: Thermax is a mid-cap capital-goods company selling boilers, heating, cooling, water and environmental systems, plus a growing green-energy and renewable-utility arm, and it benefits from India's industrial capex cycle. Consolidated revenue growth picked up to +11.4% YoY in Q2FY27 (Rs 2,756 cr), from +6.7% in Q1 and about +3-4% through FY26, but profit has not followed: Q2 PAT fell 5% YoY to Rs 113 cr (4.1% margin vs 4.8% a year ago), Q1 PAT collapsed 85% to Rs 22 cr, and Q2 was propped up by Rs 20 cr of one-off PSI incentive income alongside a Rs 15 cr Green Solutions impairment, so the core margin trend is contracting. Grading on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an order-book industrial, the stock trades at 53.5x, 57% above the 34x peer median and at the 82nd percentile, with trailing P/E of 76x well above the 28-45x sector band; that is expensive, especially with the price at about 91% of its 52-week range and sell-side FY EPS estimates cut about 14% over 30-90 days (the quoted +40% upside looks erroneous, since a Rs 3,900 mean target sits below the current price). The biggest risk is that order momentum is fading: consolidated order booking fell 8% YoY to Rs 3,259 cr, the Rs 14,250 cr backlog covers only about 1.3x annual revenue, and free cash flow was negative (FY26 FCF -Rs 411 cr, CFO/PAT 0.75x), which leaves little room for a multiple this rich.

fundamental.thesis: Supreme Industries is India's largest plastics processor, selling plastic pipes (including CPVC), industrial, packaging and consumer products through about 50,000 distributors. It is a building-materials and consumer-demand business, not an order-book capital-goods company, so the Industrials sector card fits it only loosely. The latest verified filing is the FY26 annual result: revenue of Rs 11,218 cr (+7.0% YoY) and PAT of Rs 954 cr (-1.0% YoY), with an 8.5% PAT margin. Volumes grew 12% and piping volumes 14%, beating an industry that shrank 9%, but piping value grew only 11%, so falling PVC prices are eating into growth. Profit has not kept pace with volume, and Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27 filings are not indexed (Q2 results come out today), so the trajectory cannot be confirmed. On valuation (EV/EBITDA and peer rank), the trailing P/E of 47x is above the static 28-45x Industrials band but 12.6% below the live peer median of 53.8x (P38). EV/EBITDA of 29.5x is 13% below the peer median (P41), and the stock sits at 27% of its 52-week range, which adds up to fair rather than cheap. fundamental.thesis: BHEL is India's dominant PSU power equipment and heavy engineering manufacturer, with leading exposure to thermal power, defence, and T&D — a direct beneficiary of the government-led capex upcycle in power and infrastructure. Q2FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹9,300 cr (+23.8% YoY from ₹7,512 cr), PAT surged 118.9% to ₹821 cr (margin 8.8%), confirming a clear multi-period turnaround: PAT margins have expanded from -0.7% in H1FY26 through 4.5%, 4.7%, 4.9%, to 8.8% now, with H1FY27 PAT of ₹1,198 cr vs a ₹80.6 cr loss a year ago. On the primary Industrials yardstick (EV/EBITDA), BHEL trades at 56.2× vs sector median 34.0× — P88 in sector, a 65% premium — and while the forward P/E of 29.7× is a reassuring P35 (below median), the stock is at 82.6% of its 52-week range with ROE of only 6.3% against P/B of 5.15×, graded expensive overall. The most critical data gap is the absence of current order-book and book-to-bill figures, which are the primary leading indicator for any capital-goods name; without these, it is impossible to confirm that the execution ramp is sustainable, and any government capex pause could trigger the 30–50% de-rating this sector is historically prone to from near-highs.

Jubilant FoodWorks is India's largest quick-service restaurant operator: it runs Domino's India (about 75% of orders come through delivery) and Popeyes, and owns DP Eurasia (Domino's and Coffy in Turkey), with 3,820 stores across the group. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue grew 11.8% YoY to ₹2,608 cr, but growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q4FY26 to +14.1% in Q1 and +11.8% now. EBITDA rose only 7.3% to ₹513 cr as margin fell 83 bps to 19.7%. PAT from continuing operations was nearly flat (+0.5% to ₹113.9 cr), and reported PAT fell 42.7% after the Dunkin exit, although Domino's India same-store sales (LFL) recovered from 0.2% to 2.5% to 4.1% over the last three quarters. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick because lease accounting distorts P/E, the stock is in line with peers at 21.9× (P50), but that multiple flatters a lease-heavy QSR. On earnings it looks expensive: trailing P/E of 83.7× (P82, +111% vs the 39.7× sector median) and forward P/E of 52.1× (P90) are being paid for flat continuing-operations profit, and FY EPS estimates were cut 3.0% over the last 30 days. The biggest risk is about 200 bps of input-cost inflation (cheese, dairy, LPG, wages) arriving while Domino's India LFL is still below the 5–7% medium-term target, which could stall the margin recovery and trigger a de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Petronet LNG runs India's largest LNG import and regasification terminals (Dahej, Kochi), a tariff-and-volume business that is largely insulated from gas prices, which the sector card notes. On a P/E-plus-dividend yardstick, the 10.3x trailing P/E sits inside the 8–14x Energy band, EV/EBITDA of 6.1x equals the peer median (P67 on P/E, P50 on P/B), and forward P/E of 9.5x is below trailing, so we grade it fair. The live dividend yield (372%) and debt/equity (10.51) figures are clearly data errors, since the filings show net cash and zero conventional debt, so we did not use them. The biggest risk is asset quality: GNPA rose from 1.08% at FY26 to 1.35% in Q2 (though it is 8bps better YoY), provision coverage is a thin 34.5%, and ROE slipped to 15.2% from 15.7%.

fundamental.thesis: GIC Re is India's dominant state-owned reinsurer. That means the company loses money on underwriting and relies on ₹5,015 cr of investment income. Q2 alone (about ₹2,966 cr of PAT, implied by H1 minus Q1) was much better than Q1, whose PAT fell 31%. For an insurer I grade value on price-to-book against ROE, not P/E. At 0.62x book, the cheapest in the peer set and near the bottom of its 52-week range, the stock is cheap even for a below-par 9.1% ROE, and the 4.18x solvency ratio gives a large capital buffer. The trailing P/E of 6.8x supports this but is not my yardstick. The ROE gap is the main reason the market keeps this PSU at a discount to book. The biggest risk is that underwriting losses stay above 100% of premium while estimates keep being cut (FY EPS down 10% over 90 days), so earnings would depend on volatile investment gains.

HUDCO is a government-owned (75% promoter, now held by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs) lender that funds mostly state-government housing and urban infrastructure projects; RBI classified it in the NBFC Upper Layer in August 2026, and the loan book has reached ₹1,86,502 cr. Growth is strong but cooling slightly: H1FY27 total income rose +25.7% YoY to ₹7,789 cr (vs +28.8% in FY26) and PAT rose +31.5% to ₹1,762 cr, while asset quality stays clean (gross NPA 1.08%, net NPA 0.06%, coverage ~94%) and CRAR is a comfortable 32.6%. On the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE), P/B of 2.35x against H1 annualized ROE of 15.7% is fair rather than cheap; the 10.5x trailing P/E looks low against the 18–28x NBFC band and the broad market, but P/E is not the right lens for a lender. Several snapshot figures conflict with the filings (a 263% dividend yield, ROE of 20.2% vs 15.7%, and the implied price), so the valuation read is uncertain. The main risk is that ~29% loan growth funded by wholesale borrowing at 7.2x debt/equity, concentrated in state-government exposures, leaves margins exposed to funding costs and policy-driven lending, and FY26's 30% PAT margin was flattered by provision write-backs (credit cost of -0.12%).

fundamental.thesis: IIFL Finance is a mid-size NBFC with a diversified lending book spanning home loans, gold loans, SME credit, and microfinance, recovering from an RBI embargo on its gold loan business imposed in early FY25 that drove PAT to near-zero. Q3FY26 (latest extracted official data) showed revenue of ₹3,427 cr (+40.4% YoY) and PAT of ₹464 cr (+1,040% YoY off a severely depressed Q3FY25 base of ₹82 cr), with PAT margin expanding from 6.4% (Q3FY25) to 13.5% (Q3FY26) and GNPA improving from 2.4% to 1.6% — but Q2FY27 results filed October 15 remain unextracted, leaving a ~9-month data gap that materially limits current visibility. On the appropriate lender yardstick (P/B + ROE), IIFL trades at 1.62× P/B with a 12.3% ROE — borderline cheap — confirmed by a P11 broad-market percentile rank on trailing P/E and a forward P/E of 7.66× (vs trailing 13.65×) that implies strong consensus earnings growth priced in at a meaningful discount to NBFC sector median of 18–28×. The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

fundamental.thesis: IREDA is India's government-backed specialized NBFC for renewable energy financing, a structurally advantaged lender in the clean-energy transition with a loan book growing at ~21% annually; its PSU backing and sector tailwinds provide a durable franchise but are not substitutes for credit discipline. FY26 revenue grew 23.2% YoY to ₹8,309 cr (decelerating from 35% in FY25) while PAT grew only 10.3% to ₹1,873 cr with PAT margin contracting from 24.7% (9MFY25) to 22.5%, driven by a 227% surge in impairment provisions as Gross NPA rose sharply from 2.45% to 3.49% — the growth deceleration and credit-quality deterioration are happening simultaneously, which is the most concerning combination for a lender. Valuation: using the P/B+ROE yardstick mandated by the sector card (the primary lens for lenders), P/B of 2.28× against ROE of ~13.6% falls in fair territory; however, the peer-rank data (P16 on trailing P/E, P13 on forward P/E vs broad market) and a trailing P/E of 16.1× sitting below the NBFC sector range of 18–28× are clear cheap signals — the stock near a 52-week low at 5.6% of its 52-week range reflects the market pricing in these asset-quality concerns, not oversight. The single biggest risk is that ₹394 cr of loans artificially held in Stage II due to interim High Court orders could reclassify to Stage III NPA, compounding an already deteriorating GNPA trend and potentially triggering another provision surge that could cut PAT by a further 15–20%.

fundamental.thesis: Jammu & Kashmir Bank is a mid-sized regional lender that dominates its home state and is growing its retail, agriculture and MSME (RAM) book, with gross advances up 23.7% YoY to Rs 1.34 lakh Cr. In Q2FY27 net profit rose 10.6% YoY to Rs 546 Cr and reported income rose 14.7% YoY to Rs 1,817 Cr. Much of that came from other income, which doubled to Rs 315 Cr. Core net interest income grew only 5% YoY, and NIM has slipped from 3.64% to 3.28% over the trend window, while asset quality kept improving (gross NPA fell to 2.23% from 3.32%, net NPA to 0.51%, PCR 91.8%). Using the bank yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock looks cheap at 0.97x book for a 14.6% ROE (trailing P/E 6.97x, forward 5.76x), though the peer comparison is only against the broad market and earnings estimates have been cut 6.2% over the last 30 days. The biggest risk is funding: deposits are growing 16.3% against loans at 23.7%, and CASA has fallen from 45.9% to 42.0%, which could keep squeezing margins. ROA has also eased to 1.07%, and RBI penalties of Rs 68.65 Cr so far this year add a governance and operations flag.

JM Financial is a mid-sized diversified financial group spanning investment banking and corporate advisory (IPO pipeline of about ₹1.5 lakh cr), wealth management (₹33,394 cr recurring AUM), a small asset manager (₹13,205 cr MF AAUM), affordable home loans (₹3,715 cr AUM, GNPA 0.75%) and a private-markets/distressed-credit book (₹4,045 cr). The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹883 cr, up 13.3% YoY, and PAT of ₹292 cr, down 35.7% YoY (PAT margin 33.1%), following a FY26 in which revenue fell 8.6% while PAT rose 46.3%. That pattern points to lumpy, resolution-driven earnings rather than steady compounding, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-04 have not been extracted, so the trend is stale. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE, not P/E), the stock trades at 1.12x book against an ROE of about 11%, just below the 12% hurdle for a cheap grade; I grade it fair, and the broad-market peer rank (P5–P6) is not a like-for-like comparison. The biggest risk is credit quality and earnings quality: reported GNPA of 15% with only 26% provision coverage, CFO/PAT of 0.48x in FY26, and pending tax litigation in subsidiary JMFSL now before the Bombay High Court.

fundamental.thesis: Karur Vysya Bank is a well-run, Tamil Nadu-based mid-size private bank that has become one of the most profitable lenders in its peer group, with ROE of 20.5% and ROA of 2.1% in Q2FY27. Q2FY27 PAT rose 37.3% YoY to a record Rs 788 cr and advances grew 20.4% YoY. The key bank metrics are moving the right way: NIM has widened every period, from 3.82% (H1FY26) to 4.03%, 4.18% and now 4.34%. GNPA is down to 0.69%, NNPA is 0.18% and provision coverage is about 96%, and management raised its full-year NIM guidance to above 4%. Judged on the bank yardstick (price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E), a P/B of 2.24x for a sustained 19-20% ROE is fair rather than cheap, although the 11.4x trailing P/E, 8.2x forward P/E and rising sell-side estimates (+6.6% over 30 days) show growth is not fully priced in. The main watch-point is funding: deposits grew 16.0% against 20.4% loan growth, CASA is low at about 27.5% and drifting, and cost of deposits is high at 5.49% while yields on advances fell 18 bps. Management's 18-20% credit growth guidance therefore depends on paying up for deposits.

fundamental.thesis: Bank of Maharashtra is a government-controlled (73.6%) mid-size public sector bank with a strong low-cost deposit base (FY26 CASA 52.51%), good asset quality (gross NPA down from 1.45% in FY26 to 1.25% in H1 FY27, net NPA 0.12%, coverage about 98.5%) and FY26 loan growth of 21.74%. H1 FY27 revenue rose 18.6% YoY to Rs 18,799 cr and PAT rose 31.1% to Rs 4,160 cr, but standalone Q2 figures were not extracted, and the 'accelerating' signal is unreliable because it compares a half-year with a full-year figure of only Rs 13,664 cr that appears to use a different revenue definition, while management's maintained 18% FY27 credit growth guidance implies slower growth than FY26. Using the P/B + ROE yardstick for lenders rather than P/E, valuation is fair: 2.07x book with a 22.7% ROE is attractive relative to returns but above the under-1.5x cheap threshold, the stock sits at 95.7% of its 52-week range, and the broad-market peer rank is a weak comparison for a bank, although FY-EPS estimates rose 11.3% over 30 days on thin coverage of 4 analysts. The biggest risk is that fast loan growth with an 86.48% advances-to-deposits ratio squeezes margins or weakens credit quality as new loans season, and the latest NIM trend cannot be confirmed because only the FY26 figure of 3.91% is available.

MCX runs India's dominant commodity derivatives exchange, and recent filings show it widening its product range (electricity futures, cardamom futures, exchange-discovered gold and silver spot prices). The Q2 FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-03, but no quarterly revenue or PAT figures have been extracted into the trend table (every row is blank), so I cannot cite YoY growth or margin direction. The only indirect evidence is sell-side EPS estimates, which rose 4.4% over 30 days and 8.0% over 90 days, implying strong recent prints. Since MCX is an exchange and not a lender, I used earnings and cash-flow multiples instead of the card's P/B-for-lenders yardstick. On that basis valuation is fair to stretched: trailing P/E is 53.9x (P73, 53% above the broad-market median of 35.2x), EV/EBITDA is 39.3x (P81), and forward P/E is 33.6x. The 17x P/B reflects a 37.9% ROE rather than a lending-book risk. The biggest risk is that the multiple is priced on today's very high commodity trading volumes and new-product ramp-up, so any fall in volumes or regulatory change to commodity derivatives could hit both earnings and the multiple at once.

fundamental.thesis: Motilal Oswal Financial Services is a diversified capital-markets firm covering broking, wealth management, asset management, housing finance and lending, and asset management is now its largest profit pool. In H1FY27, operating PAT grew 22% YoY to ₹1,327 cr, asset management PAT grew 69% to ₹304 cr on AUM up 26% to ₹3.2 lakh cr, and recurring revenue grew 27% to ₹1,182 cr, making up 66% of revenue. The headline +51% total PAT of ₹2,584 cr includes OCI/mark-to-market gains and is lower quality, while capital markets revenue fell 12% and wealth management PAT grew only 3%. The trend table's revenue rows mix periods and bases, and the H1FY26 row is clearly broken, so I have not used them for growth. On valuation I used P/B against ROE because the business is half lender, half capital-markets: P/B of 4.41x on 15.6% ROE is rich for a lender, but trailing P/E of 28.9x is at the top of the NBFC range (18–28x), forward P/E of 15.8x prices in growth, and the stock sits mid-pack against peers (P39 on P/E, P47 on P/B). With the consensus target about 1% below the price and the stock at 69% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair. The main risks to this view are weaker balance-sheet quality and dependence on market conditions.

fundamental.thesis: Nippon Life India AMC is a top-5 Indian mutual fund manager with ₹7.87 trillion of MF quarterly average AUM, up 20% YoY. Its market share rose 51bps to 9.02%, led by ETFs (+135bps share gain) and B30 cities. Q2 FY27 revenue, derived as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹796 cr, up 21% YoY from ₹658 cr. That is in line with the +20% to +26% range of recent quarters. Reported Q2 PAT fell about 6% YoY to roughly ₹324 cr (40.7% margin), mainly because of a one-off ₹96.76 cr SEBI settlement over the AT-1 bonds, booked as an exceptional item. Excluding it, H1 operating profit of ₹1,211 cr (77.5% operating margin) shows the core business is healthy. Two weaker signs: closing AUM growth has slowed from +27% to +14% YoY over six periods, and SIP flows grew only 4% YoY. For an AMC the right yardstick is AUM-linked earnings, not P/B. Market cap is about 8.6% of the ₹8.68 trillion closing AUM, with a trailing P/E of 49x and forward P/E of 35x. That is fair for a franchise compounding above 20% with a 34.5% ROE. fundamental.thesis: Delhivery is one of India's largest third-party logistics platforms, running express parcel delivery for e-commerce and part-truckload (PTL) freight, with ₹4,676 cr of cash on the balance sheet. fundamental.thesis: Emmvee is an integrated solar module and cell maker with 10.3 GW of installed module capacity, 2.94 GW of TOPCon cell capacity and an order book of 10.4 GW. It is tagged Industrials/IT in our data, but it really trades on the solar-manufacturing cycle. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 45.1% YoY to ₹3,132 cr and PAT rose 79.1% to ₹762 cr, a 24.3% PAT margin. Growth is clearly slowing from the +116% revenue growth of FY26. EBITDA margin is flat at around 35%, and new orders in Q2 were only 1.5 GW against 10.3 GW of module capacity running at 44% utilisation. No separate quarterly breakdown was available, so these are half-year figures. On the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, it looks cheap: EV/EBITDA is 13.4x (P21, 42% below the broad-market median of 23.3x), trailing P/E is 19.5x (below the 28–45x Industrials range) and forward P/E is 13.7x. That multiple is being applied to what look like peak-cycle 35% EBITDA margins, and the stock is already at 90% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is earnings quality. Cash from operations covered only 0.54x of PAT in H1 and 0.18x in FY26, free cash flow in FY26 was -₹453 cr, and analysts have cut next-year EPS estimates by 12.5% in the last 30 days. Together these suggest margins may fall back as module supply catches up.

Finolex Cables is a mid-sized Indian maker of electrical wires and cables (about 88% of revenue) and optical-fibre communication cables (about 9%). It is not an order-book business, so the Industrials order-cover lens does not really apply. Revenue growth has accelerated sharply from +5.0% in Q2FY26 to +19.0% in Q4FY26 and +44.2% in Q1FY27 (Rs 2,013 cr), and PAT rose +53.1% to Rs 249 cr with PAT margin up from 11.3% to 12.4%. However, that growth is mostly price-led: electrical wire volumes grew only about 7% against roughly 24.5% effective price hikes, which look like copper cost pass-through. EBITDA margin also fell from 18.6% to 16.7%, and the just-filed Q2FY27 numbers conflict between sources (yfinance Rs 1,818 cr revenue / Rs 273 cr PAT vs an unlabelled extracted row of Rs 2,269 cr / Rs 286 cr), so the latest quarter is unverified. On EV/EBITDA, the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive name, the stock trades at 22.8x, right at the broad-market median (P49), so it grades fair. The 24.8x trailing P/E looks cheap against the 28-45x Industrials band, but it is flattered by about Rs 237 cr of FY26 other income, and the stock sits at 94.6% of its 52-week range. Sell-side EPS estimates are rising (+4.8% for FY27, +7.5% for next year over 90 days), but the biggest risk is that a copper price reversal or a slowdown in price hikes exposes underlying volume growth that is only in the high single digits.

fundamental.thesis: Firstsource Solutions (FSL) is a mid-cap BPS/digital-services provider servicing Banking, CMT, and Healthcare verticals for global clients, with a growing $1m+ client roster (45 accounts), six consecutive quarters of 4+ large-deal wins, and 11 straight quarters of QoQ revenue growth — the deal pipeline signals reasonable near-term revenue visibility for its scale. Q1FY27 delivered 12.3% constant-currency revenue growth — a sharp deceleration from +24.5% a year ago — while adjusted PAT grew +31.2% YoY to ₹22cr (8.2% margin) and EBIT margin hit 12.4% for a seventh consecutive quarter of expansion; the company maintained FY27 guidance of 10-13% CC growth and 12.25-12.75% EBIT margin despite absorbing a 1-1.5% headwind from a healthcare BPaaS wind-down, a show of confidence in the deal ramp pipeline. On valuation, trailing P/E of 25.1× sits within the IT sector benchmark of 22-30×, but EV/EBITDA of 12.5× ranks at the P20 percentile of the broad market (-47% below the market median of 23.3×) and forward P/E of 15.25× trades at a -34% discount to the market median — with the stock at 18.8% of its 52-week range, the risk/reward skews cheap, though in a RISK_OFF, FII-selling environment the re-rating catalyst is absent near-term. The dominant risk is that CC revenue growth has halved over four quarters, the 27.5% voluntary attrition rate constrains margin expansion headroom, and a 66% concentration in cyclical Banking+CMT verticals leaves earnings vulnerable to any corporate IT/BPS budget tightening.

Great Eastern Shipping is India's largest private-sector shipping company, running tankers, dry-bulk and gas carriers, plus an offshore-services arm. The pack tags it Industrials, but it is really a freight-rate-driven cyclical with no order book. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 56.8% YoY to ₹3,830 cr and PAT rose 137% to ₹2,578 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 revenue of about ₹1,825 cr, up roughly 47% YoY (slower than Q1's +67%), and Q2 PAT of ₹1,269 cr. But the implied Q2 EBITDA margin of about 97% and PAT margin of about 69% suggest one-off items such as vessel-sale gains or other income, so the headline margin expansion overstates core earnings. On the asset-heavy cyclical yardstick (EV/EBITDA plus P/B with ROE), the stock looks cheap: EV/EBITDA is 4.7x (P2 vs the broad market), P/B is 1.19x against an 18.8% ROE, and the filings show net cash (net debt/equity -0.45). However, the forward P/E of 7.2x is above the trailing 6.9x, which signals that earnings are expected to fall from a cyclical peak, and low peak-cycle multiples in shipping often turn out to be value traps.

fundamental.thesis: Graphite India makes graphite electrodes for electric-arc-furnace (EAF) steelmakers. It runs 80,000 tpa of capacity at 97% utilisation, and that demand depends on the steel cycle and on EAF adoption, not on an order book, so the Industrials order-book framework fits poorly. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose 34% YoY to Rs 1,871 cr and PAT rose 26% to Rs 265 cr; subtracting Q1 (Rs 842 cr / Rs 171 cr) implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 1,029 cr (+41% YoY vs Rs 729 cr) and PAT of about Rs 94 cr (+24% vs Rs 76 cr). However, the implied Q2 PAT margin fell sharply to about 9.1% from 20.3% in Q1, so revenue is accelerating while profitability per rupee is slipping. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, and the signals conflict, so the grade is fair: EV/EBITDA of 51x (P89, +119% vs median) and a trailing P/E of 72x look expensive because trailing earnings come from the FY26 trough (PAT -62%), while a forward P/E of 12.5x (P16), P/B of 2.2x, and a mid-range 52-week position price in a sharp earnings recovery that the 30-day sell-side EPS upgrade (+8.3%) supports. The main risk is that the recovery stalls as margins compress, global steel output stays flat (-0.2% YoY, China -1.6%), and Chinese electrode pricing pressure persists; the reported debt/equity of 6.27 also conflicts with the company's historically low leverage and is probably a units error, but it should be verified.

fundamental.thesis: IGIL is India's listed entity of the International Gemological Institute — a global leader in diamond and gemstone grading services with an asset-light, high-margin business model riding the lab-grown diamond (LGD) certification wave across 16 global subsidiaries. Q1FY27 revenue grew +23.2% YoY to ₹371 cr, with PAT growing faster at +31% YoY to ₹166 cr and PAT margin expanding to 44.7% — PAT consistently outpacing revenue is a quality signal of operating leverage, and EBITDA margin recovered to 64.3% in Q1FY27 after holding at 60-61% in FY26; revenue growth has re-accelerated modestly from the steady +17–18% corridor. Trailing P/E of 30× sits at P41 in the broad market (14.6% below the median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 20.87× is also below peer median — fair to leaning cheap for a 64%-EBITDA-margin business growing at 23%, and the forward P/E of 20.28× (a meaningful discount to trailing) confirms consensus expects earnings acceleration to continue. The single biggest risk to this thesis is the reported debt/equity of 9.59 — likely legacy acquisition financing from the PE-backed IPO structure — which, combined with structural LGD average-realized-price deflation (-3% YoY in 2025), could squeeze cash flows and de-rate the multiple sharply if certification volume growth disappoints.

fundamental.thesis: Inox Wind is India's leading wind turbine manufacturer and turnkey EPC player, serving utility-scale developers including public-sector clients such as IOCL, with a growing O&M contract base (₹11,212 cr unbilled) that provides some recurring revenue visibility. The multi-quarter trajectory is deteriorating on every dimension — revenue growth has decelerated sharply from +103.7% (FY25) through +41.7% (H1FY26) to +23.6% (Q4FY26), with Q1FY27 PAT down 34.1% YoY to ₹64 cr from ₹97 cr; PAT margins have contracted from 12.8% (Q1FY26) to 9.2% (Q4FY26), and EBITDA is also softening (₹210 cr vs ₹220 cr Q1 prior year). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials (per sector card), at 17.8× vs sector median 23.3× the stock screens at P33 and appears modestly discounted, but this apparent cheapness is materially misleading — ~₹9,884 cr in contingent liabilities (₹4,306 cr EPCG customs-duty exposure + ₹5,578 cr SECI bank guarantees invoked) equate to ~64% of market cap and are absent from the EV, justifying a FAIR grade at best. Sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 43% in 90 days while all 6 analysts retain BUY — a classic pre-derating divergence — and binary resolution of the EPCG/SECI liabilities on an already-extreme D/E of 20.63× is the make-or-break risk.

IRB Infrastructure is India's largest private toll-road developer and operator, with 27 highway projects, about 1.5 million vehicle crossings a day and roughly a tenth of national toll revenue, plus an asset base of about ₹94,000 cr that it recycles through its private and public InvITs. In Q2FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,945 cr (+8.1% YoY, up from +0.4% in Q1FY27) and PAT was ₹260 cr (13.4% margin), with toll revenue growth improving to 15% from 11% a year ago and an EBITDA margin of 56.7%. However, the headline +84% PAT growth leans on InvIT distributions, and the comparison base is unreliable because the Q2FY26 row (₹175 cr revenue) does not match the current reporting basis. On the yardstick for a capital-intensive business, EV/EBITDA of 16.2× is about 30% below the broad-market median, and P/B of 1.21× looks cheap, but ROE of only 4.2% justifies that low book multiple, so overall valuation is fair rather than a clear bargain. The main risk is leverage: net debt is ₹10,283 cr (about 2.3× net debt/EBITDA, debt/equity close to 1×), so earnings depend on the pace of asset monetisation and on regulatory terms for concessions.

Valuation is unambiguously expensive: trailing P/E of 69.7x sits nearly 100% above the broad-market median of 35.2x (P83 peer rank), EV/EBITDA of 30.04x is 29% above peers (P66), and the P/B of 4.04x against a TTM ROE of only 5.8% is egregious — paying 4x book for sub-cost-of-capital returns — with the forward P/E of 28.45x implying an aggressive earnings recovery that analyst downward revisions (-24.6% EPS cut in 90 days) directly contradict. fundamental.thesis: Gujarat Fluorochemicals is a major Indian maker of fluoropolymers and fluorochemicals; its chemicals arm brings in about 98% of revenue, and it is also building a battery-materials (EV) business that is still at an early stage. Growth has picked up sharply. Revenue growth went from -1.1% in Q3FY26 to +12% in Q4FY26, +24% in Q1FY27 (₹1,588 cr) and +34.4% for H1FY27 (₹3,348 cr). That implies a Q2FY27 of about ₹1,760 cr, up roughly 45% YoY, with PAT of about ₹240 cr (about 13.6% margin). EBITDA margin rose from 22.5% to about 27%, the chemicals segment earned a 27.6% margin, and cash from operations was 1.61x PAT. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card sets for capital-intensive chemicals. At 42.2x it is far above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range and in the 84th percentile of the broad market. Trailing P/E is 85.3x and forward P/E 43.5x, the stock sits at 91.5% of its 52-week range, and the mean analyst target is only about 1.7% above the price, so it is expensive even allowing for a premium for fluoropolymer quality. The biggest risk is the gap between price and estimates: analysts have cut forecasts (FY EPS -2.5%, next-FY -5.4%) while ratings stay bullish, which often comes before a de-rating. On top of that, the planned ₹6,000 cr battery-materials capex is pushing free cash flow negative (₹-103 cr in H1) while that segment is still losing money (₹-92 cr in H1).

fundamental.thesis: Jindal Stainless (JSL) is India's #1 stainless steel producer and #5 globally ex-China, operating 4.2 MTPA capacity across 120+ product grades on a ~₹44,000 cr TTM revenue base, with strong structural demand from government infrastructure programmes (railways, highways, airports). Q1FY27 revenue grew +10.5% YoY to ₹11,279 cr (stable, not accelerating from FY26's +9.3%), but PAT margin has contracted from 7.4% in FY26 to 6.8% in Q1FY27 as raw material costs at ~70% of revenue compress the spread; PAT growth has decelerated sharply from +27.4% in FY26 to +7.7% YoY in Q1FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (the correct metric for capital-intensive steel, per sector card), JSL trades at 6.59× — inside the 5–8× mid-cycle cyclical range and at the 4th percentile vs 473 broad-market peers — grading CHEAP, corroborated by forward P/E (13.68×) sitting at a discount to trailing P/E (18.27×), pricing in continued earnings growth. The biggest risk to this thesis is raw material cost volatility (nickel, ferro-alloys at ~70% of revenue) combined with structural Chinese overcapacity, which could further erode the already-contracting EBITDA margin (13.1% Q1FY27 vs 13.7% peak in FY26).

Lloyds Metals and Energy is a Maharashtra-based iron-ore miner and pellet/sponge-iron producer expanding into downstream steel, so it is a commodity spread-cycle name within Materials rather than a consumer franchise. Q2FY27, derived as H1FY27 minus Q1FY27 from the official filings, shows revenue of about 13,009 - 7,354 = 5,655 cr (+52.5% YoY vs 3,707 cr) and PAT of about 1,057 cr (+86% YoY vs 567 cr). That is a sharp slowdown from +208.6% revenue growth in Q1FY27, with revenue down about 23% and PAT down about 39% quarter-on-quarter, and PAT margin compressing from 23.6% to roughly 18.7%; the pre-computed 'accelerating' signal is distorted by mixing half-year and quarterly rows. On the sector card's EV/EBITDA yardstick for cyclicals, 19.1x is far above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, and trailing P/E of 26.3x is above the 12-22x Materials band, so the stock grades expensive today. The 12.1x forward P/E and the +38% upward revision to sell-side estimates show the market is pricing in a large capacity ramp, which must be delivered to justify the price. The biggest risk is that this ramp is debt-funded (FY26 FCF of -1,853 cr, high debt/equity, fresh NCD issuance) while the stock sits at 84% of its 52-week range, leaving little room for an iron-ore price dip or execution slippage.

fundamental.thesis: NATIONALUM (NALCO) is a government-owned, fully integrated aluminium producer (bauxite to alumina to metal, with captive power) and among the world's lowest-cost alumina producers. It sells into global prices it cannot set, carries net cash of about ₹12,172 cr and earns about 30% ROCE. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹10,722 cr (+32.4% YoY) and PAT ₹3,838 cr (+54.7%), both records, with CFO/PAT at 1.14x. But growth is fading inside the half: Q2 implied revenue is ~₹5,420 cr, YoY growth slowed from +39.3% in Q1 to roughly +26%, and PAT growth from +91.5% to roughly +28% (~₹1,835 cr vs ₹1,430 cr). PAT margin slipped from 37.8% to ~34%, and the alumina/chemicals segment revenue fell 5.75% YoY. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a commodity cyclical, the stock trades at 7.4x, the top of the 5–8x mid-cycle band, on what look like near-peak margins (EBITDA margin ~50%), so I grade it fair. The trailing P/E of 11x looks cheap against the broad market, but that comparison means little because there are no tight peers and cyclicals always look cheapest at the top of the cycle. The biggest risk is that profits rest mostly on LME aluminium and alumina prices, which NALCO does not control, and the Q2 slowdown suggests the price tailwind is already fading.

Anthem Biosciences is a mid-cap contract research, development and manufacturing (CRDMO) business, with CRDMO at 84% of H1 revenue and specialty ingredients at 16%; it has a clean regulatory record (USFDA, TGA and ANVISA inspections) and a China+1 tailwind. Q2 recovered: subtracting Q1 (₹418 cr, -22.6%) from H1 gives Q2 revenue of about ₹594 cr, roughly +8% YoY, and PAT of about ₹211 cr. However, PAT growth (+7.2% in H1) and margin expansion lean heavily on ₹83.8 cr of other income, which is about 17% of reported EBITDA, while forex gains fell 79%. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive CDMO, the stock trades at 50.8x (P89 vs the broad market), on a trailing P/E of 76.2x against a 28–40x pharma range and P/B of 14.7x on 21.7% ROE, so it is expensive. The sell-side mean target is only about 2% above the price, and the stock sits at 74% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that a lumpy, contracting top line and other-income-flattered margins cannot support a valuation already pricing in a sharp earnings rebound.

fundamental.thesis: Aster DM Healthcare runs a multi-specialty hospital network in India. Occupancy rose 335 bps to 68% and patient volumes grew 12%. However, this is a single post-merger quarter, so we cannot yet read a multi-quarter trajectory, and the YoY base is likely pro-forma. Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive hospital operator: at 45.9x it sits at P87 versus the broad market and about 97% above the median, and the 123x trailing P/E is distorted by the merger. Even the 41x forward P/E plus a price at 85% of the 52-week range points to 'expensive'. The biggest risk is that sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut about 18% in 30 days while all 12 analysts still rate it a buy, a classic pre-derating pattern during an unfinished integration.

Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, cross-checked with P/E because no tight listed peers were available, the stock looks expensive at 37.0x EV/EBITDA (P78 and 59% above the broad-market median) and 50.8x trailing P/E against a 28-40x pharma range; the 34.4x forward P/E already prices in a strong profit recovery, and the +23.8% sell-side upside looks unreliable because the Rs 1,520 mean target is only about 5% above the roughly Rs 1,450 price implied by market cap and EPS. The biggest risk is that profit does not catch up with revenue, since FY27 EPS estimates were cut 2.8% in the last 30 days and the valuation leaves little room for further margin slippage; confidence is also limited because the FY26 revenue and PAT rows appear overstated tenfold, the 51% dividend yield is clearly wrong, and no sector KPIs or management guidance were available.

Gland Pharma is a mid-cap maker of generic injectable medicines. It sells mainly to partners in the US and Europe, and its contract-manufacturing (CDMO) arm now makes up 45% of revenue. In Q2 FY27 revenue rose 23.3% YoY to ₹1,834 cr and PAT rose 58.3% to ₹291 cr (15.9% margin), so growth has picked up from +6% a year ago to +20–23% over the last two quarters, driven by US sales up 42% and CDMO up 31%. Momentum is cooling sequentially, though: revenue was only +2% QoQ, PAT fell from ₹317 cr to ₹291 cr, and the reported EBITDA margin slipped from 27.0% to 26.2%. India, Canada/Australia/NZ and Rest of World all shrank 18–42% YoY. On valuation the stock looks fair: trailing P/E is 35.3x, inside the 28–40x pharma range and at the median of the broad market. EV/EBITDA of 20.1x is about 14% below the peer median, and forward P/E of 24.1x already prices in continued growth. Return on equity is a modest 10.5%, which limits the case for a premium, and with the stock at 76% of its 52-week range the upside looks limited. The biggest risk is concentration: 64% of revenue now comes from the US, so any end to the current tariff exemption for generics, any pricing pressure, or a bad FDA inspection result would hit the core growth engine directly.

fundamental.thesis: GLAXO is the Indian subsidiary of GlaxoSmithKline, a premium MNC branded-formulations franchise with 22–27% market shares in general medicines and vaccines respectively, operating entirely within India's domestic market with zero US generics exposure and no tariff risk from recent US pharma levies. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated sharply to +16.56% YoY (₹938 cr vs ₹805 cr in Q1FY26), a marked re-acceleration from near-stagnation at +1.9% through FY26 and -1.2% in Q1FY26, driven by Shingrix (+65% growth), vaccines therapy (+18.5%), cardiac (+16.9%), and anti-diabetic (+17.3%) segments — PAT grew 15.68% YoY to ₹237 cr but PAT margin contracted to 25.3% from 27.1% in FY26 as S&A normalises, with management guiding EBITDA margins to settle at ~34% vs the 36-38% range seen over FY26. At a trailing P/E of 44.85× (above the 28–40× pharma sector benchmark), forward P/E of 35.72× (within range, confirming near-term earnings growth priced in), and EV/EBITDA of 33.98× (P71 vs broad market), GLAXO grades as fair — the premium is defensible for a defensive, India-only, brand-led franchise with no binary US/FDA risk, but peer rank at P65 on trailing P/E confirms there is no meaningful discount on offer. The principal risk is that the guided margin normalisation to ~34% EBITDA compresses PAT margins further if the current revenue acceleration fades back toward the guided 8–10% established-business growth range, making the present fair multiple vulnerable.

Q1FY27 consolidated revenue accelerated to +17.3% YoY (₹2,229 cr), continuing a multi-quarter re-acceleration from +9.8% in Q1FY26, but PAT collapsed 45% YoY to ₹56 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from 15.9% (Q1FY26) to 12.0%, with CDMO Sterile Injectables margins imploding from 11% to 1.4% and the Generics segment swinging to a ₹10 cr operating loss — a dangerous divergence between topline and bottom-line trajectories. The biggest risk is a dual FDA compliance overhang — OAI at Montreal (remediation expenses of ₹535 mn already booked, manufacturing suspended) plus a live USFDA Spokane update — alongside a GST show-cause notice and a high debt/equity ratio (50.94×), any one of which could derail the assumed margin recovery.

fundamental.thesis: Max Healthcare is one of India's largest listed hospital chains, with about 6,100 network beds running at more than 75% occupancy. It is growing by adding beds at existing hospitals and buying new ones (Kalinga in Bhubaneswar, a land parcel in Pune, 85 more beds at its Noida hospital). Taking H1 FY27 minus Q1, Q2 FY27 revenue comes to about ₹2,569 cr, up about 20% YoY, and EBITDA margin has widened from 26.8% to 28.2% over the trend window. But revenue growth has slowed from above 30% to about 17–20%, and H1 PAT fell 7.7% YoY to ₹737 cr. Most of that fall comes from the tax rate going back to normal: it rose from an unusually low 5.6% to 24.5% because of a one-off merger-related tax reversal last year. Cash generation is solid, with operating cash flow at 1.35x PAT and ₹406 cr of free cash flow in H1. Because hospitals are capital-heavy, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, which is 45.6x, about 96% above the broad-market median (P86). Trailing P/E is 73.9x against a 35.2x median (P85), and P/B is 9.9x for only a 14.3% ROE, so the stock is expensive even with forward P/E falling to 44.9x. The biggest risk is that analysts keep cutting their EPS estimates (down 4.5% over 90 days) while capex for new beds and acquisitions stays heavy. That could lead to a de-rating even though 21 of 28 analysts still rate it a buy. Two numbers don't line up: the press release reports Q2 revenue of ₹3,219 cr and PAT of ₹448 cr (+10%), likely on a gross or network basis, while the trend table implies ₹2,569 cr and ₹414 cr. Also, the 15% dividend yield and 32.37 debt/equity in the snapshot look like data errors and were ignored.

The biggest risk is that extraordinary debt/equity of 42.28 with ₹52 cr in quarterly finance costs leaves minimal margin of safety — any delay in Zaynich commercialization or continued mixed subsidiary performance (18 of 28 subsidiaries unreviewed; 5 audited reporting a net ₹2 cr loss on ₹777 cr revenue) could strain free cash flow and force dilutive capital raises.

ABFRL is a midcap fashion retailer running Pantaloons, ethnic labels (including TCNS), the TMRW digital-brands platform and luxury retail, with about 1,286 stores. Revenue growth slowed to +2.4% YoY in Q2 FY27 (₹2,030 cr), down from +10.6-11% in Q1 FY27 and FY26, while the net loss widened 27.5% to ₹376 cr, taking PAT margin from -12.3% to -18.5% in one quarter. H1 operating margin fell to -7.3% from -2.5% a year ago, and cash burn continues (H1 FCF of -₹288 cr, CFO/PAT 0.14x). P/E is meaningless for a loss-maker, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA (18.2x, P36 vs the broad market) and P/B (1.28x, P7), with ROE at -12.7%; the low book multiple reflects equity being eroded by losses rather than a clear mispricing, so I call it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that slowing revenue plus rising losses keep consuming the balance sheet before Pantaloons' 15.9% segment margin can offset losses in ethnic (near-zero EBITDA margin) and TMRW (-19% margin).

fundamental.thesis: Bata India is India's largest footwear retailer, with about 2,000 stores and a growing franchise network. It is a mass-to-mid-market brand in a K-shaped consumer market where premium players are taking share. The trend has not recovered convincingly: Q1FY27 revenue was ₹979 cr (+4.0% YoY), only a modest pickup after five periods of flat-to-negative growth (FY26 +0.6%, H1FY26 -2.2%). FY26 PAT fell 59.5% to ₹134 cr, a 3.8% margin, partly because of ₹42 cr of VRS costs. VRS costs continued in H1FY27 (₹13 cr) along with a ₹5.8 cr forex loss, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-03 are not yet in the extracted data. Franchisee like-for-like growth in the high single digits is the one positive KPI. I graded valuation on P/E plus ROE, because the low 13.7× EV/EBITDA is inflated by lease accounting. On that basis the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E is 75.6× (P86 vs the broad market, +115% vs the 35× median) and P/B is 6.4× on an ROE of only 8.5%. That is a premium-retailer multiple for a business growing revenue in low single digits. The forward P/E of 37× assumes a profit recovery that has not shown up yet. Sell-side views are bearish (8 sell out of 14), and FY EPS estimates have been cut 8.2% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the margin recovery story keeps slipping while estimates keep being cut, which would push the multiple down further.

BLS International runs outsourced visa and consular processing for foreign governments, plus a fast-growing but lower-margin digital and e-governance services arm; it does not fit the premium consumer-discretionary template in the sector card. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 32.0% YoY to ₹973 cr, up from +25.3% in Q1FY27, but PAT rose only 8.6% to ₹202 cr (Q1: +11.4%). PAT margin has contracted from 25.2% a year ago to 20.8%, and from 24.1% for FY26. The main cause is mix: digital services (H1 revenue ₹793 cr, +50% YoY) earns a 6.2% segment margin against 39.7% in visa, and acquisition costs from Atyati and the Trefeddian hotel add to the pressure. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA and P/E together with cash conversion, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 13.8x and EV/EBITDA is 10.2x, both around the 11th percentile of the broad market (median 35.2x / 23.3x). It also has ₹1,665 cr net cash and CFO/PAT of 1.37x, though the price sitting at 11% of its 52-week range shows the market is pricing in a de-rating as profits grow far slower than sales. The biggest risk is that the shift toward digital services keeps diluting margins, so strong revenue growth fails to turn into earnings growth.

fundamental.thesis: Chalet Hotels owns and runs upscale hotels in Indian metros, mostly under the Marriott brand, and also earns from office rentals and a residential real-estate business that books revenue in lumps. The ongoing businesses held up: core hospitality grew 8.5% to ₹419 cr at a 29.3% PBIT margin, and rentals grew 18.1%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because hotels are capital-intensive. At 15.7x it sits at P27 against the broad market and well below the sector card's premium-hotel range. fundamental.thesis: Crompton is one of India's largest fan, pump and small-appliance makers. fundamental.thesis: ITC Hotels is a leading Indian luxury and upscale hotel chain, demerged from ITC, and since May 2026 has a new branded-residences arm after acquiring Kerala Luxury Resorts (Zuri) and GHK Hospitality. H1 FY27 revenue grew 20.2% YoY to ₹1,990 cr and PAT rose 44.0% to ₹385 cr, with PAT margin up to 19.3% from 16.1%; the implied Q2 FY27 alone (H1 less Q1) is about ₹1,054 cr revenue (+25% YoY) and ₹203 cr PAT, so growth sped up from Q1's +14.8%. Part of that speed-up is bought rather than organic: the core hotels segment grew 13.8%, the new residences segment added ₹109 cr, and operating cash flow is solid at 1.42x PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-heavy business, 20.8x sits about 11% below the peer median of 23.3x, P/B of 2.75x is at P30 and trailing P/E of 37x (forward 26x) is near the median, so we grade it fair with mild cheapness, and the price sits at 15% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that headline growth leans on two back-to-back acquisitions whose fair values are still provisional, while capex has nearly tripled to 22% of revenue as rising crude and a risk-off macro weigh on discretionary travel demand.

JSW Dulux (formerly Akzo Nobel India; JSW Group took control in Dec 2025) is a decorative and industrial paints maker that sold its Powder Coatings and IRC divisions and is now chasing market share. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,927 cr, up only 5.8% YoY as reported, but up 20% on a comparable retained-business basis with 23% volume growth, and the latest single quarter improved from Q1 FY27's -2.8%. Profitability is moving the wrong way: gross margin fell 1,180bp from 47.2% to 35.4%, EBITDA margin slipped to 13.2% from 14.4%, and PAT margin dropped to 7.8% from 12.1% on an operating basis, while cash conversion is weak (CFO/PAT 0.42x, FCF about ₹-8 cr). On valuation I used forward P/E and ignored the 7.45x trailing P/E, because the ₹1,874 cr one-off divestment gain inflates it; at 31.3x forward and 6.0x P/B the stock is cheap against the card's 60-100x discretionary norms, but analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (-5.8% over 90 days), so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that volume-led growth is being bought with price and margin under a new promoter, and the price increases do not restore gross margin before earnings estimates are cut further.

fundamental.thesis: Kalyan Jewellers is one of India's largest branded jewellery chains, with a pan-India and Middle East store network, and it benefits from the shift from unorganised jewellers to branded ones and from premium spending. H1 FY27 revenue rose about 35.9% YoY to roughly ₹19,300 cr and PAT rose 36.4% to ₹716 cr, but growth is slowing within the year rather than accelerating as the pre-computed signal says: Q1 FY27 grew +45.7%, so Q2 implies roughly +27%; H1 PAT also includes a ₹73 cr one-off land-sale gain, so core profit growth is closer to the low-20s%; and H1 PAT margin of 3.7% is below Q3 FY26's 4.0%. I graded valuation on trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA because no same-store-sales or store-payback data was provided: trailing P/E of 29.3× (forward 20.4×) and EV/EBITDA of 19.6× sit around the 40th percentile of the broad market, well below the 60–100× the sector card cites for premium discretionary names, and the high P/B of 6.3× is backed by 24% ROE, so this is fair with a cheap tilt, near its 52-week low. Cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 1.79×, FCF ₹1,091 cr), but the inputs conflict in several places: Q1 FY27 revenue is ₹10,589 cr in the PDF vs ₹9,325 cr in yfinance, Q1 FY26 is mis-extracted, the 40% dividend yield is bogus, and the ~₹384 price implied by the 52-week range does not match the consensus +25.7% upside, so conviction is held moderate.

fundamental.thesis: Lenskart is India's largest omnichannel eyewear retailer, running its own manufacturing and a large store network.
