The biggest risk is that any further slowdown in growth triggers the 25–40% single-reset de-rating the sector card warns about for names priced this richly.

fundamental.thesis: LG Electronics India is a leading consumer-durables maker. Home appliances (ACs, fridges, washing machines) are 88% of H1 FY27 revenue at a thin 9.4% segment margin, while home entertainment is a smaller but much more profitable 38.9%-margin business; the company holds net cash of about ₹4,569 crore. Growth has recovered sharply from a weak FY26 (revenue +1.0%, PAT -23.5%). Revenue growth went from -6.4% in Q3 FY26 to +8.1%, then +15.5% in Q1 FY27 and +17.4% for H1 FY27, which implies about +19% in Q2 alone (₹7,380 cr) and Q2 PAT of about ₹489 cr (+26% YoY), but part of this is an easy base and Q2 PAT margin (about 6.6%) fell from Q1's 9.0%. On valuation I used P/E and EV/EBITDA against the Consumer Discretionary card's 60–100× norm: trailing P/E of 64.8× sits at the low end of that range and forward P/E of 41.2× prices in continued strong growth, so I grade it fair. It still looks rich against the broad market (P81–P92) and on 42.5× EV/EBITDA for a business earning about 12% EBITDA margins. The biggest risk is that a premium multiple rests on a low-margin, highly competitive appliance business that is also spending heavily (₹1,163 cr capex in H1) on a new, unproven automotive-electronics venture with no financial guidance.

fundamental.thesis: Meesho is a value-focused Indian e-commerce marketplace with 284 million annual transacting users, and its Q2 FY27 contribution margin was 6.0% of net merchandise value (NMV). Revenue grew 34.0% YoY to Rs 4,120 cr in Q2, slowing from +48.0% in Q1 despite the trend table's 'accelerating' label, while NMV grew a slower 23% (33% on management's festive-aligned basis), orders grew 17%, and the net loss narrowed about 68% YoY to Rs 132 cr at a -3.2% margin, though that margin is roughly flat against the implied Q1 level of about -3.6%. On the sector card's platform yardstick of EV/sales, growth delivery and unit economics (trailing P/E is not meaningful), I grade the stock expensive at 6.22x price/sales and 94.9x forward P/E (99th percentile against a broad-market fallback set, so a weak comparison), with next-year EPS estimates cut 12.2% over 90 days and the mean target only about 2% above the price. The biggest risk is that a richly valued, still loss-making stock de-rates if growth keeps slowing or if the Rs 2,072 cr of tax demands, heavy New Initiatives losses (-465% margin) and the Rs 2,021 cr Kirana Club deal absorb more cash than expected.

Physicswallah is a fast-growing Indian test-prep and edtech company that sells online courses and runs a growing chain of offline coaching centres. Note that yfinance tags it FMCG, which is wrong; it belongs under Consumer Discretionary. On the latest quarter we could verify from filings (Q1 FY27), revenue was about ₹1,054 cr, up 24.4% YoY. That is slower than the 35.0% growth for full-year FY26, and EBITDA margin fell from 14.1% (FY26) to 4.9% in Q1, while FY26 PAT was a ₹24 cr loss. The Q2 FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-04 but have not been extracted into our trend table. The unverified yfinance Q2 figures (₹738 cr revenue, ₹144 cr PAT) cannot be relied on, and the store-count KPI drop from 353 to 273 looks inconsistent. Because the business is barely profitable, we grade valuation on EV/sales and EV/EBITDA rather than P/E. At 8.4× price/sales and 72× EV/EBITDA (P96 vs the broad market), with a 55.7× forward P/E and ROE of -0.8%, the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is that consensus EPS estimates are being cut (-5.8% in 30 days) while 7 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy, plus integration risk from the new Utkarsh Classes acquisition. Together these set up a classic derating if margins don't recover.

The Q2FY27 results announcement (4 Nov 2026) shows revenue from operations of ₹314.3 cr, up 37% YoY, adjusted EBITDA of ₹118 cr (+39%) and PBT of ₹85.8 cr (+43%). That is a sharp rebound from FY26, when revenue fell 15.9% to ₹985 cr, although PAT margin did improve from 18.4% in H1FY26 to 21.0% for full-year FY26. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA and P/E against the broad market because there are no tight listed peers, the stock trades at 25.5x EV/EBITDA (P58) and 43.9x trailing P/E (P64), with a 32.3x forward P/E implying expected earnings growth, so it is fairly valued with modest upside. The biggest risk is cash conversion: CFO/PAT was only 0.48x in FY26 and free cash flow was negative (₹-114 cr) because of heavy spending on acquiring catalogue and content, and the 37% jump is a single quarter off a weak base.

fundamental.thesis: The Leela Palaces Hotels & Resorts is a pure-play luxury hotel owner-operator with 14 properties at Q3FY26 and an average room rate of about ₹30,300, which puts it squarely in the premium-travel trend the sector card calls structurally strong while hotel supply lags demand until about 2027. The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹352 cr, up 28.1% YoY, and PAT of ₹49 cr, up 460% off a low base, for a 13.8% PAT margin. Revenue growth sped up from +21.0% in Q3FY26. The trend table flags margins as 'contracting' (from 32.3%/52.0% EBITDA in Q3FY26), but that compares the seasonally weak Q1 against peak-season Q3, so it is not a real deterioration. The Q2/H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-14 have not been extracted, so the latest quarter is unverified. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hotel owner, the stock trades at 22.5×, about level with the 23.3× median (P48), and P/B is 2.4× against an ROE of only 8%. That makes it fair, not cheap, despite 18 of 18 analysts rating it buy and FY-EPS estimates raised 8.7% over 90 days. The main risks are a mid-cap luxury-discretionary stock in a RISK_OFF market with rising crude, and the live price data contradicting itself: the 52-week range of ₹382–474 conflicts with the consensus target of ₹702 implying +16.9% upside, and yfinance Q1 revenue of ₹114 cr does not match the PDF figure of ₹352 cr.

Vardhman Textiles is one of India's largest integrated yarn and fabric makers, with an acrylic-fibre subsidiary. It is a cyclical, capital-heavy textile business rather than a premium consumer brand, so the Consumer Discr. sector card's 60–100× multiple norms do not apply. Growth has turned sharply upward. Revenue growth accelerated from about +1% through FY26 to +13.3% in Q1FY27 and about +15.6% in Q2FY27 (implied ₹2,866 cr vs ₹2,480 cr). Implied Q2 PAT nearly doubled to about ₹358 cr (+91% YoY), and EBITDA margin expanded from 13–17% to 21.5% in H1FY27, with cash conversion strong at 1.48x CFO/PAT. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, 15.2× is about 35% below the broad-market median, and forward P/E of 14.6× vs trailing 25.3× prices in further earnings growth. But P/B of 1.85× against a TTM ROE of only 7.3%, with the stock at 98.4% of its 52-week range, makes this fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the margin jump reflects a favourable cotton-yarn spread cycle rather than structural gains, and next-year EPS estimates are already being trimmed (-2.8% over 30 days).

fundamental.thesis: Welspun Living is a home-textiles maker with a market cap of about Rs 19,689 cr, and it is recovering from a very weak FY26. Q2FY27 revenue rose 16.9% YoY to Rs 2,870 cr and PAT rose to Rs 170 cr from about Rs 15 cr, with PAT margin improving from 0.1% in Q3FY26 to 5.8% in Q1FY27 and 5.9% in Q2FY27; however, growth slowed from +23.7% in Q1, the table's 'accelerating' signal mainly reflects a low base, and revenue is only about back to its implied Q2FY25 level. Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick: 23.2x is in line with the 23.3x broad-market median (P49), forward P/E of 22.5x is also mid-pack (P48), and the 71.6x trailing P/E (P84) looks inflated by depressed earnings, as the latest quarter annualises to about 29x; trading at 92% of the 52-week range limits upside, while the consensus target data looks unreliable because it does not reconcile with that range. The biggest risk is that the recovery has only two quarters of evidence, and this analysis had no usable management guidance or Q2 EBITDA margin to test its durability.

fundamental.thesis: Whirlpool of India is a leading single-segment home appliances manufacturer (refrigerators, washing machines, ACs) with a well-established urban franchise, though it faces intensifying competition from Haier, LG, and listed peers. Revenue inflected positively in Q1FY27 to ₹2,727 cr (+12.1% YoY consolidated, PDF-sourced), reversing prior weakness (-3.8% in Q2FY26, -1.0% in 9MFY26) — a genuine top-line recovery — but PAT collapsed -29.6% YoY to ₹103 cr with EBITDA margin compressing sharply to 7.62% from 9.77%, meaning the company is growing revenues while simultaneously destroying earnings quality. At 34.84× trailing P/E (P49 vs broad-market peers, median), EV/EBITDA of 19.1× (P39, below median), and P/B of 2.5× against a meagre 7.24% ROE (FY26), the stock is fairly valued on headline multiples but expensive on a quality-adjusted basis — a company with sub-8% ROE and accelerating downward EPS revisions (-25.2% over 90 days) does not merit a median consumer-discretionary multiple. The biggest risk is that margins continue to deteriorate under rising crude-driven input cost pressure while aggressive sell-side estimate cuts (-25.2% in 90 days) signal further earnings-led de-rating from an already distressed 7.1% of 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: Zee Entertainment is India's second-largest broadcast media group (~50 TV channels plus the ZEE5 OTT platform), structurally pressured by the secular migration to streaming and left exposed after the Jiostar/Sony merger collapsed; it now carries substantial governance and legal overhangs that suppress any re-rating. FY26 annual revenue declined 1.9% YoY to ₹7,567 Cr while PAT collapsed 82.8% to ₹120 Cr, compressing PAT margin to 1.6% and EBITDA margin to a catastrophic 2.6% (from 13.4% in FY25) — the multi-quarter trajectory shows revenue decelerating and margins contracting across every available period with no stabilisation evident in filings. Forward P/E of 13.42× (P19 vs broad-market peers, -42% below median) and P/B of 0.9× (P2 vs peers, -80% below median) both screen as unambiguously cheap; EV/EBITDA of 23× looks deceptively at median but is computed on severely depressed EBITDA — on normalised 12-13% margins the implied EV/EBITDA would be sub-5×, confirming franchise-level cheapness if operational recovery is achievable. The single largest risk to the recovery thesis is the IDBI Bank insolvency petition (filed September 2025) seeking NCLT-admitted CIRP initiation, which if granted would be existential for the business regardless of underlying brand and content-IP value.

fundamental.thesis: Amara Raja Energy & Mobility is India's second-largest lead-acid battery maker (Amaron) and is building a lithium-ion cell and pack business. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 21.2% YoY to Rs 8,323 cr, but profit fell 22.2% to Rs 343 cr. The quarter implied by the filings (H1 minus Q1) is worse: Q2 FY27 revenue was about Rs 4,108 cr (+18.5% YoY), PAT was about Rs 152 cr (-45% YoY), and EBITDA margin dropped to about 9.3% from 15.1% a year ago, so sales are accelerating while margins shrink. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick we use for this capital-heavy business, the stock trades at 10.3x, cheaper than about 89% of the broad market, and its trailing P/E of 17.4x sits just below the 18-28x auto-ancillary range. That makes it cheap on paper, but sell-side FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days, so the cheapness is partly a falling-earnings effect. The biggest risk is that lead-acid margins keep shrinking while the loss-making new-energy unit (Rs 64 cr H1 loss) and Rs 2,320 cr of new LFP capex keep free cash flow negative (Rs -161 cr in H1).

Olectra Greentech makes electric buses (Mobility, about 86% of H1 revenue) and composite insulators (Energy, about 14%), and is a mid-sized player in India's government-tender-driven e-bus market. H1FY27 revenue grew +25.7% YoY to ₹1,263 cr, but almost all of that came from Q1 (+65.7%): the implied Q2FY27 figure (H1 minus Q1) is about ₹687 cr, only about +4.6% YoY. H1 PAT rose just +4.4% to ₹79 cr as EBITDA margin fell to 10.4% (from 14.1% in H1FY26) and PAT margin fell to 6.2% (from 7.5%), so sales growth is not turning into profit growth. On trailing P/E, the usable yardstick here because the snapshot's EV/EBITDA of 1065x is clearly a data error, the stock trades at 56x against an 18–30x auto OEM band and the broad-market median of 35x (P75), so it is expensive; the 27.9x forward P/E assumes roughly a doubling of earnings that flat PAT does not yet support. The biggest risk is that margins keep falling on low-priced state transport (STU) bus contracts while net debt of about ₹268 cr and finance costs eat into already thin profits.

fundamental.thesis: ACME Solar is a mid-sized renewable power producer (IPP) with 2,990 MW running and about 5,080 MW under construction, and its 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs) are mostly with central-government buyers like NTPC. Such a company grows through new capacity and the spread between its returns and its cost of debt, and the new BESS (battery storage) and FDRE (round-the-clock renewable) projects are its growth engine. H1 FY27 revenue rose 78.2% YoY to ₹1,745 cr and PAT rose 105% to ₹504 cr. YoY growth has sped up from +59% (FY26) to +63% (Q1) to +78% (H1), and PAT margin rose from 19.9% to 24.7% to 28.9%. Within H1, the September quarter works out to roughly ₹791 cr revenue (below Q1, which fits the monsoon dip in solar output) but higher PAT of about ₹269 cr. Operating capacity barely moved in Q1 (+3.5% YoY), so near-term growth now depends on commissioning, which has started: 66.68 MW of solar plus BESS units went live in early November, and a 400 MW FDRE PPA was signed with NTPC. Valuation is fair: I graded it on EV/EBITDA, the card's yardstick for capital-heavy businesses. At 15.2x it is about 35% below the market median (P26), and the forward P/E of 13.7x is far below the trailing 40.7x, which suggests earnings growth is expected. But P/B of 4.0x against a 10.4% ROE is not cheap, and the stock sits at 80% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt/equity is about 3.9x, interest coverage is only 2.47x, finance costs take about 40% of EBITDA, and H1 free cash flow was -₹5,263 cr on ₹6,329 cr of capex. Grid connection delays (substations delivered on time only 60% of the time, about 6 months late on average) or higher interest rates could hold back the earnings ramp.

The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

Mahanagar Gas is the city gas distributor for Mumbai and nearby areas, selling CNG to vehicles and piped gas to homes and industry, with a near-monopoly in its licensed areas and network volumes edging up (about 4.5 to 4.6 mmscmd through FY26). Sales are growing but profits are shrinking. H1 FY27 revenue rose 18.5% YoY to ₹5,377 cr, and the implied Q2 revenue of about ₹2,778 cr (H1 less Q1) is the fastest growth in the window. The ₹17 cr 3EV impairment explains only a small part of that fall, so the squeeze is mainly gas costs. On valuation, the business is closest to a regulated utility, so I graded it on EV/EBITDA plus P/E: trailing P/E of 14.2x sits inside the 10–18x utilities band and EV/EBITDA is 7.4x. That makes it fair rather than cheap, because the broad-market peer discount ignores falling earnings and there are no city-gas peers in the comparison set. The biggest risk is that gas sourcing costs keep rising, for example through cuts in cheap government-allocated (APM) gas or a costlier spot-gas mix, faster than MGL can raise CNG and PNG prices, so margins keep compressing even as volumes grow.

The single biggest risk is the sequential compression in the automotive PBIT margin from 9.3% in Q4FY26 to 7.7% in Q1 FY27, combined with rising crude costs (+headwind on vehicle input costs), EV mix dipping from 9.6% to 6.4% quarter-on-quarter, and a sustained RISK_OFF FII outflow environment that keeps the Auto sector on underweight — this cocktail can extend the share-price slide meaningfully before cheap valuations matter to the market.

fundamental.thesis: Axis Bank is India's third-largest private-sector bank, with a large corporate and wholesale book, a growing retail franchise and a consolidated life-insurance associate (Axis Max Life). In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

The principal risk is that credit costs remain elevated at 2.19% and cost of borrowing continues to tick higher (7.76%, +4bps QoQ), delaying the RoA/ROE recovery the premium forward multiple demands and risking a sharp de-rating from an already near-52-week-low price.

Sundaram Finance is a conservatively run, promoter-family NBFC focused on vehicle finance. It is known for top-tier asset quality, and it also owns stakes in a home-finance arm, an AMC and the Royal Sundaram general insurance JV. In the latest results, standalone Q2FY27 PAT rose 21% YoY to Rs 475 cr and consolidated H1FY27 PAT rose 20% to Rs 1,153 cr, helped by Q2 disbursements up 28% YoY and core AUM up 19% to Rs 65,992 cr. Gross Stage 3 assets improved to 1.84% from 2.03% and provision cover rose to 51% from 45%. Below the headline, though, the numbers are softer: Q2 profit from operations grew only 11%, implied consolidated Q2 PAT (about Rs 517 cr) was up only about 9% YoY because a Rs 66 cr motor third-party claims provision dragged on Royal Sundaram, and ROA eased to 2.86% from 3.06% in Q1. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the right yardstick for a lender: 3.5x book for a 16.75% ROE is a full price, at the 67th percentile among peers on P/B and the most expensive of its 10 credit peers on forward P/E (21.2x vs a 14.6x median), so I rate it fair-to-rich rather than cheap.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance is a conglomerate with four main businesses: oil refining and chemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (now listed separately as JPL), retail (RRVL) and new energy. Per the sector card it should be valued business by business (sum of the parts), not as a pure oil company. In Q2FY27 gross revenue was a record ₹362,268 cr, up 27.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹29,550 cr, up 33.8% YoY. Revenue growth has picked up from about -8.5% in FY26 to +24.5% in Q1 and +27.8% in Q2, and PAT margin improved from 6.8% in Q1 to 8.2%. However, much of this growth came from O2C, whose EBITDA rose 67.9% because fuel margins spiked on Middle East supply disruption. Retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%, and only Jio is growing steadily (revenue +11.4%, monthly ARPU ₹218.8). We have no sum-of-the-parts data, so as a fallback we used EV/EBITDA of 12.2x and trailing P/E of 21.7x. These look expensive next to the PSU energy peers (median 9.2x P/E, 6.1x EV/EBITDA), but those peers are policy-priced single businesses and not a fair yardstick for a conglomerate. With forward P/E at 18.0x, earnings estimates raised 15-21% over the last 30 days and the price near its 52-week low, we grade valuation fair, not expensive. The biggest risk is that record O2C margins are a temporary geopolitical windfall while retail and media are shrinking, at a time when ROE is only 9.1% and finance costs are up 24.2%.

Bharti Airtel is India's number-two telecom operator by revenue share and the premium player in a 2.5-player market, with added growth from Africa, home broadband, enterprise and Airtel Money. In Q2 FY27 mobile ARPU rose to ₹271 (+5.9% YoY, up from ₹257 in Q4 FY26), the customer base grew 11.1% to 692.6 mn, and the extracted Q2 figures show revenue up 16.7% YoY and PAT of ₹889 cr up 30.8% YoY at a 57.9% EBITDA margin. Those Q2 revenue and PAT figures (₹6,088 cr) are far below consolidated scale and do not match the Q4 FY26 (₹21,097 cr) or FY26 (₹2.11L cr) rows, so the table mixes reporting bases and the 'decelerating/contracting' trajectory signals are probably artefacts that I have discounted. On the sector card's EV/EBITDA yardstick, 10.5× sits inside the 9–12× India-mobile band, which makes it fair rather than cheap. Supporting factors are a forward P/E of 21.6× against 40.7× trailing (earnings growth expected), net debt/EBITDA of 1.18× with 7.9× interest coverage, ROCE of 22.7%, and a price at only 15% of the 52-week range, which gives a better entry point. Against that, FY EPS estimates have been trimmed slightly (-0.5% over 90 days) despite 32 of 34 analysts rating it a buy. The biggest risk is that the next tariff hike, which re-rating depends on, keeps slipping while ARPU growth runs at only about 6%.

State Bank of India is India's largest lender, with a ₹78.88 trillion balance sheet, best-in-two-decades asset quality (Gross NPA 1.39%, Net NPA 0.36%, PCR 74.4%) and strong capital (CET-1 13.34%). That profit is flattered by a one-time ₹7,288 cr gain from selling part of the SBI Funds Management stake (versus a ₹4,593 cr Yes Bank gain a year ago), while non-interest income fell 4.9% and whole-bank NIM slipped to 2.94% from 3.03% in Q4FY26, so core earnings growth is closer to moderate. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, the stock looks fair: P/B of 1.53× (P57 among 15 regional-bank peers, in line with the 1.5× median) against a TTM ROE of 15.5%, trailing P/E of 10.8× and forward P/E of 9.6×, sitting mid-range at 45% of its 52-week band. The main risk is funding: loans are growing 17.8% but deposits only 12.3%, and CASA has fallen to 38.3% from 39.5%, which could keep pressure on margins. Management's mention of an expected RBI rate hike also conflicts with the easing-cycle backdrop and adds rate uncertainty.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Unilever is India's largest FMCG company, with leading brands across home care, personal care and foods. Revenue growth sped up from +10.1% YoY in Q1FY27 to +14.5% in Q2FY27 (₹18,226 cr). Profit did not follow: PAT was flat at ₹2,790 cr (+0.3% YoY, after -3.2% in Q1), so PAT margin shrank from 17.5% a year ago to 15.3%. We also have no volume-growth figure for Q2; the last reported figure was 6% for Q4FY26, so we can't tell how much of the 14.5% is real demand and how much is price or mix. On P/E, the standard yardstick for FMCG, the stock trades at 46.6x trailing and 39.4x forward, inside the 40-60x sector range and only slightly above the peer median of 43.8x (P60 in its sector; P80 on forward P/E and EV/EBITDA), so we grade it fair. Being near its 52-week low gives some comfort on entry price, but it is not a bargain. The biggest risk is that sales keep growing while profit stays flat, which suggests input costs or extra spending are eating the gains.

Maruti Suzuki is India's largest passenger-car maker and, per its own October filing, the country's top EV exporter. The fundamentals data is unreliable: the 1H FY26 row, the guidance and the sector KPIs (JPY figures, motorcycles, marine) belong to parent Suzuki Motor Corporation, not Maruti, and the Q2FY27 quarterly row is blank. The one row that looks like Maruti, H1FY27, shows revenue of ₹100,575 cr (+31.0% YoY) but PAT of ₹5,767 cr (-18.3% YoY), with PAT margin down to 5.7%, so growth is not reaching profit. On valuation, a trailing P/E of 27.6x and EV/EBITDA of 18.3x sit at the peer median (P60 and P50) and inside the 18-30x OEM band from the sector card, which grades as fair; the stock trades at 19.5% of its 52-week range and analysts have cut next-year estimates by 7.5% in 30 days and 8.4% in 90 days. The biggest risk is that the market prices further profit downgrades while 35 of 40 analysts still rate it buy, and the clean quarterly figures needed to confirm or reject this are missing.

fundamental.thesis: ONGC is India's largest oil and gas producer, a government-controlled upstream company whose profits rise and fall with crude prices and government policy on windfall taxes and subsidy sharing. The extracted trend table stops at FY26, when revenue fell 3.9% to ₹132,508 cr and PAT fell 7.6% to ₹32,894 cr, after revenue declines of 6-9% in earlier periods; the 5 Nov Q2 FY27 filing headline reports Q2 net profit of ₹15,489 cr and a record H1 profit of ₹32,522 cr, but that period has not been extracted or checked, so Q2 growth cannot be confirmed on a like-for-like basis. Using the sector card's yardstick of P/E plus dividend yield and EV/EBITDA, ONGC trades at 8.0x trailing earnings and 4.6x EV/EBITDA against peer medians of 9.2x and 6.1x, with the cheapest forward P/E in the sector (6.1x); that sits inside the 6-10x band the market applies to all PSU energy names, so I grade it policy-priced (fair) rather than cheap, though rising FY EPS estimates (+5.2% over 30 days) and strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT about 2x) are supportive. The biggest risk is that elevated crude near $86 brings back windfall taxes or subsidy-sharing demands, which would cap realisations while production volumes stay flat to declining.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Finserv is a financial holding company that owns 51.3% of Bajaj Finance (consumer and retail lending) along with life and general insurance, housing finance and an AMC, so its value comes mostly from Bajaj Finance. On a consolidated basis, H1 FY27 revenue grew +17.9% to ₹85,453 cr, against +11.8% in H1 FY26 and +19.2% in Q1 FY27, so growth is running firmly in the high teens. Bajaj Finance AUM grew 26.5% while gross NPA improved to 1.06% from 1.24%, and Bajaj Life VNB rose 53%. The reported PAT margin jump from about 6.5% to 14.3% does not reconcile with prior periods: ₹12,249 cr appears to include minority interest, while the ₹5,033 cr H1 FY26 base looks owner-attributable. Treat that apparent margin expansion as a likely basis artifact, not a real gain. Using the card's P/B-vs-ROE yardstick for a holding company, P/B of 3.53x against ROE of 14.6% sits at P73 among Financials peers, with trailing P/E at 28.2x versus a 17.5x sector median. The lower forward P/E of 18.7x and a price at about 21% of the 52-week range make this fair rather than expensive, though the NAV discount was not available to confirm it. The main drags are Bajaj General Insurance, whose combined ratio of 104.7% means an underwriting loss and whose PAT fell 24%, and the ₹5,800 cr of capital Finserv is committing to Bajaj Finance warrants, alongside mild downward estimate revisions of about -3% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: POWERGRID is India's dominant regulated power-transmission utility: it earns a regulated return of about 15.5% on the assets it has commissioned, so its earnings follow how fast it builds and commissions capex rather than power prices. Growth is slow but steady. H1 FY27 revenue rose 2.8% YoY to ₹23,313 cr and PAT rose 3.7% to ₹7,465 cr. Backing out Q1 (₹11,497 cr revenue, ₹3,598 cr PAT, PAT down 0.9%) gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹11,816 cr (roughly +3% YoY) and PAT of about ₹3,867 cr (32.7% margin). So the quarter improved a little, but the trend is flat in the low single digits and the pre-computed 'accelerating/contracting' signals mix half-year and full-year periods, so I set them aside. Valuation is fair on the yardsticks that fit a regulated utility. Trailing P/E is 14.2x, inside the 10–18x utilities range. EV/EBITDA is 10.7x, 7% below the peer median (P25). P/B is 2.64x against an annualised ROE of about 14–16.5%, and the dividend yield is about 4.3% (the snapshot's '430%' is a units error). That is a slight discount to peers, not a mispricing. The main risks are slow earnings growth combined with high debt (₹1.51L cr borrowings, D/E about 1.42), H1 free cash flow slightly negative (₹-245 cr) on ₹18,913 cr of capex, and sell-side EPS estimates cut 2.4–3.4% over the last 90 days even though most analysts still rate it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: JSW Infrastructure runs ports with about 186 MTPA of capacity, targeting 400 MTPA by 2030, and is building a fast-growing rail and logistics arm. PAT fell 11.1% YoY to ₹328 cr, a deeper drop than Q1's -8.2%, as finance costs rose about 125% and the PAT margin shrank from about 29-31% in FY26 to 22.1%; cargo volume growth was only 4% for H1, while logistics revenue grew about 71%. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy port business, the stock trades at 25.6x, around P58 of the peer set, and its 42.2x trailing P/E sits inside the 28-45x Industrials band, so it is fairly valued. Forward P/E of 27x already assumes a strong earnings rebound, while consensus estimates are being trimmed slightly (-0.4% for FY, -1.8% for next FY). The main risk is that heavy capex and acquisitions keep pushing up interest costs and free cash flow stays negative (₹-384 cr in H1), so earnings per share keep falling, made worse by dilution from the ₹6,555 cr QIP.

fundamental.thesis: PTC Industries is a specialty investment-casting manufacturer supplying precision components to aerospace, defence, and energy sectors, having scaled consolidated revenue from ₹308cr (FY25) to ₹603cr (FY26, +95.7% YoY) on India's defence indigenisation and PLI tailwinds. Q1FY27 marks a sharp trend break: revenue declined to ₹71cr vs ₹97cr in Q1FY26 (approximately -27% YoY, reversing from +107% a year prior), PAT collapsed to ₹2cr at a 2.7% margin (vs 5.3% in Q1FY26), and the business has generated chronically negative FCF in every measured period (FY26 FCF -₹386cr, CFO/PAT -0.68×), confirming earnings are not cash-backed — EBITDA margin has also contracted sequentially from 35.2% (FY25) to 25.2% (FY26) to 18.9% (Q1FY26). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial, PTCIL trades at 203× EV/EBITDA (sector median 28–45×) and 259× trailing P/E, ranking at P100 (most expensive) among 473 market peers, while a P/B of 18.4× against a 7% ROE and Debt/Equity of 17.34× signals extreme valuation risk with no earnings support. Sustained EPS estimate cuts (-13.1% over 90 days, -14.6% on next-FY) while sell-side ratings stay uniformly bullish is a textbook pre-derating pattern, and any further slip in the defence order pipeline or margin recovery could catalyse a 30–50% de-rating — the historical norm for industrial cycle disappointments.

fundamental.thesis: FACT is a PSU fertilizer producer (primarily complex fertilizers under the FACTAMFOS brand) operating as a near-monopoly in Kerala/South India, heavily dependent on government subsidy disbursements and imported raw materials — a price-taker in both inputs and outputs. Revenue recovered sharply to ₹1,484 cr in Q1 FY27 (+41.9% YoY, accelerating from the -24.9% trough of 9M FY2025), but this top-line bounce has not translated into operating profits: the fertilizer segment PBIT margin sits at -1.86%, the Q1 FY27 operating loss before finance costs was ₹36.51 cr, and the headline PAT of ₹3 cr (0.21% margin) is a statistical artefact of non-operating income rather than genuine operational recovery — full-year FY26 PAT was -₹40 cr. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per the sector card), FACT trades at 120.63× vs a fertilizer/chemicals cyclical mid-cycle norm of 5–8×, ranks P99 among 403 broad-market peers, and carries a P/B of 36.81× on a near-zero ROE — this is unambiguously expensive; the ₹50,886 cr market cap is disconnected from any demonstrated earnings power. The single largest risk is the compounding of a post-Q1 raw-material supply shock (West Asia geopolitical disruptions already causing plant shutdowns) on top of extreme financial leverage (D/E 295×) where quarterly finance costs of ₹61.98 cr structurally exceed operating income, leaving zero buffer for further stress.

fundamental.thesis: India Cements is a mid-sized South India cement maker with 14.75 MT of capacity (Q1FY26). It is now controlled by UltraTech, so the story depends on a turnaround under new ownership rather than on stand-alone strength. The latest extracted figures are stale: they run only to 9MFY26 (filed Jan-2026), and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-17 have not been indexed yet. In those older numbers, cumulative revenue growth picked up from -0.2% YoY in Q1FY26 to +4.8% in H1FY26 and +10.9% in 9MFY26 (₹3,256 cr). The company was still losing money, though the loss margin narrowed from -13.0% to -3.9% (9M PAT ₹-127 cr), while EBITDA margin slipped from 9.4% (H1) to 7.5% (9M), so the fall in costs per rupee of sales has not held. Because cement is capital-intensive, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 25.9× it sits well above normal cement multiples and above the broad-market median of 23.3×, and the 116× trailing P/E reflects barely positive earnings. The 1.06× P/B and the price near its 52-week low look cheap only on the surface. The 20.6× forward P/E already assumes a turnaround, while analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by about 21% in the last 30 days. Grade: expensive. The biggest risk is that EBITDA per tonne keeps lagging the healthy ₹900–1,100 band. Rising crude-linked fuel and freight costs and a risk-off market make that more likely, and the turnaround that today's price assumes would then be pushed back.

fundamental.thesis: Nuvoco Vistas is an East- and North-focused cement and ready-mix concrete (RMC) maker with about 35 MTPA of target capacity. It is a mid-tier player in a sector where UltraTech and Adani now control about 45% of capacity. Using the filings trend table (the yfinance rows are inconsistent and were ignored), Q2FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹2,790 cr, up from +9.0% in Q1, and cement volumes grew 9% YoY against 5% in Q1. Profit quality is thinner than the headline suggests. PAT rose 78% YoY, but only to ₹65 cr, a 2.3% margin. EBITDA margin fell to 14.7% from 18.3% in Q1 and 15.1% a year ago. Implied EBITDA per tonne is about ₹875, below the healthy ₹900–1,100 band and down from roughly ₹1,080 in Q1. Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cement maker, not P/E. At 8.6x (P8 of the broad market, no close peers in the universe), with P/B of 1.09x, forward P/E of 20.5x against trailing 31x, and the price at 18% of its 52-week range, the stock looks cheap against typical cement multiples. Much of that discount is justified by an ROE of only 3.7% and high debt. The biggest risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is ₹5,028 cr, current ratio is 0.57x, free cash flow was -₹246 cr in H1 because of capex, and legal disputes are pending: the ₹490 cr CCI penalty and about ₹454 cr of West Bengal incentive provisions. fundamental.thesis: JK Tyre is one of India's largest tyre makers, with 11 plants (9 in India, 2 in Mexico), about 38 million units a year of capacity, and a strong truck/bus and OEM franchise. In Q2FY27 consolidated revenue hit a record ₹4,841 cr, up 20.7% YoY (a rebound from -6.6% in Q1), helped by 32% domestic sales growth and 65% OE growth after GST 2.0. Profits have not kept up. EBITDA margin has roughly halved, from 13.3% in Q2FY26 to 7.1%, Q1 PAT fell 75% YoY to ₹44 cr (1.1% margin), and Q2 free cash flow was -₹447 cr. On the usual EV/EBITDA yardstick for a capital-intensive auto ancillary, the stock looks cheap at 7.7x EV/EBITDA and 14.6x trailing P/E against an Auto sector range of 18–28x (P6–P14 vs the market). However, those trailing multiples still include the high-margin quarters, analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 57% over 90 days, and annualised current-run-rate PAT would put the stock well above sector P/E, so we grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is further margin squeeze: about 70% of raw materials are petro-based, crude is above $102, debt is meaningful and cash flow is negative, so volume growth may not turn into earnings.

fundamental.thesis: CCL Products is one of the world's largest private-label instant coffee makers, with plants in India and Vietnam (Ngon Coffee, which earned ₹53 cr PAT in Q2 alone), plus a small but growing branded domestic business; it trades as FMCG but is mostly a B2B coffee processor exposed to green-coffee price swings. Q1FY27 revenue surged +52% YoY to ₹1,394 cr driven by capacity additions, but PAT fell 1.2% to ₹225 cr as PAT margin compressed severely from 24.8% to 16.1% — a pattern that has deteriorated every quarter for six periods, with EBITDA margin also contracting from ~88% to 66%, reflecting rising interest burden on a highly leveraged balance sheet (D/E 2.25×, DSCR 0.60 — a 40% shortfall in debt servicing). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive regulated utility, at 15.88× SJVN sits within the regulated-utility peer range and at P28 vs broad market, while P/B at 1.86× (P16 vs peers) and forward P/E at 14× (P22 vs peers, deep discount to trailing 38×) reflect market pricing in earnings recovery — grading overall as fair, but the 52-week position at 12.8% of range and ongoing sell-side EPS cuts of -13.3% over 30 days caution against treating the cheapness as a catalyst. The DSCR of 0.60 combined with a current ratio of 0.54 means near-term liquidity is structurally stressed, and the NJHPS tariff determination pending since April 2024 (₹3,200+ cr billed provisionally under an expired 2019 tariff) creates a binary earnings event with no resolution timeline visible.

Bajaj Holdings is a near-debt-free holding company: its earnings come from dividends, interest and its share of profits from its large stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv, so revenue (₹576 cr in H1FY27) is a small figure next to profit. Reported H1FY27 PAT fell 6.7% YoY to ₹4,845 cr and revenue fell 20.1%, but that is mainly because last year included a one-off ₹1,522 cr gain from selling Bajaj Finserv shares. Without that gain, PAT rose about 37%, and the share of associate profits grew 32% to ₹4,626 cr, helped by Bajaj Auto Q2 PAT up 62% and Bajaj Finserv up 23%. Reported growth has slowed sharply, from +65.6% to -6.7% half-year on half-year, but the underlying associate engine is accelerating. Using the holding-company yardstick (discount to NAV, not P/E or EV/EBITDA, which mean little here), the stock trades at about a 52% discount to the reported NAV of ₹21,578 per share (estimated price around ₹10,300). That sits in the middle of the usual 40–60% holdco discount band, and peer P/E of 11.4x (P33) and P/B of 1.5x with ROE of 12.6% back a 'fair' grade, with the stock in the lower third of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is concentration: value depends almost entirely on Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv share prices, and the holdco discount may not narrow, so this is a leveraged-looking proxy on two group stocks rather than an independent earnings story.

fundamental.thesis: Vedanta is a diversified natural-resources producer (aluminium, zinc, oil & gas, iron ore, power) that sells at global commodity prices, so it is judged on its cost position and balance sheet. Its continuing operations shrank after the demerger: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹59,872 cr, down 22.9% YoY, and Q2 revenue fell to ₹26,356 cr from ₹33,515 cr in Q1. Profit is improving even though sales are shrinking: H1 PAT rose 83% YoY to ₹9,123 cr, but Q2 PAT of ₹3,650 cr was below Q1's ₹5,473 cr, with PAT margin slipping from 16.4% to 13.8%. Prior periods were restated for the demerger, so the YoY comparisons are not clean. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, as the sector card advises for commodity names, the stock is cheap: 5.71x is the lowest of 16 Materials peers (sector median 17.9x) and at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle band. Forward P/E of 12.7x vs trailing 17.75x, and analysts raising FY EPS estimates by 25% over 90 days, point the same way. fundamental.thesis: Carborundum Universal is a mid-cap maker of abrasives, industrial ceramics and electrominerals, with a large standalone India business and overseas subsidiaries in Russia, Germany and South Africa. Revenue growth has picked up from about +2-4% YoY through FY26 to +17.0% in Q1FY27 and +13.1% in Q2FY27 (₹1,455 cr), and standalone revenue grew 28% on Ceramics (+36%). Reported Q2 PAT, however, fell 83% to ₹12 cr (0.9% margin) because of an ₹80 cr charge for closing the German subsidiary CAAG. Before exceptional items, profit (PBEBT) rose 22% to ₹138 cr, but Abrasives grew only 4% and Electrominerals profit fell 21%. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for this capital-intensive Industrials name, the stock trades at 34.5x (P72 vs the broad market), and forward P/E is 40x (P82). The headline 115x P/E is inflated by the one-off charge. Against a 4.4% ROE and P/B of 5.8x, and with the price at 86% of its 52-week range, valuation looks expensive. Sell-side (4 sell, 2 hold) puts its mean target at roughly today's price. The biggest risk is the international subsidiaries: VAW in Russia is now on the US OFAC sanctions list, FZL in South Africa is being accounted for as not a going concern, and CAAG is winding down. Together they could bring more write-downs and keep weighing on reported earnings.

Solar Industries makes commercial explosives for coal miners such as CIL and SCCL, and it is now growing fast as a defence ammunition and energetics supplier. It sits under the Materials label, but it is really an explosives and defence business, so steel and chemical multiples do not apply. In the half-year to September 2026 (HY27, from the official filing), revenue grew +69.7% YoY to ₹7,187 cr and PAT grew +84.3% to ₹1,316 cr. That is faster than FY26 (+30.0% revenue) and Q3FY26 (+29.0%), and defence revenue more than doubled (+109% to ₹1,935 cr). EBITDA margin widened about 140 bps to 28.4%, so the pre-computed 'contracting' margin flag looks like a period-ordering artefact. The ₹20,178 cr order book (87% defence) covers roughly 2 years of revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business. At 65.8x EV/EBITDA, 101.7x trailing P/E and 32x P/B, the stock is at P93–P99 versus the broad market, well above the 12–22x Materials range and rich even for a defence name. The forward P/E of 63x and estimate upgrades (+11% FY-EPS over 90 days) show strong growth is already priced in, and the price is at 97% of its 52-week range. So: expensive. The biggest risk is that the defence order flow is lumpy and largely export-driven, so any slip in orders or execution would hit a stock priced for perfection.

fundamental.thesis: Balrampur Chini Mills is one of India's largest integrated sugar makers, with 80,000 TCD of cane crushing, 1,050 KLPD of distillery capacity and 175.7 MW of saleable co-generation, and it is building an 80,000 TPA PLA bioplastics plant. It is really a commodity agri-processor rather than a branded FMCG company, so the FMCG sector card's 40-60x P/E norms do not fit it. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 12.3% YoY to ₹1,876 cr and PAT rose 81.6% to ₹104 cr (PAT margin 5.5%), recovering from a weak Q1FY27 (+6.1% revenue, PAT -14.4%). Still, revenue growth has slowed from +18-22% a year ago to +9.3% for H1FY27, and EBITDA margin has fallen from 13.9% in Q3FY26 to 9.1% in Q2FY27. Because the business is capital-intensive, I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA: 25.0x is high for a sugar/ethanol business and sits only around the broad-market median (P56), while the trailing P/E of 38x is P55. The forward P/E of 18.5x and rising sell-side estimates (+12.7% over 90 days) already assume strong earnings growth, so on balance I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the large PLA capex (FY26 FCF of -₹349 cr) and continued margin compression fail to deliver the earnings growth the forward multiple already prices in.

fundamental.thesis: Sun Pharma is India's largest pharma company by revenue. Its earnings come from leadership in Indian branded formulations, where market share rose 0.3pp to 8.6% and formulations sales grew 16.6% in H1, and from a growing global innovative-medicines (specialty) business that is now about 21.5% of sales. H1FY27 revenue grew 11.0% YoY to ₹31,499 cr, and Q2 (₹16,315 cr, worked out as H1 minus Q1) grew 11.8%, a little faster than Q1's 10.1%. The bigger trend is slowing: growth was +15.1% in 9MFY26, and EBITDA margin has slipped from 31.9% to about 29%. Implied Q2 reported PAT of about ₹1,988 cr gives only a 12.2% margin after large Organon-acquisition and US pricing-settlement charges, and US formulations fell 8.2% in Q2 as Lenalidomide sales eroded. On the yardstick that suits a branded/specialty pharma, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E is 37.4x, inside the 28–40x sector band and at P54 among peers. Forward P/E of 27.7x (P62) and EV/EBITDA of 24.2x (13% above the peer median) leave no room for a re-rating. The biggest risk is integrating the USD 14bn Organon deal. It is several times Sun's ~₹17.7k cr net cash, so the clean balance sheet will likely take on debt, and more deal costs are flagged for coming quarters. Meanwhile sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 2.9–3.4% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: NTPC is India's largest power generator. Most of its earnings come from a regulated return (about 15.5% ROE) on the plants it has commissioned, with a fast-growing solar and renewables arm on top. H1 FY27 headline revenue was ₹100,262 cr, up 19.9% from ₹83,660 cr a year ago, but the company's core capacity-plus-energy billing grew a more modest 9.65%. Within that, capacity charges rose 6.7% to ₹35,909 cr, energy charges rose 11.6% to ₹55,845 cr and solar revenue rose 64.9% to ₹2,456 cr. Revenue growth has turned up from about -1.5% to -3% in FY26 to +7.0% in Q1 FY27 (PAT ₹6,896 cr, +12.9%, 13.6% margin), though H1 PAT was not extracted. For a capital-intensive utility I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, backed by P/B with ROE. On that basis it looks cheap against peers: EV/EBITDA is 8.4x against a peer median of 11.6x (cheapest in the peer group) and trailing P/E is 11.9x against 14.7x. P/B is 1.7x with ROE of 13.7%. It is only fair against the static 10–18x utilities P/E band. The forward P/E (12.8x) is above the trailing P/E, and this year's EPS estimates were trimmed 0.9% in the last 30 days, so near-term earnings look roughly flat. The main risk is earnings quality: CERC 2024 tariff orders are still pending, so bills are provisional and later adjusted (₹2,825 cr energy adjustment in H1), and large regulatory-deferral and deferred-tax swings make reported PAT hard to compare across periods.

fundamental.thesis: Nestle India is a leading packaged-food company (MAGGI, NESCAFE, KITKAT, infant nutrition) with deep rural and urban distribution and a premium brand franchise. Growth is slowing slightly from Q1FY27, when revenue grew 25.4% and PAT 47.9%. EBITDA margin dipped slightly to 23.8% from 24.2%, and ad spend rose 46%, so margins are not being protected by cutting brand investment. On the P/E yardstick for FMCG staples, trailing P/E of 77x sits above the sector norm of 40-65x and above the peer median of 51.5x (P83), and forward P/E of 59x is the most expensive in the sector (P100), so the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is a valuation de-rating: the current 11% volume growth is far above the company's 5-year volume CAGR of 4.2%, and the price assumes it lasts while cocoa and milk costs keep pressing on margins.

fundamental.thesis: Coal India is the state-controlled near-monopoly coal miner that supplies most of India's thermal power fuel, and it earns a steady return from domestic volumes, e-auction premiums and a high dividend payout. In H1 FY27 revenue rose +13.8% YoY to ₹90,434 cr and PAT rose +18.9% to ₹15,397 cr (PAT margin 17.0%), recovering from a weak FY26 (revenue -0.5%, PAT -12.3%). The quality of that growth is mixed: offtake rose +7.6% to 384.2 MT while production fell -2% to 321 MT, so part of the growth came from selling down inventory, which fell 49% to 130.3 MT. Cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 2.21x, FCF ₹26,270 cr). I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/E and yield, as the sector card prescribes for PSU energy names. At 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 9.2x trailing P/E the stock sits exactly at the Energy peer median (P50) and inside the 6–10x policy-priced band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is at 85% of its 52-week range and EPS estimates are drifting slightly lower (-0.9% over 30d), which limits upside. The main risk is that volume growth cannot continue once the inventory buffer is used up while production is still falling, and administered pricing caps any offset from price.

fundamental.thesis: DLF is NCR's leading luxury housing developer, and it also earns rental income through its DCCDL office and retail arm, which brings in about ₹6,800 cr a year. The 'expanding margin' signal mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so I don't treat it as a real trend; the stronger evidence is cash from operations at 1.43x PAT and a net cash balance of ₹9,300–15,000 cr (the filings disagree) even after a ₹1,980 cr dividend. For valuation I used the sector yardstick (pre-sales, net cash and the rental annuity) instead of P/E or EV/EBITDA, since both are distorted by the revenue lag; at a ₹1.4L cr market cap, P/B of 3.2x with 10% ROE, and the stock at 23.5% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair. fundamental.thesis: Lodha (Macrotech) is one of India's largest residential developers, mainly in Mumbai (MMR) and Pune, and is expanding into Bangalore and rental income (annuity assets and data centres). Its reported numbers look strong: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹9,464 cr (+29.8% YoY) and PAT was ₹2,387 cr (+62.9%), with PAT margin up to about 25% from 20% in FY26. But revenue growth slowed from +43% in Q1 to roughly +30% for the half, and in this sector reported profit reflects sales booked 2–4 years ago. The forward-looking numbers are weaker: pre-sales were ₹96.7bn, up only 7% YoY, and collections fell 7%. Hitting the ₹240bn FY27 pre-sales guidance means H2 must deliver about ₹143bn, roughly 1.5x H1, which depends heavily on launching a ₹190.7bn H2 pipeline on time. On valuation I used the sector yardstick, EV/pre-sales, rather than P/E: an enterprise value of about ₹95k cr is roughly 4x guided FY27 pre-sales, or about 4.9x H1 annualised. P/B of 3.9x with ROE of 15.7% and a trailing P/E of 26.5x (inside the 20–35x real estate range and P34 vs the broad market) support a 'fair' grade. The stock sits at 29% of its 52-week range and earnings estimates are being raised, so the entry point is reasonable but not a bargain. The biggest risk is that slow pre-sales and falling collections signal the plateau typical of a late upcycle, and a shortfall against the back-ended guidance would hit the stock.

fundamental.thesis: Polycab is India's largest wires and cables maker, with about 30-31% share of the organised market. It is scaling a consumer electricals (FMEG) business and a smaller EPC arm, and has net cash of ₹4,520cr and an 11-day working-capital cycle. Revenue growth sped up from +39% YoY in Q1 FY27 to +53% in Q2 FY27 (₹9,900cr), and PAT rose 43% to ₹990cr. PAT margin edged up to 10.0% from 9.4% in FY26. FMEG grew 124% and posted its first double-digit EBIT margin (10.1%). Much of the headline growth is copper price pass-through, though: copper rose 40-45% in H1, while wire volumes grew only 10.5% and cable volumes about 5%. Underlying demand is healthy but well below the +53% headline. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, which suits this capital-intensive business. At 35.0x it sits close to the sector peer median of 34.0x (P53). Trailing P/E is 53.8x (P50) and forward P/E is 38.5x, which points to expected earnings growth. On the sector card's 50-80x range for electricals this is fair, not cheap, and the stock is at 99.8% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that copper-inflated revenue and record margins revert as commodity prices normalise or UltraTech's entry into wires squeezes pricing. That risk is larger because, in a risk-off market, a stock priced for perfection can lose 30-50% of its valuation multiple quickly.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC AMC is one of India's top-two mutual fund managers, with about 13% QAAUM market share, roughly ₹9.3 lakh cr of QAAUM and around ₹6 lakh cr in equity AUM. It runs an asset-light, debt-free model whose earnings move with equity AUM and SIP flows; its retail franchise is strong, with 16.7M unique investors and SIP/STP flows of about ₹4,880 cr a month, up 33% YoY. The latest quarter we have read is Q1 FY27: revenue rose 13.6% YoY to ₹1,100 cr and PAT rose 12.0% to ₹837 cr. That is a slowdown from FY26, when revenue grew +17.8% to ₹4,122 cr and PAT grew +16.2% to ₹2,858 cr. The 'accelerating' revenue signal in the trend table reads the series in the wrong order, and two of its rows (Q4FY26 ₹41 cr, 9MFY26) have broken units, so we ignored them. One important caveat: the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 have not been read, so all figures here are one quarter stale. We graded valuation on earnings multiples suited to an AMC, as the sector card says, not on P/B against lenders. On that basis it is fair: 35.5x trailing and 27.4x forward P/E for a debt-free business with ROA around 29% and a payout near 80%. The 'expensive vs peers' tag and P/B of 11x compare it with banks and NBFCs, which is the wrong peer set, and the snapshot's 222% dividend yield and 2.36 debt/equity are data errors for a debt-free AMC. The stock sits at 26% of its 52-week range, which is a reasonable entry point. Against that, sell-side EPS estimates are being cut steadily (-1.4% over 30 days, -2.0% over 90 days) even though 25 of 27 analysts rate it Buy, which points to a slower earnings path ahead.

fundamental.thesis: Max Financial Services is the listed holding company for Axis Max Life Insurance, a large private life insurer in which it owns 80.01%. Q2FY27 revenue rose 18.5% YoY to ₹11,601 cr, with premium income of ₹10,187 cr, while PAT of ₹100 cr jumped from a very low ₹5.91 cr base but fell from ₹118 cr in Q1, taking PAT margin from 1.6% to 0.9%; the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' signals are unreliable because they mix quarterly and 9-month periods, Q4FY26 and FY26 data are missing, and H1 revenue of ₹17,484 cr does not match Q1 plus Q2 (₹18,876 cr). The right yardstick for a life insurer is P/EV, but neither P/EV nor VNB margin or APE growth was provided, so the 'expensive' grade is provisional and rests on peer multiples: forward P/E of 102.3x vs a 46.0x median, P/B of 20.3x vs 6.8x, and EV/EBITDA of 69.1x vs 58.8x, with the 682.7x trailing P/E given little weight because accounting profit understates life insurer economics. The biggest risk is paying a top-of-peer-group price without evidence of new-business value growth, while the planned merger into Axis Max Life still needs IRDAI and shareholder approvals, and the peer table's labelling conflict and the consensus upside figure (+54.8% stated, about +14% implied by a price near ₹1,618) both need checking.

fundamental.thesis: Oracle Financial Services sells core banking and financial-crime software to banks worldwide, with products about 90% of FY26 revenue, a 44% operating margin and 10% attrition, though no deal-pipeline (TCV) data is available. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹5,032 cr (+38.2% YoY) and PAT ₹2,118 cr (+78.2% YoY) at a 42.1% margin, compared with FY26 growth of +12.0% in revenue and +11.0% in PAT at a 34.4% margin, but the pre-computed 'accelerating' and 'expanding' signals compare a half-year with full-year rows, one of them mis-scaled (₹767 cr vs ₹7,672 cr), and no Q1 or Q2 split or driver is available, so this may not be a lasting trend. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA against peers, valuation is expensive: trailing P/E is 33.4x vs a 26.9x peer median (P82), forward P/E is 26.3x vs 17.9x (P82) and EV/EBITDA is 23.7x vs 15.2x (P78), with the stock at 88% of its 52-week range, although the trailing P/E appears to use FY26 earnings and would be about 25x on my rough trailing-12-month PAT of ₹3,569 cr, so the premium is less clear-cut if H1 profits prove durable. The biggest risk is that H1 was lifted by lumpy or one-off items, which the mere +1.9% to +2.4% rise in estimates from two analysts could hint at, leaving little room for disappointment at this price.

IPCA Laboratories is a mid-sized Indian pharma maker with a chronic-therapy branded business at home (about 45% of revenue, ranked 16th in India) plus formulation and API exports through its Unichem subsidiary. Profit has risen faster than sales over the last six periods: H1 FY27 revenue grew 17.1% YoY to ₹5,698 cr and PAT jumped 50.7% to ₹814 cr, with EBITDA margin up 280 bps to 22.9%, ahead of the 22-22.3% FY27 guidance. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹2,910 cr (+14% YoY), slower than Q1's +20.8%, at a PAT margin of about 13.4%. Domestic formulations grew 13% and export formulations 33%. Using P/E with an EV/EBITDA cross-check, the stock looks fair: trailing P/E of 38x sits at the top of the 28-40x pharma range and at the 69th percentile of its peers, forward P/E is 28x and EV/EBITDA is 22.6x, about 6% above the peer median. With the price at 96% of its 52-week range and the average analyst target only about 5% above it, the earnings growth is mostly priced in.

fundamental.thesis: SRF is a diversified Indian chemicals and packaging-films maker; most of its profit comes from refrigerant gases and specialty chemicals for agrochemical and pharma clients. The SECTOR CARD places it in specialty chemicals, with the ref-gas cycle turning up. The latest quarter in the official trend table is Q1FY27, which showed revenue of ₹5,033 cr (+31.8% YoY) and PAT of ₹759 cr (+75.5% YoY), with EBITDA margin rising to 25.2% from about 18-20% through 9MFY26 and FY26 (FY26 revenue grew only +7.5%, so growth has re-accelerated sharply). However, the Q2FY27 results filed on 21 Oct are not yet in the extracted table, the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹2,600 cr looks inconsistent with that run-rate (likely standalone or partial), and the H1FY26 row appears mislabelled, so the newest quarter is unverified. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the card names for chemical cyclicals: 19.2x EV/EBITDA, 34.6x trailing P/E and 27.9x forward P/E sit well above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle EV/EBITDA and the 12-22x Materials P/E band, so it grades expensive. The 'cheap vs peers' verdict is not usable because the peer set is capital-goods names (ABB, CGPOWER, HAL) after a yfinance Industrials mis-tag; the stock sitting near its 52-week low (19% of range) only partly offsets this. The biggest risk is earnings quality and cycle dependence: H1 cash conversion was weak (CFO/PAT 0.63x, FCF -₹180 cr) during a heavy capex phase (₹974 cr in H1), with ₹165 cr of forex losses, so any cooling in refrigerant-gas pricing would hit a peak-margin earnings base.

fundamental.thesis: Deepak Nitrite is an integrated Indian chemicals maker with a leading position in phenol and acetone (Phenolics), plus an Advanced Intermediates (AI) business serving agrochemical and other customers. Quarterly revenue growth has accelerated from +3.0% in Q3 FY26 and -3.0% in Q4 to +36.4% in Q1 FY27 and about +62% in Q2, while H1 FY27 revenue was Rs 5,654 cr (+49.0%) and PAT Rs 743 cr (+222%); Q2 is derived as H1 minus Q1 (revenue about Rs 3,076 cr, PAT about Rs 398 cr, margin about 12.9% vs 13.4% in Q1), and the gain leans on Phenolics, with H1 EBIT of Rs 933 cr, while AI margin fell to 7% from 10%. Using EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for chemical cyclicals, I grade valuation fair: the 24.6x headline (+37% vs the 17.9x peer median, P67) and 41.6x trailing P/E appear to use FY26 earnings, and my rough trailing-12-month estimates are about 14x EV/EBITDA and 22x P/E, which is below the headline but still above the card's 5-8x mid-cycle range on what may be peak earnings, while the 27.6x forward P/E implies PAT of only about Rs 830 cr, so either that figure is stale or earnings are expected to fall despite upward EPS revisions (the snapshot's dividend yield and implied price also look unreliable). The biggest risk is that Phenolics spreads normalise, as management itself signals with its 'new normal' language, just as the long-dated polycarbonate project (FY27 capex plan Rs 2,500 cr vs FY26 FCF of Rs 348 cr, commercialisation targeted by end FY2030) adds debt without near-term earnings.

fundamental.thesis: United Breweries is India's largest beer maker, owning Kingfisher and selling Heineken, with growth increasingly led by premium brands. Revenue growth improved from +10.0% in Q1 FY27 to +23.7% in Q2 FY27 (₹4,623 cr), with volumes up 16% and premium volumes up 38%, while PAT rose 190.9% to ₹135 cr from a low base of about ₹46 cr after falling 9.6% in Q1; however, the 'accelerating' and 'expanding' trajectory signals are unreliable because they mix quarterly and full-year figures, and the 5.3% PAT margin appears to use net sales (about 2.9% on the listed gross revenue), against about 2.4% on the FY26 gross basis. Using the FMCG card's 40-65x P/E norm, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E of 84.0x is above the range and at P92 among peers, EV/EBITDA of 47.9x is at P83, and forward P/E of 46.3x is within the range but implies roughly 82% EPS growth, although the price near its 52-week low (2.6% of range) offers some sentiment support. The biggest risk is that this low-base rebound fades before earnings grow into the valuation, with next-year EPS estimates already cut 8.8% over 90 days and the ₹751.83 cr CCI penalty still before the Supreme Court; the 80% dividend yield and consensus upside figure appear to be data errors and were ignored, and the 29.08 debt/equity is likely a percentage (about 0.29x) but is unverified.

fundamental.thesis: Oberoi Realty is a Mumbai (MMR) ultra-luxury residential developer that is also building a rental income base (offices, malls and hotels), and it runs a very clean balance sheet: debt/equity is 0.14x, interest coverage is 13.6x and net debt is only ₹830 cr. H1FY27 revenue rose 7.4% YoY to ₹2,972 cr and PAT rose 10.4% to ₹1,305 cr. However, Q1 alone was +31.7% (₹1,301 cr), so the implied Q2 revenue of about ₹1,671 cr is roughly 6% below last year, and implied Q2 PAT of about ₹761 cr is flat. The headline 'accelerating' signal therefore hides a slowdown in Q2, although this is normal for a developer that recognises revenue only when projects are handed over. Following the sector card, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/B rather than P/E: EV/EBITDA is 17.6x (about 25% below the broad-market median) and P/B is 3.5x for a 42% PAT-margin business, with the stock mid-way in its 52-week range, which I grade as fair. Conviction is held back because the key forward metrics (pre-sales/bookings, collections and the launch pipeline) are missing from the data provided. I also ignored two obvious data errors: the 45% dividend yield and the 15.77 debt/equity figure.

fundamental.thesis: Aditya Birla Capital is a diversified financial-services holding company with an NBFC, a housing finance arm, an AMC, life and health insurance, and a growing digital platform; lending AUM is ₹2.34 lakh cr, up 32% YoY. The Q1 FY27 row (₹316 cr revenue) looks like a standalone figure, so I am not reading the 'accelerating' signal as a real quarter-on-quarter pattern; the cleaner signals are NBFC PBT +41%, HFC PBT +73%, NBFC ROA up 25bps to 2.45%, Stage 2+3 assets improving 72bps YoY to 2.31%, and life VNB margin up 447bps to 16.1%. Because this is a lending-led holding company, I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, as the sector card says, and called it fair: P/B is 2.82× on a modest 11.2% TTM ROE, which is close to the 'expensive' line, but forward P/E of 15.1× (down from 26× trailing) shows earnings growth is expected and estimates were raised about 2.8% over 90 days. The stock sits at 96% of its 52-week range with all 14 analysts rated buy, so much of the good news looks priced in; the AMC is barely growing (QAAUM +4%) and health insurance is still losing money on underwriting (combined ratio 107%).

fundamental.thesis: Anand Rathi Wealth is a capital-light HNI/UHNWI wealth management distributor earning trail commissions and distribution fees on a growing AUM base — an asset-light model that structurally warrants premium P/E multiples over traditional lenders. H1FY27 revenue grew +17.4% YoY to ₹646 cr (decelerating from FY26's +22.3%), while PAT surged +26.4% YoY to ₹322 cr with PAT margin expanding sharply to 49.8% from 34.5% in FY26, suggesting strong operating leverage — though this margin step-up from ~34% to ~50% in a single half-year warrants scrutiny for one-off items and seasonal AUM tailwinds. The stock trades at a trailing P/E of 80.3× and P/B of 36.78× — at P88 and P100 respectively vs the broad 499-stock market — with sell-side mean targets implying −26.8% downside and zero buy recommendations from only 2 analysts, while the 52-week position at 95.1% of range signals the stock is priced for near-perfection; using EV/EBITDA of 56.3× as the primary yardstick (per sector card for capital-light/platform-adjacent names), this is unambiguously expensive versus any reasonable comparable. The single largest risk is valuation derating from extreme multiples if AUM growth decelerates or equity markets correct, compounded by recent promoter pledge disclosures (SAST Reg 31 filings on Oct 16) which are a governance flag for a MIDCAP, thin sell-side coverage, below-1.0 CFO/PAT ratio (0.71×), and a high reported D/E of 8.25 whose nature warrants clarification.

fundamental.thesis: BSE is India's oldest stock exchange and a capital-markets infrastructure monopoly, earning revenues through transaction charges, listing fees, clearing/settlement, and investment income — it is not a traditional bank, so the relevant yardstick is P/E and EV/EBITDA (not P/B+ROE). Q1FY27 revenue grew +63.5% YoY to ₹1,566 cr and PAT grew +62.1% YoY to ₹873 cr at a 55.7% margin; while the absolute growth rate is still exceptional, the trajectory has decelerated from +116% in FY25, and PAT margins are broadly stable (55.7% vs 56.3% a year ago) rather than meaningfully expanding. At 48.1× trailing P/E (P68 vs broad peers) and EV/EBITDA of 28.4× (P63), the stock screens as fair against headline P/E metrics, but the forward P/E at 37.8× sits at P78 (expensive), P/B at 17.4× is at P94 (extremely elevated even for an asset-light exchange model), and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut sharply over the past 90 days (FY-EPS −6.6%, next-FY −9.8%) — a classic pre-derating signal that makes the 'fair' grade conditional on growth sustaining. The single biggest risk is that BSE's transaction-charge revenues are directly levered to equity market volumes and IPO activity, both of which face acute pressure from FII outflows of ₹44,000+ cr over 30 days, a RISK_OFF macro regime, and rising regulatory contribution costs (₹193 cr, +66% YoY), which could compress earnings faster than consensus currently models.

fundamental.thesis: CreditAccess Grameen is India's largest pure-play microfinance lender, with a gross loan book of about ₹29,294 cr that grew 21.5% YoY as of H1 FY27 and 2,276 branches lending mostly to rural women borrowers. Earnings are recovering sharply from last year's microfinance stress: Q2 FY27 PAT, derived as H1 ₹995 cr minus Q1 ₹493 cr, is about ₹502 cr on total income of about ₹1,904 cr. That is roughly 7-8x the year-ago quarter, but off a provisioning-hit base, so the +691% H1 PAT and +144% revenue figures overstate the underlying growth, and the revenue figure also mixes NII with total income across periods. Asset quality is the real story: GNPA improved from 4.04% (9M FY26) to 3.17% (FY26) to 2.18% (Q1 FY27), with collection efficiency at 97.4% and provision coverage holding around 65%. Using the sector card's P/B-vs-ROE yardstick for lenders, a P/B of 2.91x against a TTM ROE of 16.4% (annualised H1 ROE about 24%) looks fair rather than cheap. The low forward P/E of 11x simply reflects the earnings normalisation, and analysts have raised FY EPS estimates by 9.8% in the last 30 days. The main risks are a fresh stress cycle in unsecured rural lending, a borrower count that is shrinking (-2.4% YoY) even as loan size grows, and a risk-off macro backdrop for a leveraged midcap lender.

fundamental.thesis: Billionbrains Garage Ventures (Groww) runs one of India's largest retail investing platforms: broking, mutual-fund distribution, an AMC (State Street now holds 22.94% of the economic interest) and a fast-growing lending and margin-funding book. So it is best judged as a capital-markets platform on P/E against growth and P/B against ROE, not as a bank. H1FY27 revenue rose 56.2% YoY to ₹3,003 cr and PAT rose 71.8% to ₹1,460 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹1,502 cr (+47% YoY on a weak, -9.5% base) and PAT of about ₹725 cr (+54%), so growth slowed from +66% in Q1. The 'accelerating' signal relies on a Q4FY26 revenue row (₹147 cr) that doesn't fit the FY26 total, and H1 PAT includes a one-off ₹81 cr gain from the AMC stake sale. Valuation is expensive: trailing P/E is 59.2x against a broad-market median of 35.2x (P77) and P/B is 12.8x (P90), well above what a 28.7% ROE supports. The 32x forward P/E needs roughly 80% earnings growth, yet sell-side FY-EPS estimates were cut 5.4% in the last 30 days. Earnings are not converting to cash: H1 operating cash flow was -₹828 cr as the loan book grew 51% to ₹5,294 cr, debt/equity is 3.0x, and this is a high-beta stock in a RISK_OFF regime with heavy FII selling.

Using the sector-card mandated P/AUM-linked earnings yardstick, the stock trades at 51.33× trailing P/E and 35.11× EV/EBITDA (P74 vs broad market peers, +50% premium to median), with forward P/E of 36.77× implying priced-in earnings recovery — graded fair given the ROE-justified premium, but the stock at 83% of its 52-week range with consistently negative estimate revisions (FY-EPS cut –5.8% in 30d, next-FY cut –10.5% in 90d) provides very limited margin of safety. The biggest risk is a classic pre-derating setup: sell-side estimates being quietly cut while ratings remain bullish and the pending PMS acquisition from ICICI Securities adds regulatory and integration overhang.

In Q2FY27, reported total income rose only +2.8% YoY to ₹9,865 cr and PAT fell -39% to ₹2,205 cr (PAT margin 22.3% vs 62.8%), but that drop mostly reflects a ₹1,699 cr one-off NSDL stake-sale gain in Q2FY26. The underlying business is growing well: net interest income +29% to ₹4,228 cr, NIM up 40 bps YoY to 4.11%, advances +18%, deposits +17%, gross NPA down 53 bps to 2.12%, net NPA 0.17%, provision coverage 99.24% and capital adequacy 27.1%. The main risks are the NIM jump, which runs against the easing cycle, internally inconsistent prior-quarter figures (Q1 NIM shown as 2.5% while the 50 bps QoQ change implies ~3.6%), and uncertainty around the government divestment process flagged in the October 14 exchange clarification.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Energy Exchange runs India's dominant power exchange, an asset-light trading platform where most revenue (77-78%) comes from transaction fees. Real-Time Market volumes have grown from 20% of its electricity volumes in FY23 to 41% in H1 FY27. In Q2FY27 revenue rose +10.8% YoY to ₹203 cr and PAT rose +12.9% to ₹139 cr, a 68.5% PAT margin. Revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q1FY26 and +14.6% for FY26 to roughly 10-11% over the last three periods, though margins are steady to rising. Cash conversion is only moderate, with CFO/PAT of 0.73x in H1FY27 versus 0.88x in FY26. Because this is a fee-based exchange rather than a lender, I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA, not the bank P/B yardstick. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.3x is 37% below the broad-market median of 35.2x, EV/EBITDA of 14.2x is at P24, ROE is 39%, and the stock sits at about 9% of its 52-week range. Part of that discount is fair given the regulatory overhang, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 5.5% over 90 days, so the stock is not mispriced beyond doubt.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Overseas Bank is a mid-sized public sector lender with advances of about Rs 3.46 lakh crore, growing well above the roughly 16% FY26 sector credit growth in the sector card at +24.35% YoY. In Q2FY27, revenue growth decelerated from +23.3% to +13.2% YoY (Rs 10,428 cr), while PAT growth accelerated from +45.7% to +56.0% (Rs 1,912 cr), helped by NIM of 3.49% vs 3.35% in FY26, gross NPA of 1.19% vs 1.83% in H1FY26, and credit cost of 0.17%; the pre-computed 'accelerating' revenue signal is unreliable because it reads newest-to-oldest across mixed periods and FY26 revenue (Rs 17,900 cr) is below H1FY26 (Rs 18,084 cr). Using P/B plus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, valuation is fair: P/B of 1.63x sits just above the 1.5x cheap threshold despite 16.5% TTM ROE (the bank reports 24.58%), trailing P/E of 11.03x is not the basis for the grade, the 'cheap vs peers' rank is against the broad market rather than banks, and the 36.51x forward P/E conflicts with recent earnings and needs checking, though being 15.7% up the 52-week range offers a better entry point. The biggest risk is that profit growth depends on unusually low credit costs while loans grow rapidly, with non-interest income down 10.11% YoY, CRAR down to 18.60% from 19.36% in a quarter, and a CFO change effective 01.11.2026 adding a governance item to monitor.

fundamental.thesis: L&T Finance is a large retail-focused NBFC (₹1.32 lakh crore loan book) under the L&T Group umbrella, operating across rural/farm finance, two-wheelers, housing, and consumer lending segments with strong parentage and a well-capitalised balance sheet (CAR 18.67%). Revenue growth has sharply accelerated from +10.1% in H1FY26 to +24.4% in H1FY27, with PAT rising +31.6% YoY to ₹1,889 cr and PAT margins expanding from 16.5% to 17.6%; critically, the primary NBFC KPIs are moving in the right direction — Gross NPA has improved consistently from 3.19% to 2.75% over four periods, Net NPA from 0.96% to 0.85%, and ROA has risen to 2.39% from 2.27% in FY26, confirming this is not just revenue-led growth. Using P/B+ROE as the mandated NBFC yardstick (not P/E), LTF at 2.76× P/B with rising ROA ranks at P30 vs broad-market peers on both P/E and P/B (below sector median by 30–40%), and its trailing P/E of 24.57× sits within the 18–28× NBFC benchmark range while a forward P/E of 15.83× — a 36% discount to trailing — prices in strong near-term earnings growth, placing it at fair value with a modest cheap lean. The primary risk is that impairment provisions grew 15.6% YoY and credit cost remained elevated at 11.29% of total income, sell-side next-FY EPS estimates have been trimmed -3.2% over 30 days, and the highly leveraged balance sheet (D/E 393×) leaves LTF exposed to any funding-market stress or a slower-than-expected credit cost normalisation.

fundamental.thesis: One 97 Communications (Paytm) is a pre-scale digital payments and financial-services platform with net cash of Rs 12,714 cr, so we judge it on EV/sales, growth delivery and unit economics rather than lender P/B or trailing P/E. Q2 FY27, derived as H1 less Q1, shows revenue of about Rs 2,648 cr, up 28.5% YoY, with growth improving from +24.2% in Q2 FY26 to +27.6% in Q1 FY27; EBITDA margin rose from 8.3% to about 16.9% over the year, but PAT was nearly flat sequentially at about Rs 225 cr versus Rs 220 cr, and the 209% H1 PAT growth is flattered by a very low Rs 21 cr base in Q2 FY26. Valuation is fair but not cheap at about 6x EV/TTM sales (our calculation from market cap, net cash and filed revenue), mid-range in the 52-week band; the 128x trailing P/E and 112.9x EV/EBITDA look stale against about 79x annualised H1 PAT, while the 34.9x forward P/E already assumes about Rs 2,000 cr of PAT, roughly 2.25x the current run-rate. The biggest risk is that earnings fail to reach that level, especially as H1 free cash flow was only Rs 42 cr after Rs 434 cr of capex and cash fell Rs 790 cr, with FEMA and GST matters still unresolved.

fundamental.thesis: Pine Labs is India's leading merchant commerce platform operating ~2.17 million POS/DCP devices with embedded affordability finance, UPI infrastructure, and an expanding international footprint (UAE, Malaysia) — a high-growth fintech rather than a traditional lender despite its Financials sector tag. Q1 FY27 revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹737 cr (stable within the 18-24% band across the last four quarters, showing consistent rather than truly accelerating growth), while PAT surged ~4× to ₹20 cr from ₹5 cr YoY, but EBITDA margin contracted sharply from 23% in Q3 FY26 to 17.1% in Q1 FY27 as technology/cloud spend (+33% YoY to ₹64 cr) and international investments eroded profitability — the trajectory signal of 'EBITDA contracting' is the dominant margin read. Valuation is expensive on most yardsticks: trailing P/E of 147× sits at P98 vs peers and far above any sector benchmark (IT 22–30×, Financials 12–18×); EV/EBITDA of 25.7× is more moderate at P58, and forward P/E of 31.7× (P67) is reasonable IF the earnings ramp materialises, but ROE of only 2.4% with D/E of 7.47 makes the P/B of 2.9× difficult to defend — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card's platform guidance, 'fair-to-expensive' is the honest grade, leaning expensive given the ROE/leverage combination. The biggest near-term risk is that the effective tax rate of 48% (vs guided 28-30%) and persistent EBITDA margin compression prevent the PAT inflection on which the forward multiple entirely depends, exposing the stock — already at its 52-week low — to further de-rating.
