fundamental.thesis: Tata Investment Corporation is a Tata Group listed investment holding company (middle-layer NBFC by RBI classification), whose income is overwhelmingly driven by dividends from investee companies (75% of Q1 FY27 revenue) and realized/fair value gains on its equity portfolio — making it a market-beta proxy, not a lending or operating business. Q1 FY27 revenue grew modestly +4.3% YoY to ₹152 cr, while PAT declined marginally by -1.9% YoY to ₹143.51 cr (PAT margin 94.6%), with the drag coming from a 51.6% collapse in net fair value gains (₹21.96 cr vs ₹45.44 cr in Q1 FY26), a structurally volatile income line; the full-year FY26 picture was stronger (+38.9% PAT growth, +30.2% revenue), but that was driven by buoyant equity markets and realized gains, not earnings quality improvement. Using the appropriate holding-company yardstick (P/B vs NAV discount, per Sector Card) rather than P/E: at P/B of 1.07×, the stock trades at essentially zero NAV discount — yet historically listed holding companies command 40–60% NAV discounts, making this expensive by sector norms, despite appearing cheap at P4 on the broad-market P/B peer rank (which is misleading given operating companies dominate that peer set). The biggest risk is that 75% of income depends on Tata investee dividend decisions plus equity portfolio performance, with OCI swings of ±₹4,000–5,000 cr per quarter confirming that NAV — and thus the fundamental floor — is highly sensitive to a RISK_OFF equity drawdown, which the current macro regime directly exacerbates.

fundamental.thesis: Blue Dart Express is India's dominant integrated express logistics company and a DHL Group subsidiary, operating time-definite air and ground freight networks with significant pricing power in the premium segment. Q1FY27 showed a sharp positive inflection: revenue grew +15.0% YoY to ₹1,658 crore (accelerating from a flat +7% range across all FY26 quarters), while PAT surged 81.2% YoY to ₹88 crore with EBITDA margin expanding to 16.7% — the operating-leverage story is finally showing up in PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the preferred yardstick for capital-intensive logistics (EV/EBITDA is unavailable in the snapshot), the fallback trailing P/E of 40.4× sits within the Industrials sector range of 28–45× (fair), but forward P/E at 26.5× — below the 28× lower bound — implies the market is pricing in substantial earnings growth; the stock at 10.6% of its 52-week range (near ₹4,883 vs a 52-week high of ₹7,036) at a fair-to-cheap forward multiple presents a potentially asymmetric setup, though the falling-knife risk at this proximity to the low demands caution. The single biggest fundamental risk is that crude oil at $89.72 and rising directly compresses unit economics since freight and handling costs constitute 58% of revenues, and the 90-day EPS revision of -24.3% signals the sell side is already cutting numbers — a classic pre-derating pattern that could undermine the inflection narrative.

Apar Industries is a leading Indian maker of power-transmission conductors, specialty oils and cables, and it benefits directly from the grid-capex cycle. H1 FY27 revenue rose +25.0% YoY to ₹13,522 cr, and Q2 alone grew +21.3% to ₹6,931 cr. Revenue growth has held steady at +22% to +25% over the trend window. PAT jumped +77.7% to ₹915 cr, PAT margin widened from 4.8% to 6.8% and EBITDA margin from 9.2% to 11.8%. The conductor order book is a record ₹12,025 cr (+67% YoY) and Q2 order inflow rose +123%. Volume quality is weaker than the headline, though: conductor volumes fell 8% and oil volumes fell 17% in H1. So growth is coming mainly from higher prices (elevated metal and base-oil costs passed on) and a richer product mix, not more units sold. Valuation is expensive. Graded on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive names, it trades at 32.2x vs a peer median of 23.3x (P68). Trailing P/E is 59.2x, above the 28-45x Industrials band, at P77 on P/E and P90 on P/B. The stock sits at 90% of its 52-week range. The forward P/E of 46x and +21% upward revisions to FY EPS estimates offset this only partly. The biggest risk is earnings quality: H1 operating cash flow was -₹863 cr (CFO/PAT -0.94x) because of a ₹900+ cr inventory build and higher receivables, while US and export revenue are shrinking.

H1 FY27 revenue grew about 15% to Rs 7,935 cr (an alternate extraction shows Rs 7,541 cr), up from about 10-12% growth in FY26 and led by chemicals (+33.6%), but the reported PAT of Rs 799 cr (+193%) includes about Rs 474 cr of one-off tax gains, and PAT excluding them is about Rs 325 cr (about +19%), while derived Q2 PAT fell about 33% to about Rs 106 cr from Rs 159 cr and EBITDA margin compressed from 11.9% in Q2 FY26 to about 7-8%. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, 11.9x looks cheap against the broad-market median of 23.3x (P17), but that is a fallback peer set rather than true peers, and the 10.9x trailing P/E is flattered by one-offs (about 17x excluding them, within the 12-22x Materials range, which is the closest fit), while the 23.3x forward P/E sits at the median, so the overall grade is fair even with the stock near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that the weak Q2 marks continued margin erosion rather than a temporary dip, with sugar and ethanol at a 0.93% margin, Bioseed loss-making and rising crude adding pressure, although H1 cash generation is a real offset (CFO about Rs 986 cr, 1.23x PAT, FCF Rs 644 cr).

Cemindia Projects (formerly ITD Cementation, now promoted by the Adani Group) is a mid-sized EPC contractor in marine, urban infra, hydro and foundation work. Its order book hit a record ₹32,715 cr in Sep-2026, about 3x trailing revenue, up from ₹18,820 cr in Q1FY26, which gives over two years of work in hand. Revenue growth has picked up: from +5.6% YoY in Q1FY27 to +25.2% in Q2 (₹2,749 cr), and +14.6% for H1 (₹5,470 cr). Profit has not kept pace: Q2 PAT rose 21.3% to ₹131 cr, H1 PAT grew 10.8%, and EBITDA margin slipped from 11.1% to 10.2% YoY. Graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive contractor, the stock is fair: 19.9x versus a broad-market median of 23.3x, and trailing P/E of 34.3x sits inside the 28–45x Industrials range. The high P/B of 8.5x is backed by about 28% ROE. But the price is at 91% of its 52-week range, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 7.9% over 90 days, so the upside looks limited. The biggest worry is cash: H1 operating cash flow was negative (−₹78 cr; CFO/PAT −0.29x) because ₹474 cr got tied up in unbilled contract work. That means the faster growth is not yet turning into cash.

fundamental.thesis: Engineers India is a state-owned engineering consultancy and turnkey contractor for hydrocarbon, refinery and petrochemical projects, so its revenue comes from working through its order book. That makes revenue a clear deceleration story: Turnkey revenue collapsed 46.7%, while the higher-margin Consultancy segment grew 32.9%. That mix shift lifted H1 PAT 138% to ₹355 cr, PAT margin from 8.3% to 21.6% and EBITDA margin to 28.4%. Cash conversion was strong at 1.76x CFO/PAT. Using EV/EBITDA, the Industrials sector card's preferred measure for order-book businesses, the stock trades at 16.75x against a market median of 23.3x (P30), and trailing P/E is 20.6x against the 28–45x Industrials range, so it looks cheap. But it sits at 87% of its 52-week range, and next-FY earnings estimates were cut 8.1% over 90 days, which tempers the upside. The biggest risk is that the margin jump depends on mix (shrinking low-margin turnkey work) and possibly other income, and no order-inflow or order-book figure was given to show that revenue can grow again.

Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive shipbuilder, 29.34× sits within the 28–45× Industrials range but at P65 vs the broad market, rendering valuation fair; the forward P/E of 27.33× at a meaningful discount to trailing 34.84× confirms analysts expect continued EPS growth, while the P/B of 10.59× (P84 vs peers) signals the PSU defence franchise premium is already well-embedded at current prices. R R Kabel is a mid-sized wires and cables maker with a smaller, loss-making FMEG (fans, lights, appliances) arm. Wires and cables bring in about 91% of H1 revenue (₹5,890 cr, up 54.8%), so the company rides the same power, real-estate and data-centre demand as the bigger cable makers. Growth is strong: H1 FY27 revenue rose 52.8% to ₹6,452 cr and PAT rose 87.2% to ₹386 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,284 cr (+51.8% YoY) and PAT of about ₹181 cr (+56%). That is still faster than the +19.5% of a year ago, but the Q2 PAT margin slipped to about 5.5% from 6.5% in Q1, and EBITDA margin fell from 10.4% to roughly 9.2%. So profitability is rising year on year but has come off its Q1 peak. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick this sector card calls for, the stock trades at 32.0×, about 37% above the broad-market median (P67). Trailing P/E is 52.7× (P71) against a forward P/E of 34.0×. That multiple sits above the static 28–45× industrials P/E band, but the forward P/E and roughly 21% ROE give a fair, fully priced grade rather than a cheap one, especially with the stock at 94% of its 52-week range. There are no tight cable peers in the comparison set, so the peer rank is only broad-market context. The biggest weakness is cash: H1 operating cash flow was only 0.31× PAT and free cash flow was -₹159 cr. Capex of ₹280 cr in H1 pushed net debt from ₹147 cr to ₹455 cr and finance costs rose 87%. Real leverage is still modest at roughly 0.18× equity; the 13.09 debt/equity figure in the snapshot is most likely a percentage, not a multiple.

The implied Q2FY27 is about ₹1,191 cr revenue (+57% YoY vs ₹758 cr) and ₹270 cr PAT (+82%), and EBITDA margin rose to 33.7% from 28.6% a year ago, though cash conversion slipped to 0.89x CFO/PAT as receivables grew. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive chemicals business, the stock trades at 34.6× against 5–8× for mid-cycle chemical cyclicals, alongside 56× trailing P/E, 38.8× forward P/E and around P75–P79 across all four peer metrics; with the price at 93% of its 52-week range, it is expensive even after strong upward EPS revisions (+22.6% over 90 days). Hindustan Copper is India's only vertically integrated copper miner, a PSU with mines such as Malanjkhand, so its earnings depend on the global copper price. In Q1 FY27 revenue rose 81.4% YoY to ₹936 cr and PAT rose 162.5% to ₹352 cr, so growth sped up from +4.6% a year earlier, and PAT margin widened to 37.6% from 26.0% while EBITDA margin hit 56%. Cash conversion is less clean: FY26 free cash flow was ₹-182 cr and cash from operations was only 0.76x PAT. Because this is a commodity price-taker, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says to do. At 33.4x EV/EBITDA it trades far above the 5-8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals and about 43% above the broad-market median of 23.3x. P/B of 14.8x sits at P92, so the stock looks expensive and appears to price these strong earnings as permanent, even though the 25.6x forward P/E reflects estimates that were raised 10% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that a high-copper-price year is being valued like steady growth, and Q2 FY27 results come out tomorrow (2026-11-11), so the next data point could move the view either way.

For a cyclical miner I graded on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names: at 7.8x it sits at the top of the 5-8x mid-cycle range, so the stock is fair rather than cheap, even though trailing P/E of 10.5x is below the 12-22x Materials band and the broad-market peer rank (P6-P7) looks cheap, because that rank compares NMDC with all sectors, not with miners. The biggest threats are on the balance sheet: a possible ₹15,786 cr Karnataka mineral-tax liability (about 2x annual PAT) and roughly ₹11,000 cr of receivables from NMDC Steel and RINL. Q2FY27 results are due on 12-Nov-2026, which makes this view time-sensitive.

International sales grew 34.5% (Europe +34.6%, Rest of World +42.8%, Canada +24.3%), while India formulations grew about 10%, an average pace for the sector. On valuation I mainly used P/E against the pharma range and EV/EBITDA against the broad market: trailing P/E of 37.1x is near the top of the 28-40x pharma range, but forward P/E of 25.5x, EV/EBITDA of 20.3x (13% below the market median) and steadily rising analyst estimates (+9.7% over 90 days) make it fair, not cheap, with the price at 91% of its 52-week range, which leaves limited room for upside. But growth has slowed from the +27% to +29% seen in FY26, and margins have slipped: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1,213 cr (+17%) and PAT ₹172 cr (+19%), with EBITDA margin down from 34% in Q3 FY26 to 28% and PAT margin down from 18% to about 14%. For a capital-heavy contract manufacturer, EV/EBITDA is the main yardstick (cross-checked with P/E): it trades at 40.6x EV/EBITDA and 73.5x trailing P/E, roughly double the broad-market medians (P83–P92) and well above the 28–40x pharma P/E band, near the top of its 52-week range, so it is expensive even though forward P/E of 49x and rising FY earnings estimates (+8.5% in 30 days) show growth is expected. fundamental.thesis: IRCTC is the government-backed monopoly on Indian Railways' internet ticketing, catering, tourism, and packaged drinking water (Railneer), benefiting from structural exclusivity but exposed to policy risk and PSU governance constraints. At 30.1× trailing P/E (P41 vs 473 broad-market peers, -14% discount to median 35.2×, and only 10.2% above its 52-week low), headline valuation looks fair-to-cheap on P/E and at the median on EV/EBITDA (23.4×), but the forward P/E of 23× being priced in is contradicted by 90-day sell-side EPS estimate cuts of -14%, suggesting the market has not fully absorbed the margin deterioration — graded 'fair' with downside skew. The primary risk is a convergence of core ticketing saturation, material GST litigation (₹397+ cr debited in FY26 alone, plus a ₹50 cr anti-profiteering case pending at GSTAT since 2022), and sustained downward EPS revisions that carry a pre-derating pattern in a RISK_OFF macro regime.

The sector card has no diagnostics yardstick, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E. The stock is expensive: trailing P/E of 82.8x against a healthcare band of 28–40x, EV/EBITDA of 41.9x, the 83rd–94th percentile of the broad market on every multiple, and a price at 90% of its 52-week range. The consensus target is only about 8% above the price, so most of the strong delivery already looks priced in. The biggest risk is that this rich multiple depends on new hubs in Bengaluru, Kolkata and the North-East ramping up on time, while finance costs rose 46% YoY and Hyderabad still dominates revenue.

Q2 FY27 revenue rose 47.0% YoY to Rs 2,945 cr and PAT rose 68% to Rs 153 cr, with revenue growth picking up from +30.5% in Q3 FY26 to +36.3% in Q1 FY27 (although below the +55% to +65% of H1 FY26), but EBITDA margin fell from 16.8% to 14.0% in one quarter and PAT rose only 1.3% QoQ despite about 21% more revenue. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 23.5x only matches the median of a broad-market peer set rather than close auto-parts peers, and it looks full next to a 60.98x trailing P/E (P79, above the 18-28x auto benchmark), a 32.98x forward P/E and 8.53x P/B, so the valuation is expensive. The main risk is that this price needs a margin recovery while FY-EPS estimates have been cut 6.2%, FY26 FCF was Rs -667 cr and two more plants are being built, and confidence is limited by data problems: Q3 FY26 revenue of Rs 206 cr looks wrong (its PAT and margin imply about Rs 2,058 cr), the price implied by the sell-side target conflicts with the 94.2% 52-week position, the 9.0% dividend yield looks unreliable, and debt/equity of 111.01 is probably 1.11x but unconfirmed.

Asahi India Glass is India's leading automotive glass supplier and also has a growing float (architectural) glass business; in H1 FY27, auto glass made ₹2,015 cr of revenue and float glass ₹1,153 cr. Growth is speeding up. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹2,999 cr (+26.0% YoY) and PAT was ₹316 cr (+179.8%). Taking H1 minus Q1 gives an implied Q2 of about ₹1,586 cr revenue (+36.5% vs ₹1,162 cr) and ₹167 cr PAT (+188% vs ₹58 cr), so quarterly revenue growth went from -0.1% to +15% to about +36%. PAT margin roughly doubled from 4.7–5.0% to 10.5%, and EBITDA margin rose from 16.9% to 22.4%, with float glass the standout (+49.7% growth, 22% PBIT margin). Because this is a capital-intensive business, I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA. At 25.0x it is only 7% above the broad-market median (P55), which makes it fair. The P/E numbers look stretched, though: trailing 55.7x and forward 41.8x (P84) are well above the 18–30x auto norm, and even the annualised H1 run-rate is about 39x. Much of the PAT jump is a base effect against a weak FY26, so the price already assumes the recovery lasts.

Minda Corporation is a mid-cap auto-component maker supplying mechatronics, security and access systems, wiring harnesses and a growing range of electronics and EV systems to Indian two-wheeler, passenger-vehicle and commercial-vehicle makers, with some export business. Revenue growth has picked up sharply, from +10.3% in FY25 and +22.3% in FY26 to +33.2% in Q1FY27 and a record Rs 2,189 cr (+42.6% YoY) in Q2FY27. H1FY27 revenue was Rs 4,036 cr (+38.1%). Much of this jump comes from consolidating Minda-VAST from April 2026 rather than organic demand, and EBITDA margin has slipped from 14.2% in FY25 to about 11.6-11.8%. Reported H1 PAT of Rs 349 cr (+132.9%) includes a one-time Rs 106 cr gain, so underlying Q2 PAT is about Rs 143 cr, a 6.5% margin. Using P/E as the auto yardstick, the stock is expensive: trailing P/E is 43.3x against an 18-28x auto benchmark (and the one-time gain flatters even that number), forward P/E of 29.2x is still at the top of the range, and it trades at 88% of its 52-week range. EV/EBITDA of 23.3x is only in line with the broad market, so the call rests mainly on P/E; analysts have nudged estimates up (+3% FY EPS over 90 days), but the price already reflects much of that.

fundamental.thesis: Gillette India is a P&G-affiliate premium FMCG company with a near-duopoly position in branded men's grooming (razors/blades) and a fast-growing oral care segment, operating debt-free with consistently strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.93× in FY26). Tenneco Clean Air India makes emission-control and clean-air systems for Indian vehicle makers. It is a recently listed midcap auto-parts supplier with very high returns (ROE about 43%) and strong cash generation: FY26 operating cash flow was 2.37x PAT on ₹5,404 cr revenue (+10.5% YoY) and ₹604 cr PAT (+9.3%). The latest fully extracted quarter, Q1 FY27, showed revenue growth speeding up to +20.2% YoY (₹1,545 cr), but PAT fell 1.7% to ₹165 cr and PAT margin slipped to 10.7% from 11.2% in FY26, so the extra sales are not yet turning into extra profit. H1 FY27 PAT of ₹339 cr implies about ₹174 cr in Q2, which is a small step up from Q1, but the Q2 revenue figures filed on 4 Nov have not been extracted, so year-on-year growth for Q2 cannot be checked. I graded valuation on trailing P/E plus EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an auto-parts maker. At 38.2x trailing P/E it trades well above the 18–28x range for Auto and ancillaries, and 24.3x EV/EBITDA is rich for a parts supplier. The forward P/E of 27.7x is only at the top of that range, the comparison peers are the broad market rather than true industry peers, and the stock sits mid-way in its 52-week range, so overall it looks expensive. Main risks: margin pressure from rising crude and commodity costs while volumes grow, and data gaps or oddities that lower confidence. The Q3FY26 revenue of ₹129 cr looks like a bad extraction, the 4.29x debt/equity does not fit the strong free cash flow, and the consensus upside of +48% does not match the stock's place in its 52-week range.

PAT roughly doubled (+103%) to ₹164 cr, PAT margin widened to 11.0% from 8.4% in FY26, and EBITDA margin rose to 16.7% from 12.1%. Volume grew 30.5% against only 1.5% from price/mix, so this is real demand rather than price hikes. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA, the yardsticks for profitable FMCG names: trailing P/E of 66.3× is above the 40–65× sector band, EV/EBITDA of 62.4× ranks 93rd percentile against the broad market, and the stock sits at 83% of its 52-week range. fundamental.thesis: Tata Elxsi is a Tata Group engineering R&D services company specialising in embedded systems design for automotive, media & entertainment, and healthcare verticals — a niche deep-tech services player distinct from commodity IT outsourcers, with a strong domestic and global client base in high-complexity design programmes. Revenue growth has inflected sharply from a -3.9% trough in Q2FY26 to +14.7% YoY in H1FY27 (₹2,077 cr), with PAT rising +13.9% to ₹341 cr and PAT margin holding steady at 16.4%; the System Integration segment contributed 28.9% YoY growth, signalling service diversification — however, EBITDA margin has contracted ~290 bps from its peak of 28.1% (Q3FY26) to 25.2% (H1FY27), driven by New Labour Code wage provisions and rising employee benefits costs. Trailing P/E of 40.78× is above the IT sector benchmark upper bound of 30× (expensive on that metric alone), but the forward P/E collapses to 26.22× — within the 22–30× sector range, confirming earnings recovery is priced in — and peer-rank analysis places TATAELXSI at P60 on both trailing and forward P/E (fairly valued per the ≥P75 expensive threshold); at 6.7% of its 52-week range the stock appears sentiment-oversold relative to an improving earnings trajectory, consistent with the FY26 exceptional charge now cycling out of the base. The primary risk is sustained EBITDA margin compression from structural wage inflation and New Labour Code costs, amplified by a persistent negative EPS revision trend (-0.9% over 90 days, -1.2% next-FY) that historically flags further analyst downgrades ahead, and a long-run AI-driven structural threat to engineering services demand that the sector card explicitly flags as unproven in revenue terms.

C.E. Info Systems (MapmyIndia) is India's leading digital maps and location-intelligence company, selling map data, APIs and IoT/telematics devices to auto makers, enterprises and government. H1FY27 revenue grew +15.3% YoY to ₹271.5 cr, up from roughly +2-3% through FY26, and consolidated PAT rose +32.1% to ₹85.0 cr; Q2 alone works out to about ₹131 cr of revenue (about +16% YoY) and ₹35 cr of PAT (H1 minus Q1). The growth quality is weak, though: almost all of it came from the device segment (+161% to ₹56.2 cr), while the core map data and services business, about 79% of revenue, grew just +0.7%, and the PAT margin fell to about 27% in Q2 from 35.6% in Q1. On the IT yardstick of P/E, the trailing 36.9x sits above the 22-30x sector band, but forward P/E of 22.5x falls inside it and the stock ranks in the middle of the broad-market peer set (P53 on P/E, P64 on EV/EBITDA at 29.1x), so I grade it fair rather than cheap, even though it trades near its 52-week low. The biggest risk is that the high-margin core map business has stalled while sell-side EPS estimates keep falling (-3.0% FY over 90 days, -4.1% next-FY), so the low price may be a falling knife rather than a value entry.

fundamental.thesis: Dixon Technologies is India's largest contract electronics maker (EMS). The filed H1 FY27 figures show revenue of ₹37,938 cr and PAT of ₹1,129 cr, with PAT up 51% YoY. Q1 revenue grew +21% to +25% (the two extracted Q1 rows disagree). The reported +147% H1 revenue growth and the ₹4,959 cr FY26 row do not reconcile with the quarterly figures, so the growth rate cannot be trusted. Margins are being diluted as volume grows faster than profit. Because this is an assembly-heavy, low-margin business, I graded on EV/EBITDA plus trailing P/E. EV/EBITDA is 32.3x, and trailing P/E of 42.9x sits at the top of the 28–45x Industrials range, so I grade it fair-to-full rather than cheap even though the stock is only 22% up its 52-week range. The peer-rank block compares Dixon with IT-services companies (WIPRO, INFY, PERSISTENT), which are not real peers, so I gave its 'P100 expensive' verdict little weight. The forward P/E is above the trailing P/E, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 7% over 30 days and 10% over 90 days while ratings stay 22 buy. That pattern often comes before a de-rating. Nutrient segment margin is only 8.25%, and H1 operating cash flow was just ₹54 cr against ₹1,220 cr of profit before tax, so the subsidy-heavy working capital is absorbing cash. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive, subsidy-dependent processor: at 17.3x it sits almost exactly on the 17.9x Materials peer median (P47). Trailing P/E is 31.6x, below the 37.3x peer median but above the 12-22x commodity-Materials range. The forward P/E of 20x looks unreliable after a 19% cut to FY EPS estimates in the last 30 days, so overall I call it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that analysts are still cutting estimates while 8 of 9 keep a buy rating, and subsidy dependence plus import reliance on ammonia and sulphur leave margins exposed to rising input costs and to delays in government subsidy payments.

fundamental.thesis: Angel One is one of India's largest retail stockbrokers by active clients, so it earns mainly from broking fees (heavily F&O-linked), interest on client margin funding and distribution. The latest extracted quarter is Q1FY27, where revenue rose +25.4% YoY to ₹1,430 cr and PAT doubled (+102%) to ₹231 cr, with PAT margin up from 10.0% to 16.2%. But this follows a weak FY26 (revenue -1.9%, PAT -21.9%), so much of the rebound is a recovery from a low base rather than proven new growth. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 are not yet in the extracted data. The main risk is that profits depend on market-linked and one-off gains that are not turning into cash. fundamental.thesis: Canara HSBC Life Insurance (CANHLIFE) is a bancassurance-focused life insurer distributed primarily through the Canara Bank and PNB branch networks, giving it a structural reach advantage over standalone agency-model peers; however, for a life insurer the correct valuation yardstick is P/EV (Price-to-Embedded Value), not P/E, and P/EV data is absent from this pack. Revenue growth has been strong at +25% YoY in FY26 (peaking at +31.6% at 9M before settling), but PAT has grown only +8.5% as PAT margin contracted from 1.6% (H1 FY26) to 1.3% (FY26 full year), meaning topline momentum is not converting to bottom-line expansion — a concerning quality signal; crucially, H1 FY27 results were filed on 9-Oct-2026 but remain unextracted, leaving the current trajectory blind. As the best available proxy, P/B at 8.29× against a TTM ROE of only 8.1% is clearly expensive (P/B < 1.5 + ROE > 12% = cheap; this is the inverse), and broad-market peer rank at P94 on trailing P/E (107×, +205% vs median 35×) and P98 on forward P/E confirm top-decile expensiveness with no margin of safety. The single biggest risk is that thin, contracting PAT margins (1.3%) combined with a ₹287.5 cr NCD issuance signalling capital needs leave the earnings base fragile — any claims spike, cost overrun, or distribution slowdown would disproportionately impair an already leverage-heavy, low-ROE profile in a RISK_OFF macro regime where Financials are macro-underweight.

fundamental.thesis: Central Bank of India is a mid-sized public-sector lender whose recent story has been cleaning up bad loans: gross NPA fell from 3.02% (H1 FY26) to 2.67% (FY26), net NPA is about 0.5%, and provision coverage is very high at about 96%. Loan growth has been strong at 17.7–20.7% YoY. FY26 PAT was ₹4,531 cr, up 15.0%, and Q3FY26 PAT was ₹378 cr, up 33.5% in the extracted series. However, margin health is weakening: NIM fell from 3.12% to 2.69%, ROA slipped from 1.07% to 0.92%, and capital adequacy fell from 17.34% to 16.13% as fast lending used up capital. Because this is a lender, I graded valuation on P/B and ROE, not P/E. At 0.77x book with an 11.9% ROE (trailing P/E 6.6x against a 12–18x bank range, P1 on P/B in the broad-market peer set), the stock looks cheap, sits at 33% of its 52-week range, and the market seems to be pricing in an ROE just below the 12% mark. The Q2FY27/H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-17 have not been read, so all figures here are stale. That, plus NIM compression, an underweight Financials tilt and a risk-off macro backdrop, keeps conviction moderate.

Tata Chemicals is a global soda ash producer (India, US, UK, Kenya) with a smaller Living Essentials consumer business and a stake in Rallis agrochem. It sells at global market prices, so its earnings depend on where it sits on the cost curve and how strong its balance sheet is. H1 FY27 consolidated revenue rose 11.0% YoY to ₹8,432 cr. That implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹4,177 cr, up roughly 8% YoY, so growth slowed from +13.9% in Q1. Profit is collapsing: H1 PAT fell 98% to ₹10 cr, and Q2 was a consolidated loss of ₹50 cr against a ₹219 cr profit a year ago, hit by UK gas costs, the Kenya suspension and weak global soda ash prices. India operations and standalone EBITDA (+22% to ₹292 cr) were the only bright spots. Using the sector card's EV/EBITDA yardstick for commodity chemicals, 14.5x is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm, though that multiple is inflated by trough EBITDA. P/B of 0.82x is the cheapest in the sector, a typical trough-cycle discount, so the net grade is fair, not clearly cheap. Trailing P/E cannot be used because trailing earnings are negative. The biggest risk is that soda ash oversupply lasts longer than expected while net debt sits at about 10x EBITDA. Analysts have already cut next-year EPS estimates by 25.6% over 30 days, and the rating mix leans to sell.

Revenue growth has eased slightly over six periods, from about +22% to about +19%, but the lending engine is speeding up: CIFCL disbursements rose 47% to Rs 35,872 cr, CIFCL PAT rose 41% to Rs 1,630 cr, and group AUM reached about Rs 2.68 lakh cr. The biggest risks are that the holding-company discount persists or widens, insurance losses continue, and current-year EPS estimates have been cut 6.1% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Go Digit is a digital-first general insurer, mostly motor, with about 3.9% of the motor market. For an insurer, underwriting quality matters more than headline growth, and the H1 FY27 filing shows revenue up only 4.5% YoY to ₹5,386 cr. That follows a -8.4% Q1 premium decline, so growth has slowed from +16.2% at FY26. Underwriting got worse: the combined operating ratio rose to 94.1% from 83.9%, claims to 60.9% from 53.2%, and expenses to 33.3% from 30.7%, which is above IRDAI limits. Reported H1 PAT of ₹521 cr (-3.2% YoY, 9.7% margin) does not match the yfinance quarterly rows (₹86 cr + ₹142 cr). Ind AS restatement may explain the gap, so treat that margin with caution. Judged on P/B against ROE, the right yardstick for an insurer, the stock looks expensive: 4.95x book against an H1 annualised ROE of only 6.6% (17.7% in FY26). Trailing P/E is 47x, and the stock is in the 67th percentile of the broad market on P/E and the 71st on EV/EBITDA. Earnings estimates have been cut 11.7% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the Motor OD book keeps losing money (₹297 cr loss in H1), which would keep ROE low and could bring IRDAI action over the expense breach.

fundamental.thesis: HDB Financial Services is a large-scale NBFC and HDFC Bank subsidiary providing retail, commercial vehicle, and enterprise loans across a ₹1.31 lakh crore asset base, with strong parentage constituting its primary competitive moat and funding advantage. Revenue growth has decelerated from a peak of +21.4% (Q3FY26) to +10.3% in H1 FY27 with loan growth similarly slowing from 14.1% to ~11%, while PAT recovered sharply to +36.2% YoY (₹1,565 cr in H1 FY27 vs -2% in H1 FY26) as GNPA improved from 2.81% to 2.43% and Net NPA from 1.34% to 1.09% — partially offset by structurally elevated credit costs (2.58% in FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT -0.34×), which flag earnings quality concerns. Using the P/B+ROE lender yardstick mandated by the sector card, P/B 2.79× against ROE 13.9% places the stock in fair territory (not cheap: P/B > 1.5×; not expensive: P/B < 3× with ROE > 12%); peer-relative ranking at P27 in the broad market and a ~40% discount to sector median P/B, combined with forward P/E 14.7× vs trailing 22.5×, suggest the market has already priced in a meaningful earnings recovery. The primary risk is that loan/AUM growth deceleration (tracking toward low-double-digits) persists in a RISK_OFF macro environment with rising crude costs and an elevated credit cost base, stalling the earnings normalisation that currently drives the bull case.

fundamental.thesis: IFCI is a government-owned Development Financial Institution effectively in run-off mode — its active lending business has collapsed, with the loan book shrinking -23.56% YoY to ₹1,194cr, and the company now derives income primarily from residual assets and investments rather than fresh origination. FY26 revenue grew a modest +2.5% to ₹2,069cr and PAT rose +5.7% to ₹181cr, with PAT margin recovering from -2.1% (H1FY25) to 8.7% (FY26), a directional positive — but this improvement reflects the tail of provisioning cycles on a dying book, not a genuine lending franchise revival; Gross NPA stands at a catastrophic 95.79% and CAR is deeply negative at -18.78%, far below RBI's regulatory minimum, meaning IFCI is technically insolvent on a banking capital-adequacy basis. Using P/B + ROE (the correct yardstick for a lender per the Sector Card — NOT P/E), P/B of 2.43× against an implied ROE of roughly 2% (₹181cr PAT ÷ ~₹9,100cr implied book) signals expensive — the P/B > 1.5 with ROE < 12% heuristic squarely flags this; trailing P/E of 119.29× (vs 12–18× bank sector median) confirms the same; forward P/E of 23.38× implies a heroic earnings recovery that is entirely dependent on the DFS-approved group consolidation/restructuring, a binary outcome with no earnings visibility. The single biggest risk is that the pending merger/amalgamation of IFCI subsidiaries fails to deliver value to minority shareholders, while the negative CRAR (-18.78%) and near-total NPA book leave no fundamental floor — any positive thesis is a restructuring bet, not a lending franchise bet.

3M India is the listed Indian arm of the 3M group. It sells into four segments: safety and industrial (₹465 cr in Q1FY27), transportation and electronics (₹503 cr), healthcare (₹297 cr) and consumer (₹148 cr). The last quarter we could verify from the filings is Q1FY27: revenue of ₹1,423 cr was up 19.0% from a year earlier, and profit (PAT) of ₹233 cr was up 31.1%, a 16.4% margin. Revenue growth has picked up from +12.7% in Q3FY26 to +19.0%, and growth has been double-digit for 5 quarters in a row. But the operating margin (EBITDA) slipped from 20.3% in FY26 to 17.6%. The Q2FY27 results filed on 6 Nov have not been extracted yet. The rough data feed shows revenue of only ₹902 cr and PAT of ₹158 cr for Q2, which could be the healthcare-business restructuring announced on 26 Oct, so we cannot yet tell whether growth has held. The main risk is that analysts have cut this year's earnings estimates by 6.5% in the last 30 days, while the stock trades on a forward P/E of 42x that already assumes strong growth.

fundamental.thesis: BEML is a Schedule-'A' defence PSU under India's Ministry of Defence, manufacturing heavy equipment across mining, construction, defence platforms, and metro/rail segments, with revenue heavily dependent on government order execution. Q1FY27 revenue accelerated to ₹820 cr (+29.3% YoY from ₹634 cr) and the operating loss narrowed substantially (EBITDA swung from -₹41 cr to +₹3.6 cr YoY), yet PAT remained negative at -₹27 cr (-3.3% margin); more critically, FY26 full-year PAT collapsed 49.7% and order inflows landed at only ₹1,286 cr vs a ₹6,800 cr target — an 81% miss that is the single most important leading indicator for an order-book business. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial (Sector Card guidance), the stock trades at 48.4× (P88 among peers, 107% premium to sector median 23.3×) and trailing P/E of 94× versus the sector benchmark range of 28–45×, placing it firmly in expensive territory despite a more palatable forward P/E of 28× that already discounts a sharp earnings recovery. The biggest risk is that FY27 order inflows remain structurally below target, eroding book-to-revenue cover and triggering a 30–50% de-rating (consistent with Industrials sector card cycle-risk warning) before the earnings recovery the valuation demands actually materialises.

fundamental.thesis: Escorts Kubota is one of India's major tractor makers and also sells construction equipment. Agri EBIT margin fell 340 bps to 9.3% on higher commodity costs and a weaker product mix, operating cash flow turned negative (-₹107 cr) as inventory and receivables built up, and management now expects margins to return to normal only in FY28. I graded valuation on P/E and EV/EBITDA against farm-equipment and auto peers, because the Industrials order-book yardstick does not fit this business. A trailing P/E of 22.6x is mid-range for auto (18-28x) and well below the Industrials band, EV/EBITDA is 16.3x and P/B is 2.5x against a 12% ROE, so it is fair, not cheap. Analysts have cut this year's EPS estimate by 11.6% in 30 days, which explains the discount and the stock sitting near its 52-week low. Some inputs conflict: the dividend yield, the price implied by the 52-week range versus the analyst target, debt/equity of 1.31 against a reported net-cash position, and a Q2 EBITDA margin that works out to an implausible ~2.6%. So I am trusting the reported revenue and PAT more than the derived ratios.

fundamental.thesis: Gallantt Ispat is an integrated long-steel maker with captive power and a pellet plant, and it claims about 25% share in its addressable regions; it behaves like a steel-spread business rather than an order-book Industrials name, so EBITDA per tonne matters more than the sector card's order-book metrics. EV/EBITDA, the preferred yardstick here, is unavailable, so on P/E and P/B I grade the stock expensive: the 36.9x trailing P/E is above the 12-22x Materials range, appears to reflect FY26 PAT of about Rs 484 cr, and is closer to 44x on my estimate of trailing-twelve-month PAT (about Rs 406 cr), while P/B is 5.4x and the broad-market peer rank (P53) is a weak comparison because it has no true steel peers. The biggest risk is that the price assumes a margin recovery while costs are rising, utilisation is stuck at 70% and a Rs 3,000 cr capex plan is absorbing cash; identical Rs 1,146 cr revenue in Q1 and Q2, a volume decline implied by the EBITDA figures despite 13% revenue growth, and the 14% dividend yield also need checking against the source filings, which limits conviction.

GMR Airports is India's largest private airport operator, running Delhi, Hyderabad, Goa (Mopa), Medan, and newly Nagpur and Vizag. Its earnings depend on regulated aero tariffs plus a fast-growing non-aero business (retail, F&B, real estate, hotels). Revenue growth has slowed sharply: from +48.6% YoY in Q3FY26 to +23.0% in Q1FY27, and to about +11.6% in Q2FY27 (implied ₹4,188 cr, from H1 ₹8,273 cr minus Q1 ₹4,085 cr). EBITDA margin has slipped from 43.8% to 37.9% and passenger traffic grew only about 1%, so growth now rests on tariffs and non-aero income. Implied Q2 PAT is only about ₹65 cr (1.6% margin) after ₹1,931 cr of H1 interest, and yfinance shows a ₹15 cr loss, so profit quality is thin. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive, regulated-asset business and P/E is not meaningful: at 25.1x EV/EBITDA, 82.6x forward P/E (P98 among peers), negative book value and 98% of the 52-week range, it is expensive. Sell-side EPS estimates have also been cut 37–42% over 90 days while 7 of 8 ratings stay Buy, a classic sign of a possible de-rating. The biggest risk is that weak traffic (Hyderabad -11.7%, Mopa -14.4%) plus a heavy debt load leaves the stock leaning on the Delhi CP-4 tariff being implemented on time.

fundamental.thesis: GPIL is an integrated steel and power producer (iron ore pellets → sponge iron → billets/wire rods with captive power) headquartered in Chhattisgarh, recently allotting industrial land at AURIC Bidkin, Maharashtra, signalling a next-phase capacity push. Revenue has deteriorated from near-flat +0.8% YoY in H1FY26 to -11.4% YoY in Q3FY26 (₹1,166 cr), while PAT margin compressed steadily from 16.3% in Q1FY26 to 12.3% in Q3FY26 — both revenue growth and margins are moving in the wrong direction over four consecutive periods. Assessed on EV/EBITDA of 13.5× (the appropriate yardstick for a capital-intensive steel business; P/E is secondary), GPIL trades at a 42% discount to the broad-market median of 23.3× and sits at P22 of 473 peers — genuinely cheap, but the discount reflects real fundamental headwinds rather than neglected quality; a forward P/E of 10.9× versus trailing 19.5× implies the market is pricing in an earnings recovery that the current revenue trajectory has not yet validated. The primary threat to any recovery thesis is extreme financial leverage (D/E 7.58) paired with sustained sell-side EPS cuts (-19.1% over 90 days from only one covering analyst), which compresses the margin of safety materially if the steel-price downcycle extends into FY27.

fundamental.thesis: GE Vernova T&D India is India's leading power transmission and distribution equipment maker (transformers, switchgear, grid substations), directly leveraged to the government's ₹9 lakh cr grid build-out through 2032 and a structural T&D order-book upcycle. Q1FY27 revenue grew +38% YoY to ₹1,836 cr with PAT up +24.6% to ₹363 cr, sustaining a consistent multi-quarter ~38% execution run-rate — but EBITDA margin contracted 300 bps YoY from 30.4% to 27.4%, operating profit grew only 25% against 38% revenue, and PAT margin fell 210 bps to 19.8%, signalling negative operating leverage as costs scale faster than revenue. Using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials per sector card), the stock trades at 73.2× versus the sector median of 28–45×, sits at the P95–P97 of the broad peer universe with a 214% premium to the median, and is at 99.5% of its 52-week high — unambiguously expensive by every lens. The critical risk is a violent de-rating: sell-side 90-day estimate revisions have been cut by 100%, EBITDA margins are compressing despite volume strength, and any government capex pause or execution miss on an order book priced for perfection historically triggers 30–50% drawdowns in this sub-sector.

Godrej Industries is a holding company for the Godrej group. It runs its own chemicals business and controls Godrej Properties (real estate), Godrej Agrovet (animal feed, veg oils, dairy, crop care) and a growing lending arm. Its 'Industrials' tag fits poorly, so the industrials order-book KPIs do not apply. Revenue growth sped up from about +5% YoY through FY26 to +22.2% in Q1FY27 (₹5,448 cr), led by veg oils (+42.8%), finance (+43.5%) and chemicals (+31.4%). But profit went the other way: PAT to owners fell 36.5% YoY to ₹239 cr, PAT margin dropped from 7.8% to 4.4%, and real-estate revenue fell 17.5%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is a leveraged, capital-heavy group. At 23.8× it sits almost exactly at the broad-market median (23.3×, P51), and trailing P/E of 32.1× (P45) and P/B of 3.4× (P38) are also mid-pack. With the stock at 54% of its 52-week range, I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest worry is the balance sheet: gross debt/equity rose from 1.90× to 2.38×, and FY26 free cash flow was about -₹9,883 cr. Q2FY27 results are due on 13 Nov 2026, and the current numbers are one quarter stale.

fundamental.thesis: After the HEG Composite Scheme took effect on 1 Sep 2026, H.E.G. no longer holds the graphite electrode business, which was moved into a separately listed HEG Limited. What remains is a mix of businesses at very different stages: 292 MW of debt-free green power (mostly hydro, about ₹300 cr of stable yearly cash flow), a 20,000 MT anode plant under construction (61% done, COD June 2027), early-stage battery storage (BESS) and a planned graphene project. Q2 FY27 revenue from continuing operations was ₹430 cr with PAT of ₹209 cr (a 48.6% margin), and H1 FY27 revenue was ₹726 cr with PAT of ₹269 cr (37.1%) and EBITDA margin of 60.4%. The trend table's 'accelerating growth, expanding margins' signals compare the old electrode-heavy business with the new hydro-heavy one, so they don't hold, and no clean YoY growth figure can be computed. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive business: at 19.0x it is about 19% below the broad-market median, and trailing P/E of 27.3x sits just under the 28–45x Industrials range, so the stock is fair rather than cheap, especially with ROE of only 7.3% against P/B of 2.2x. The forward P/E of 18.1x and rising FY estimates (+6.7% over 90 days) suggest earnings growth is expected, but that depends on anode projects that don't produce revenue until mid-2027.

fundamental.thesis: IRCON is a government-owned railway and highway construction contractor (EPC). About 76% of its ₹21,296 cr order book is railway work and 17% is highways. Revenue has turned around: after falling about 20% YoY through FY26, it grew 9.5% in Q1FY27 and an implied 14.9% in Q2FY27 (about ₹2,272 cr, worked out as H1 minus Q1), for H1 revenue of ₹4,228 cr, up 12.3%. The biggest risk is that order intake keeps lagging execution while margins and cash conversion stay weak: FY26 free cash flow was -₹1,150 cr and operating cash flow was -1.04× PAT.

On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card uses for capital-intensive industrials, the stock trades at 31.6× (about 36% above the broad-market median of 23.3×), and its 47.4× trailing P/E sits at the top end of the 28–45× industrials range, so we grade it fair, close to expensive; the 28.3× forward P/E and a price at only 21% of its 52-week range already assume a sharp profit recovery that the falling margins do not yet support. fundamental.thesis: RHI Magnesita India is one of India's leading refractories manufacturers, supplying high-temperature resistant materials primarily to steel, cement, and glass industries; it sits within the RHI Magnesita global group and commands meaningful market share in domestic installed capacity. Q1FY27 revenue grew 5.6% YoY to ₹1,014 cr — decelerating from a peak of +14.3% in H1FY26 — while PAT surged 83.2% YoY to ₹65 cr on a low base; more importantly, EBITDA margins expanded to 14.5% (vs 10.8% a year ago), recovering toward FY25 levels of 13.6% and signalling genuine operational improvement after FY26 was distorted by a ₹556 cr goodwill impairment on the RHIMIRL subsidiary. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for this capital-intensive business, the stock trades at 17.82× vs a broad-market peer median of 23.3× (P34 rank), which the system flags as fairly valued — not cheap enough to compensate for the elevated risk profile given the impairment history and debt load. The single biggest risk is the extreme financial leverage (D/E of 12.6) which, combined with revenue growth decelerating to low single digits and a brand-new MD/CEO at the helm, leaves the business highly exposed if steel/cement end-market demand softens.

fundamental.thesis: Shipping Corporation of India is India's largest state-owned shipping company, running tankers, liner, bulk carriers and offshore vessels. It is a freight-rate-driven, capital-intensive cyclical, so the Industrials order-book sector card does not really apply. H1 FY27 revenue rose 55.8% YoY to ₹4,137 cr and PAT rose 120.4% to ₹1,197 cr, faster than Q1 FY27 (+40.3% revenue, +74.9% PAT) and FY26 (+3.1% revenue). PAT margin widened to 28.9% from 20.5% a year ago, cash backed the profit (CFO/PAT 1.10x), and tankers led the growth (+62.5%, 44% PBIT margin), helped by Middle East disruption. On the yardsticks for a capital-intensive lender-funded shipper, EV/EBITDA and P/B, the stock looks cheap: P/B is 1.69x and trailing P/E is 10.65x against a broad-market median of about 35x. The live EV/EBITDA (35x), forward P/E (94x), dividend yield (424%) and debt/equity (29.45) readings look broken and were not used. My rough check puts EV/EBITDA near 5x on trailing EBITDA of about ₹3,500 cr. But these are probably peak-cycle, geopolitics-boosted earnings, and the stock is already at 66% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that tanker rates fall back as Middle East disruption eases. On top of that come stress in the LNG joint ventures (₹240 cr ILT-3 provision; auditors flag going-concern doubts at ILT-1/2/3), board committees still short of SEBI listing-rule requirements, and a government stake sale stuck since 2020.

fundamental.thesis: NIACL is India's largest PSU general insurer (85.44% government-owned), writing motor, health, marine, and fire coverage domestically and internationally, with a regulatory solvency ratio of 1.80×; however, the franchise is structurally loss-making at the underwriting level and profits depend entirely on investment income. Using P/B + ROE as the correct yardstick for an insurer (not P/E), P/B of 0.76× ranks NIACL at P1 in the broad peer set and appears cheap on its face, but a TTM ROE of only 3.4% fully explains this discount — it is structural cheapness, not mispricing — and analyst EPS estimates have been cut –47% in just 30 days, a classic pre-derating signal that the forward P/E of 9.2× bakes in recovery assumptions the combined-ratio trend does not yet support. The dominant near-term risk is a qualified audit conclusion on unreconciled reinsurance recoverable balances (₹75,490L gross, ₹13,783L doubtful-debt provision), compounded by a new CMD appointment in September 2026 and a mandatory Ind AS accounting transition due April 2027, leaving both governance and accounting transparency materially unresolved.

On the capital-intensive yardstick, EV/EBITDA of 9.9x is above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for chemical cyclicals, while trailing P/E of 15.3x sits inside the 12–22x Materials band; I grade it fair, not cheap. fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver miner (Vedanta Group subsidiary) with near-monopoly status in domestic mined zinc and structural cost advantages that produce world-class EBITDA margins of 62.4% — a level no domestic peer can match. H1FY27 revenue surged 76.7% YoY to ₹28,840 cr (accelerating sharply from -4.4% in Q1FY26), PAT grew 143.4% YoY to ₹11,881 cr, and PAT margin expanded to 41.2% from 29.9% — a five-period trajectory of simultaneously accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins driven primarily by elevated zinc and silver commodity prices, with cash quality strong (CFO/PAT 1.12×). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive commodity miner, the stock trades at 10.59× — P13 among 473 peers and a 54.6% discount to the broad-market EV/EBITDA median — with trailing P/E of 17.46× squarely inside the Materials sector range (12–22×), grading cheap on peer-relative metrics, though 10.59× sits above the 5–8× typical mid-cycle range for base-metals cyclicals, signalling that some commodity-cycle-peak risk remains unpriced. The thesis is materially constrained by an unresolved ED/FEMA investigation (search and seizure June 2026, no regulatory communication as of the October 2026 filing) and SEBI observations on related party transaction disclosures — governance headwinds typical of Vedanta Group that can trigger a de-rating independent of commodity fundamentals, and are weighted heavily under the midcap governance overlay.

Jain Resource Recycling is a non-ferrous metal recycler that makes copper, lead and aluminium from scrap. It is a commodity-spread business, recently listed, and copper is now about two-thirds of its revenue. Revenue is growing fast, but much of that comes from copper prices and profit is not keeping up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 65.5% YoY to ₹6,061 cr while PAT rose only 3.1% to ₹160 cr. Taking Q1 out of H1 suggests Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,337 cr (around +58% YoY, slower than Q1's +75.9%) and PAT of about ₹91 cr, which is roughly 8% lower than a year ago. EBITDA margin has fallen from 7.0% (9M FY26) to 5.7% (Q1) to 4.5% (H1), and PAT margin from 4.4% to about 2.7%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because the sector card says to judge cyclical, commodity-spread businesses that way. On that measure the stock looks expensive. EV/EBITDA is 25.1×, against roughly 5–8× for cyclicals at mid-cycle, and trailing P/E is 35.8×, against a 12–22× Materials benchmark. The 19.9× forward P/E depends on earnings growth, but analysts have cut those estimates by about 19% over the last 90 days. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking while net debt is high (about 3.3× EBITDA, debt/equity about 82%). If copper prices or recycling spreads reverse, earnings could fall sharply.

fundamental.thesis: Neuland Laboratories makes APIs (active drug ingredients) and does contract development and manufacturing (CDMO) for global drugmakers. H1FY27 still looks strong, with revenue up 35% to ₹1,091 cr, PAT up 80% to ₹199 cr and cash flow from operations at 1.8x PAT. On valuation I used trailing and forward P/E and P/B, because the reported EV/EBITDA of 401x and debt/equity of 16x are almost certainly data errors for a company the filings show as net cash. At 60.6x trailing earnings (sector range 28–40x), 11.8x book and the P78 peer percentile, the stock is expensive. The 37.6x forward P/E already assumes the H1 growth rate carries on. The biggest risk is that the Q2 drop marks a pause in big customer orders rather than normal quarter-to-quarter swings, which would leave a premium valuation without the earnings to support it.

fundamental.thesis: Blue Star is a leading Indian room air-conditioning (RAC) and electro-mechanical projects (EMP) company, positioned as a mid-tier premium brand competing with Voltas and Daikin in a structurally growing cooling market. In Q1FY27, revenue accelerated to +13.3% YoY (₹3,378 cr) driven by EMP (+15%) and unitary products (+12.7%), but PAT declined 15.1% YoY to ₹103 cr as EBITDA margin contracted sharply from 6.9% to 5.4% — the multi-quarter trajectory shows revenue growth re-accelerating while margins are compressing across all periods (PAT margin: 4.1% H1FY26 → 3.6% 9MFY26 → 4.2% FY26 → 3.0% Q1FY27), a structurally concerning divergence. At a trailing P/E of 62.75× against the Consumer Discretionary/Industrials sector median of ~28–45×, and with BLUESTARCO ranked at P80 in the broad market (78% premium to median P/E of 35.2×) alongside EV/EBITDA of 38.4× at a 65% premium to median, the stock is clearly expensive by both absolute and relative measures — the forward P/E at 40.4× does price in meaningful earnings recovery, but downward estimate revisions of -16.6% over 90 days suggest the market is still re-rating expectations lower. The biggest risk is that cost pressures (crude rising, competitive intensity in RAC) persist through FY27, making the earnings recovery priced into the forward multiple elusive and triggering a de-rating in a premium-multiple name where any guidance miss historically compresses valuation 25–40%.

Q1FY27 revenue grew 16.5% YoY to ₹1,580 cr — holding steady from prior-quarter acceleration — with PAT turning positive at ₹17 cr (1.1% margin) driven by KFC (+3.3% SSSG, +38% operating EBITDA YoY) and own brands, but badly offset by Pizza Hut India which collapsed -24.9% YoY with 13 net store closures and SSSG of -1.9% for a second consecutive negative quarter. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this Ind AS 116-heavy QSR (per sector card guidance on capital-intensive businesses), 21.06× sits near the broad-market peer median (P45), which might suggest fair, but reported EBITDA is inflated by ₹103.7 cr of lease-accounting treatment vs. operating EBITDA of only ₹151 cr (9.6% margin); the 103× forward P/E at P100 vs. all peers, a negative ROE of -2.6%, and D/E of 203× collectively signal the market is pricing in flawless execution of the Sapphire merger and a Pizza Hut turnaround management itself only expects in FY28. The biggest structural risk is that Pizza Hut's decline deepens post-merger integration while high finance costs (₹70 cr/quarter, 4.4% of revenue) keep PAT margins razor-thin, with sell-side EPS estimates already revised down -8.4% over 90 days despite a still-bullish analyst mix — a classic pre-derating pattern.

H1 FY27 PAT was Rs 320 cr vs Rs 106 cr in the H1 FY26 row (about +202%, not the +526% shown), and implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 264 cr matches yfinance's Rs 263 cr, but the growth trend is unreliable: H1 revenue of Rs 2,717 cr (shown as -21.2%) is -17.5% against Rs 3,292 cr, its 8.4% PAT margin implies about Rs 3,800 cr (+16%), and the 'decelerating revenue' and 'expanding margin' signals mix H1 and quarterly rows, with Q1 FY26 revenue of Rs 147 cr looking like a 10x error, so Q1 FY27's +11.9% is the last usable growth figure. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive, lease-heavy business, 7.41x (P6 vs a broad-market peer set, not cinema peers) with P/B of 1.27x and a price at 14% of the 52-week range grades cheap, with modest confidence because the 53.06x trailing P/E appears to exclude H1 FY27 profit, the 16.16x forward P/E needs earnings to roughly triple, ROE is only 2.4%, and the consensus '+7.7% upside' implies a price near Rs 1,524, well above the Rs 1,250 52-week high. The biggest risks are that a weak film slate hits a high fixed-cost business and that the recovery proves less durable than the +27.6% estimate upgrades suggest; separately, the promoter's Regulation 31 disclosure dated 2026-11-03 needs checking for any share pledge, and no footfall, ticket-price or management guidance data was available.

TBO Tek runs a B2B travel-distribution platform that connects travel agents worldwide to hotel and airline inventory, and since the Classic Vacations acquisition it also has a North American leisure arm. In Q2FY27 reported revenue of ₹866 cr grew 52.5% YoY, slower than Q1's +81%, and most of that headline growth comes from the acquisition: organic GTV grew 22% and organic gross profit 21%, while organic adjusted EBITDA grew 36%. Consolidated EBITDA margin has contracted from 22.5% to 17.6% over the trend window, and the last PAT margin we have is 9.0% in Q1FY27, down from about 14% a year earlier, because the lower-margin Classic Vacations business now makes up more of the mix. Q2 PAT was not available from the filings, and the revenue scale in the trend table does not match the yfinance rows, so treat the absolute figures with some caution. On valuation, the sector card says platform names should be judged on EV/EBITDA and growth delivery, not P/E alone: at 39.3x EV/EBITDA (P81 vs the broad market) and 68.4x trailing P/E (P83), with the stock at 88.8% of its 52-week range, the shares look expensive even though the forward P/E of 33.5x assumes strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that the price assumes perfection while FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days and governance issues are piling up: an unprovisioned ED/FEMA penalty of about ₹22 cr, an ₹8.1 cr employee fraud at an overseas subsidiary, and ₹8.9 cr of FX losses.

About 76% of its H1 revenue came from India and 24% from its plants in Italy and Germany. In H1FY27, revenue grew +31.6% YoY to ₹9,159 cr and PAT grew +14.4% to ₹519 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives an implied Q2 revenue of about ₹4,811 cr (+33.5% YoY, up from +29.6% in Q1) and PAT of about ₹274 cr (+21% YoY, up from +8% in Q1). Profits are growing much more slowly than sales, though. EBITDA margin fell from 13.1% in Q1 to about 12.1% in Q2, PAT margin is stuck near 5.6–5.7%, and analysts cut their FY earnings estimates by 4% over the last 90 days. The biggest risk is that the very strong sales growth keeps failing to lift profit margins while estimates keep getting cut, which would squeeze the premium the stock trades at.

fundamental.thesis: Motherson Sumi Wiring India makes wiring harnesses for Indian carmakers and two-wheeler makers, and its sales depend mostly on Indian volumes, which makes it a direct play on India's premium-vehicle and EV mix. The profit margin fell from 6.0% to 4.3% and the operating margin from 10.2% to 7.7%. There are early signs of a recovery: the half-year filing implies Q2 profit of about Rs 224 cr (+35% YoY, which matches yfinance's Rs 223 cr), FY EPS estimates were raised +7.3% in the last 30 days, and the half-year revenue figure is labelled H1FY26 in the table but is probably H1 FY27. The biggest risk is that margins stay squeezed by copper and commodity costs, rising crude and a new-plant ramp-up, so revenue keeps growing without profit following it.

Using the sector card's FMCG P/E norm, cross-checked with broad-market EV/EBITDA and P/B ranks because there are no tight peers, the stock is expensive at 77.3x trailing P/E against 40-65x, with EV/EBITDA of 34.5x and P/B of 10.7x against 13.6% ROE; the 39.9x forward P/E implies EPS nearly doubling while near-term estimates are slipping about 1%. fundamental.thesis: Tata Consumer Products is India's second-largest branded foods-and-beverages company, with leading positions in tea (Tata Tea, Tetley) and salt (Tata Salt), supplemented by an inorganic expansion into nutrition and adjacent FMCG via Capital Foods, Soulfull, and Organic India acquisitions. Q1FY27 revenue grew +11.9% YoY to ₹5,349 cr — a meaningful deceleration from +15.0% in Q3FY26 — though PAT surged +28.8% YoY to ₹427 cr (margin 8.0% vs 7.0% a year ago), powered by lower tea input costs and gross-margin expansion from 40.1% to 42.7%; volume growth in the India business was ~13%, solid but to be weighed against the sector card's caution on >10% volume claims. At a trailing P/E of 60.51× — at the upper bound of the FMCG benchmark range of 40–60× and ranked P78 among broad-market peers — the stock screens as expensive even near its 52-week low; however, a forward P/E of 41.78× (31% below trailing) signals the market is pricing in a meaningful earnings step-up from acquisition integration and tea-cost tailwinds. The principal risk is sustained revenue growth deceleration toward sub-10% alongside a reported Debt/Equity of 12.16 (reflecting heavy acquisition financing), which leaves the stock highly exposed to multiple compression if earnings delivery disappoints or high-rate conditions pressure interest coverage.

UNO Minda is a domestic auto-component supplier that sells lighting, switches, alloy wheels, sunroofs and EV parts to Indian two-wheeler and car makers, so it benefits from premiumisation and the rising share of EVs. Growth is accelerating: H1 FY27 revenue was ₹12,212 cr (+31.3% YoY) and PAT was ₹756 cr (+19.7%), up from Q1 FY27's +23.8% revenue and +2.1% PAT. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives a Q2 of about ₹6,655 cr revenue and ₹440 cr PAT, in line with the company's own press release reporting 38% YoY growth in both. Profitability is not keeping pace, though: EBITDA margin fell from 11.76% to 10.69% YoY and H1 free cash flow was negative (₹-96 cr) after ₹806 cr of capex. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA for an auto ancillary, the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E of 53× and forward P/E of 35.5× are both well above the 18–28× auto range, EV/EBITDA is 29×, P/B is 10×, and it sits at P71–P82 versus the broad market. The stock is near the low end of its 52-week range (27%) and the average analyst target is about 1% below the current price. The main risk is that the high multiple is priced for growth while margins and cash conversion keep slipping.

fundamental.thesis: Affle 3i is a mobile ad-tech platform that sells cost-per-converted-user (CPCU) advertising, mainly in India and emerging markets; it is a platform business, not a headcount-based IT services firm. Growth is steady but not speeding up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 20.8% YoY to ₹1,531 cr and PAT rose 19.5% to ₹258 cr. Subtracting Q1 from H1 gives Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹784 cr (around +21% YoY) and PAT of about ₹130 cr (about 16.6% margin), so YoY growth has held in a tight 19–21% band for six periods with PAT margin flat at 16.6–17.2%. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA (31.6x) plus forward P/E (29.7x), not the static IT-services P/E table, because Affle is a platform business. Trailing P/E of 46x is above the 22–30x IT range and about 31% above the broad-market median (P66). Forward P/E is at the top of that range, and the stock sits at 25.5% of its 52-week range. For a business growing about 20% with a ₹1,752 cr net cash cushion, I grade it fair, not cheap. Several things just added risk. The company agreed to acquire Israel-listed Perion Network, cancelled its earnings call citing a 'material development', and still has a ₹1,358 cr Bobble investment caught in insolvency, with a Supreme Court hearing on 25 Nov 2026. fundamental.thesis: JSW Energy is a large private power producer with 15.1 GW of installed capacity, about 61% of it renewable, and a stated path to 30 GW by 2030 built on long-term power contracts. Margins are shrinking because employee costs rose 21.8% YoY and now take 68.8% of revenue, and outside Industrials (+21.4%) the segments are barely growing (Financial Services +3.5%, CPG/Retail +2.7%). On valuation I used the IT sector P/E range plus EV/EBITDA. Trailing P/E is 32.3x, a little above the 22–30x IT range. Forward P/E is 22.1x and EV/EBITDA is 24.2x, close to the broad-market median (about P50). That makes it fair overall, not cheap, since estimates are being cut. The biggest worry is earnings quality: in H1 only about 26% of profit turned into operating cash (CFO/PAT 0.26x, down from 0.60x), and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 6% over 90 days. Both suggest the growth premium could shrink further.

fundamental.thesis: Tata Power is India's largest integrated power utility — spanning thermal generation (Mundra), renewables (4+ GW operational, TP Solar manufacturing), and T&D distribution in Mumbai/Delhi — and is structurally positioned at the intersection of India's energy-transition and electrification themes. Q1FY27 revenue grew 5.6% YoY to ₹19,051 cr with PAT up 11.0% YoY to ₹1,401 cr (7.4% PAT margin), representing a meaningful acceleration from the -1.8% revenue trough of 9MFY26 — EBITDA margin expanded to 23.6% from 21.2% YoY driven by a high-margin renewables segment (32.1% EBITDA margin) and T&D revenue surging 13.5% YoY; TP Solar's 2GW H1FY27 output milestone further validates the manufacturing flywheel. Using EV/EBITDA of 15.23× as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive hybrid (the sector card explicitly calls for EV/EBITDA over P/E), Tata Power sits at the 26th percentile vs broad-market peers and 34.7% below the median — fairly valued to modestly cheap — though the trailing P/E of 34.41× far exceeds the 10–18× utilities sector benchmark, an artefact of high financial leverage (D/E 168×) and a renewable-growth premium embedded in the equity. The single biggest risk is a USD 490 million (≈₹4,100 cr) contingent SIAC arbitration liability (Kleros Capital NDA breach) with no provision recorded — an adverse ruling would effectively erase roughly three full quarters of PAT and could necessitate dilutive equity issuance against an already stretched balance sheet.

Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

fundamental.thesis: Vodafone Idea is the third and weakest player in India's telecom market, which has roughly 2.5 players. It runs on a large government-linked debt and dues structure and is trying a capex-led turnaround while Jio and Airtel hold most of the industry's revenue. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 6.0% YoY to ₹11,689 cr, up from +1.9% in Q3FY26, and EBITDA margin rose to 43.1% from 42.5%; ARPU climbed 10.2% YoY to ₹195 and subscribers grew for the first time since the merger (193.1 mn), but the PAT loss was still ₹3,754 cr, a -32.1% margin, after ₹5,120 cr of finance costs and ₹5,467 cr of D&A. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive telecom. On that basis the stock is expensive: 28.6x versus the card's 9–12x norm for Indian mobile operators, 63rd percentile against the broad market, and the price sits at 90% of its 52-week range. The 4.3x trailing P/E is meaningless because a one-off FY26 gain distorts it, book value is negative, and the forward P/E is also negative. The biggest risk is solvency: negative net worth of ₹38,327 cr, deferred spectrum and AGR dues of about ₹1.56L cr with ₹9,259 cr due by June 2027, and a turnaround that depends on lender support and ₹45,000 cr of capex. The Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov are a near-term event risk.

fundamental.thesis: Indus Towers rents mobile tower space to telecom operators, with about 2.7 lakh towers and 1.63 tenants per tower in the latest KPI data. Revenue growth slowed from +7.9% in Q3 FY26 to +4.6% in Q1 FY27 and +4.0% (₹8,516 cr) in Q2 FY27, while PAT growth went from +0.5% to -2.5% (₹1,793 cr), leaving H1 PAT down 1.6% at ₹3,519 cr; I treated the row labelled Q2FY26 as Q2 FY27 because H1 less Q1 revenue is exactly ₹8,516 cr, but the same subtraction gives PAT of ₹1,773 cr and the 55.3% H1 EBITDA margin sits above both quarters (53.6% and 54.4%), so the margin figures are only approximate. On EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, 8.12× is below its 9-12× range, which is written for mobile operators rather than tower companies, so I grade the stock cheap, helped by a 15.29× trailing P/E and H1 free cash flow of ₹4,332 cr, though the bottom-quartile peer ranks are against the broad market rather than true peers and slowing growth justifies part of the discount. The biggest risk is a major customer under AGR-related stress that is paying only monthly billings, which has already kept ₹198 cr of revenue unrecognised in H1, while the 13.31× forward P/E assumes roughly 15% EPS growth even as PAT falls and estimates are being cut (FY EPS -1.4% over 90 days); leverage is also unclear, because the reported 2.33× net debt/EBITDA does not reconcile with debt of about ₹21,000 cr implied by the 53% debt/equity, or roughly 1.1× annualised EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: ITI Limited is a Government of India-owned telecom equipment manufacturer (PSU under Department of Telecommunications) engaged in defence communication, broadband gear, and telecom network products — a structurally impaired business currently in a BIFR-supervised revival plan, NOT a telecom service operator and therefore the Telecom sector card (ARPU/EBITDA framework) does not apply here. Revenue declined -14.6% YoY in Q1 FY27 (₹425 cr vs ₹498 cr), continuing a severe multi-quarter deceleration that saw -39.5% over 9MFY26 and -32.2% over H1FY26; PAT remains deeply negative at -₹32 cr (-7.4% margin), though marginally better than -₹64 cr a year ago — the 'PAT margin expanding' trajectory signal is misleading as it simply reflects a slightly smaller loss on a shrinking revenue base. Valuation is strikingly expensive: trailing P/E of 79.4× sits at P87 among 473 broad-market peers (+126% premium to market median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 483× is economically meaningless for a loss-making entity — the ₹25,371 cr market cap is pricing in the ₹8,280 cr ASCON Phase IV defence order optionality and GoI backing, not current earnings power. The single biggest risk is the material audit qualification — auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion citing Ind AS 115 revenue recognition failures on complex engineering contracts, inventory obsolescence, and inadequate internal controls, which means reported numbers cannot be relied upon and could be restated downward.

fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue grew +12.8% YoY to ₹1,075 cr — a clear acceleration from +5.4% in Q1FY26 — with PAT rising faster at +22.9% to ₹395 cr and PAT margin expanding to 36.7% from 25.3%; the EBITDA margin, however, contracted to 54.7% from 62.5% quarter-on-quarter, the residential segment effectively shut down at -92% YoY, and FY26 full-year CFO/PAT of 0.34× signals that a large portion of reported earnings is not yet converting to operating cash. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

Brigade Enterprises is a Bengaluru-focused developer with residential projects plus a steady leasing and hospitality annuity business; its leasing segment earns a 67.5% margin and grew 1.3% YoY. H1FY27 consolidated revenue fell 13.2% YoY to ₹2,312 cr, mainly because real-estate segment revenue dropped 26.6% to ₹1,374 cr. PAT still rose 32.7% to ₹436 cr, lifting the PAT margin to 18.9%, and the implied Q2 alone (about ₹1,133 cr revenue, ₹219 cr PAT) was similar to Q1. The forward-looking metrics are thin: Q1FY27 bookings were ₹1,061 cr on 0.74 mn sq ft and collections were ₹1,856 cr, with no year-ago figure to show the trend. Cash conversion weakened to 0.42x CFO/PAT in H1, against 1.63x in Q1. Following the sector card, I judged valuation on bookings, collections and net debt, not P/E. On that basis, net debt/EBITDA of 2.1x, gross D/E of 0.79x, a forward P/E of 17x and a price at 53% of its 52-week range point to fair, not cheap, value. The snapshot's P/B of 30.5x and EV/EBITDA of 143.6x look like data errors, since net worth of about ₹7,155 cr against a ₹20,830 cr market cap implies P/B near 2.9x. The biggest risks are the revoked environmental clearance on a large Chennai project and a ₹860 cr landowner JDA dispute. Analysts also cut current-year EPS estimates by 6.1% in the last 30 days.

fundamental.thesis: NHPC is India's largest hydropower generator, a government-owned company that earns a regulated return on the power plants it has commissioned, so its profits grow with commissioned capacity rather than with power prices; the Subansiri Lower project (1,250 MW of a planned 2,000 MW now running) is its main growth driver. In H1 FY27, revenue grew 26.0% YoY to ₹8,291 cr and PAT grew 20.6% to ₹2,836 cr (PAT margin 34.2%), faster than the +14.5% revenue growth a year earlier; however, ₹918 cr of that revenue is provisional Parbati-II income still awaiting CERC tariff approval, finance costs more than doubled (+115%), and EBITDA margin fell from 65.7% to 63.0%. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive utilities, NHPC trades at 25.5x, slightly above the broad-market median of 23.3x; its trailing P/E of 27.4x is well above the 10–18x utilities range, and a P/B of 1.85x against an ROE of only 9% is not cheap, so I grade it expensive on current earnings. The low forward P/E of 11.9x (estimates raised 3.9% over 90 days) and the stock sitting near the bottom of its 52-week range are the main counterpoints. The biggest risk is that heavy borrowing (net debt about ₹56,700 cr, debt/equity 1.36, negative free cash flow) keeps pushing up interest costs faster than new capacity adds earnings, especially if the remaining Subansiri units are delayed or the Parbati-II provisional revenue is cut when CERC sets the tariff.

fundamental.thesis: Prestige Estates is a Bangalore-anchored, multi-city branded developer with residential, office, retail and hospitality arms, and it is one of the larger listed players in the consolidating RERA-era sector. H1 FY27 reported revenue was flat at about ₹4,735 cr (-0.1% YoY), down from +72.7% growth in FY26. PAT fell 31.4% to ₹528 cr (11.2% margin), the owners' share fell 36.4%, and EBITDA was down 5.7% as land, contractor and finance costs rose. One caveat: reported P&L here trails bookings by 2-4 years, and the Q2 pre-sales and collections figures from the Oct-13 operational update were not in the extracted data, so I cannot assess the metric that matters most for a developer. Using EV/EBITDA and P/B+ROE rather than P/E (55x trailing is not meaningful for developers), the stock looks roughly fair. EV/EBITDA of 21.6x sits about 7% below the broad-market median, but a 4.0x P/B for an 8% ROE is rich, and with the stock at 60% of its 52-week range the margin of safety is limited. The CPPIB hospitality deal (₹15,000 cr first tranche closed Oct 2026, up to ₹30,000 cr committed) and strong H1 operating cash flow (₹1,311 cr, CFO/PAT 2.5x) are real positives. Against them, debt/equity is about 1.05x and consensus EPS has been cut 7-11% over 90 days even though 19 of 21 analysts rate it a buy, which is a classic pre-derating pattern.
